2
Automated Approaches for the Development of Genome-Scale Metabolic Network Models

Emma M. Glass

1University of Virginia, Department of Biomedical Engineering, 415 Lane Road, Charlottesville, VA 22904, USA
2University of Virginia, Department of Biochemistry & Molecular Genetics, 1415 Jefferson Park Avenue, Charlottesville, VA 22908, USA

2.1 Introduction

Metabolism is a system of biochemical pathways that convert nutrients into energy, complex biomolecules, and waste; together these conversions enable essential cellular functions for growth and homeostasis. Consequently, improving our understanding of how metabolism affects phenotypes for cellular function and growth can have important implications for health and disease. Two distinct but complementary approaches are often taken when studying metabolism: deep characterization of individual biochemical pathways as well as broad characterization of a whole metabolic system. A systems approach can be particularly valuable for linking the mechanisms of individual reactions and pathways to whole metabolic systems, probing the cellular genotype–phenotype relationships and guiding disease treatments.

Genome-scale metabolic network models (GSMs), as introduced in Chapter 1, are valuable tools for analyzing metabolic states in a variety of organisms. GSMs are a mathematical framework that represents the metabolic network of an organism; they are constructed using a set of gene-protein-reaction (GPR) rules formulated from the whole-genome sequence of an organism and a stoichiometric, mass-balanced matrix of all the metabolic reactions of an organism. There is a generally accepted and standardized protocol for generating metabolic models from genome sequencing data, including four main steps as follows: (1) Draft reconstruction, (2) refinement of reconstruction, (3) conversion of reconstruction into a compatible format, and (4) network evaluation [1]. Following reconstruction and curation, high-throughput omics data, such as proteomics, transcriptomics, and metabolomics, can be integrated with the reconstructed networks to create contextualized models with enhanced biological plausibility and predictability (Figure 2.1).

The first GSM was created manually in 1999 for the opportunistic bacterial pathogen Haemophilus influenzae [2]. By 2019, merely two decades later, there were over 6,000 GSMs created through both manual methods and automated computational pipeline [3]. However, in the past five years, explosive development of automated GSM tools has led to the publication of several large collections of GSMs, including assembly of gut organisms through reconstruction and analysis (AGORA1) [4] (773 GSMs), AGORA2 [5] (7,302 GSMs), PATHGENN [6] (914 GSMs), EMBL GEMs [7] (5,587 GSMs), MetaGEM [8] (447 GSMs), and most recently APOLLO [9] (247,092 GSMs). Currently, including the APOLLO resource, there are over 250,000 GSMs of prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, resulting in novel discoveries related to human health. For example, GSMs from the AGORA1 and AGORA2 collections have been used to discover links between the gut microbiome and colorectal cancer [10], elucidate how metabolism is modulated in microbial irritable bowel disease communities [11], predict personalized short-chain fatty acid production profiles in the human gut [12], growth dependencies of Aspergillus fumigatus strains on the lung microbiome [13], and many more clinically relevant applications. These examples highlight the potential impact GSMs can have on solving important biomedical problems.

In this chapter, we will first discuss the process for manually and automatically creating a GSM from a genome sequence. Then, we will provide an overview of tools in the field that have been developed for automated GSM construction, as well as tools that can be used to modify and visualize GSMs. Finally, we will discuss applications of large GSM collections that led to important biological discoveries, as well as current gaps in the field and future directions.

2.2 Manual GSM Creation

To generate a GSM from a genome sequence, it is necessary to consider necessary to consider GPR associations. Not all genes have a one-to-one relationship with their corresponding enzyme or metabolic reaction. For example, multiple genes could code for multiple protein subunits that come together to form one enzyme complex, or one protein could be used in multiple reactions. Therefore, it is necessary to precisely define the relationships between genes, proteins, and reactions.

After formulating the GPR rules, we must define the list of biochemical reactions in the network. Prior to the advent of genomics, these reactions were identified through experimental studies: an enzyme was isolated from an organism, and its function was demonstrated. This type of biochemical experiment provides the strongest evidence for the presence of a given metabolic reaction in an organism. However, using genomic tools, we can now functionally annotate whole-genome sequences based on DNA sequence homology to determine which reactions to include in the GSM. Since few organisms have extensive experimentally derived biochemical information available, GSM reconstruction today relies heavily on the annotated genome sequences to identify metabolic reactions present in a given organism.

After determining GPR-associations and identifying the metabolic reactions for inclusion in the GSM, we build a stoichiometric (S) matrix using the stoichiometric coefficients of the reactions that will comprise our network model. The columns of the S matrix represent individual reactions, the rows represent each compound, and the values in the S matrix are integers corresponding to the stoichiometric coefficients of each compound in each reaction. The architecture of the S matrix allows for the storage of both chemical information and network information, and explains how reactions within the network are interconnected. In general, the S matrix represents a reaction map that is topologically nonlinear: there are joint reactions between nodes in reversible reactions. Once completed, the S matrix represents the connected network of biochemical reactions in your organism.

After reconstructing the biological network in the form of the S matrix, we can compute possible functional network states directly related to cellular phenotypes. Cells are subjected to constraints arising from natural laws, environmental limitations, and physical space, limiting the range of possible behaviors. In our GSM, we can impose constraints on the network to obtain a set of solutions that are representative of a variety of functional states of the cell. We can capture different solution spaces and cellular phenotypes by altering what we are constraining and how stringently the constraints are imposed on the network.

2.3 Automated GSM Development

2.3.1 General Approach for Automated GSM Methods

In recent years, there has been significant effort in developing automated methods for GSM development based on the manual GSM construction framework described above (delineating GPR rules, selecting reactions, constructing the stoichiometric matrix, imposing constraints). Typically, automated network reconstruction pipelines follow several major steps for generating a high-quality draft model from a genome sequence: (1) BLAST search, (2) reference biochemical databases, (3) reaction inclusion, (4) gap-filling step (optional). The output of these automated tools is a GSM that is either simulation-ready or that can be further manually curated prior to simulation (Figure 2.2).

Automated GSM methods begin with either a raw or annotated genome sequence, which can be obtained from a variety of publicly available genome sequence databases such as GenBank [14], BV-BRC [15], and RefSeq [16]. The genome is then aligned to a biochemical database using a BLAST search algorithm to find orthologs. Subsequently, gene-associated reactions are identified using a chemical reaction database like KEGG [17], BiGG [18], or MetaCyc [19], which provides comprehensive mappings between genes, proteins, and metabolic reactions. These gene-associated reactions are then added to a draft GSM. Oftentimes, draft GSMs built only from gene-associated reactions will have network gaps, leading to impaired pathway connectivity and ultimately incorrect simulations and predictions. To correct these errors, some automated GSM construction methods include a gap-filling step to establish network connectivity by adding reactions to the GSM in either a probabilistic, machine-learning-based, optimization-based, or heuristic-based manner, depending on the method at hand. The final GSM is then typically saved in the Systems Biology Markup Language (SBML) format or JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) as these are community standards for cross-tool compatibility.

In this chapter, we will discuss methods for automated GSM development. We will discuss de-novo reconstruction tools including those that begin with (1) a raw genome, protein, or metagenome sequence, (2) annotated sequences, (3) biochemical databases, and (4) existing models. Additionally, we will discuss several tools that can be used to modify and visualize existing GSMs. A summary of all GSM methods discussed in this chapter is available in Table 2.1.

2.3.2 GSM Construction Tools

2.3.2.1 From Raw Sequences

ModelSEED ModelSEED [20] is a web-based platform for automated GSM reconstruction that is tailored to prokaryotes. The input to the ModelSEED tool is either an assembled genome sequence or a list of SEED subsystems. The genome sequence or subsystems are then annotated using the Rapid Annotations using Subsystems Technology (RAST) annotation server. The GPR associations for each reaction in the network are based on the functional role assigned to the genes during RAST annotation which are subsequently mapped to reactions in the ModelSEED biochemistry database. After GPR association, a preliminary reconstruction is generated by adding all reactions associated with one or more enzymes encoded in the organism's genome, as well as a set of spontaneous reactions that do not require enzymatic catalysis. After preliminary draft GSM construction, reactions are added back to the model in a gap-filling step called “Auto-completion.” In this step, a minimal set of reactions is added through an optimization process so that the model can simulate growth in silico.

Following auto-completion, all models are simulation-ready; however, ModelSEED has additional built-in methods for model optimization. These methods include Biolog consistency analysis, gene essentiality consistency analysis, and GapFill/GapGen steps. These model optimization methods help ensure that the final GSM is as biologically plausible as possible.

CoReCo Comparative metabolic reconstruction (CoReCo) [21] is a python-based software that simultaneously generates GSMs of multiple related species and has been shown to be specifically useful for the generation of fungal GSMs. This comparative approach is key for generating GSMs of species that are phylogenetically distant from extensively studied model species, when the genome sequence has low coverage, or when only incomplete genome reference sequences are available. The first phase in CoReCo GSM creation is to quantify evidence of known enzymes in a species. Given the input of a genome sequence, homologous sequences are found by both BLAST and Global Trace Graph (GTG, for more distant homologs). The quantitative results of BLAST and GTG are integrated into a Bayesian network model, resulting in the probability of an enzyme in each present and hypothetical ancestral species. The topology of the Bayesian network is based on the phylogenetic tree, and conditional probability distributions describe the probability of an enzyme in each ancestral species. In the second phase, a metabolic model is constructed for the present and ancestral species. Using the enzyme probabilities computed in phase one, CoReCo creates a highly probable network of reactions in the KEGG namespace. Only highly probable reactions are included unless inclusion of a highly probable reaction would leave a gap in the model, in which case, a low-probability reaction would be included in its place. The result of CoReCo is a gapless GSM in SBML format containing annotations with enzyme probabilities.

metaGEM metaGEM [8] reconstructs GSMs directlyfrom raw metagenome sequences. The pipeline used in metaGEM enables modeling of communities of multiple species directly from metagenome sequences, with automation of all steps, from extraction of context-specific prokaryotic GSMs from metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) to community-level flux balance analysis (FBA) simulations. The metaGEM pipeline is designed and implemented in Snakemake (an open-source bioinformatics workflow engine) and can be run by end-users in the command-line interface.

The input to metaGEM is raw FASTQ files, and the first step in the metaGEM pipeline includes metagenome reconstruction. After assembly of the MAGs, FBA-ready GSMs are constructed using CarveME (see 3.2.2.1) and then quality checked using MEMOTE. Additionally, the Species METabolic ANAlysis (SMETANA) framework is integrated into the metaGEM pipeline, and can be used for sample-specific community interaction modeling. The pipeline can also perform automatic assignment of taxonomic classification to the reconstructed MAGs and GSMs, calculate relative/absolute abundance for generated MAGs, estimate growth rates for high-coverage MAGs, and perform pangenome analysis. The metaGEM pipeline is versatile, combining many existing high-quality metagenomic and GSM tools into one user-friendly pipeline.

Merlin Metabolic models reconstruction using genome-scale information (Merlin) [22] is a user-friendly Java-based GEM creation tool that can be used for any organism that has a sequenced genome. Merlin can annotate a prokaryotic or eukaryotic genome with both enzymatic and transport functions, and build a compartmentalized draft GSM with minimum user interaction.

The input to Merlin is a raw amino acid or nucleotide FASTA file. Enzymatic functions are then assigned to genes using the homology search tools BLAST and HMMER. An enzyme commission (EC) number and corresponding confidence level are then assigned to each gene based on a weighted score. The user can also define an EC inclusion threshold, allowing for more specific annotation curation. After enzymatic function assignment, transporter annotations and compartment predictions are determined. Following the genome annotation step, model building begins with loading an internal biochemical database, which includes compound, glycan, drug, reaction, module, pathway, and enzyme information from KEGG. GPR rules are defined for all genes in the genome by cross-referencing the biochemical database to identify gene-associated reactions. Finally, there is a module in Merlin that identifies gaps in the model but does not employ a gap-filling algorithm to fill those gaps. Ultimately, the final GSM created with Merlin includes only gene-associated reactions. The final SBML GSM with minimum information required in the annotation of models (MIRIAM) [38] annotations can be exported and used for simulation or modification with other tools.

MS2/OMEGGA on KBase KBase [23] is the United States Department of Energy Systems Biology Knowledgebase, which is an open-source, web-based, and user-friendly software and data platform. KBase has an internal database of over 90,000 microbial genomes from RefSeq, 50 plant genomes from Protozyme, >30,000 reactions and compounds from KEGG, BIGG, and MetaCyc. This data can be integrated and analyzed through over 160 applications in Kbase, which offer diverse scientific functionality for metagenome assembly, comparative genomics, and RNA-seq processing, among others. Most importantly, in the context of this chapter, KBase offers a user-friendly web-based app for generating GSMs from genome sequences called MS2/OMEGGA, which is based on the ModelSEED reconstruction pipeline (see 3.2.1.1).

In the MS2/OMEGGA pipeline, genomes are first annotated using the RAST annotation server, and then GPR rules are determined. The functionally annotated genes are then mapped to reactions in the ModelSEED database. Next, the draft model is created by adding all gene-associated reactions to a GSM. In the KBase reconstruction pipeline, there is an optional gap-filling step for identifying the minimal set of biochemical reactions to add to the draft model to enable the simulation of biomass synthesis on a specified media. After the model is created, it can be analyzed with other KBase tools or downloaded for analysis with external tools.

2.3.2.2 From Pre-annotated Sequences

CarveME CarveME [7] is a command-line, python-based tool for GSM generation using a top-down approach. In general, GSMs are created using a bottom-up approach where reactions are iteratively added to a draft model to gap-fill and enable the simulation of growth under different media conditions. The alternative top-down approach used by CarveMe begins with a universal metabolic model, which is “carved” to remove reactions and metabolites not predicted to be present in given organisms based on their genome sequence.

The CarveMe workflow begins with the creation of a universal draft model, which is a simulation-ready model consisting of all biochemical reactions in the BiGG database. The user input is a pre-annotated DNA or protein FASTA file; raw genome files are not supported. DIAMOND is used to align the input genome to the BiGG database to find all homologous genes. The homologs identified are mapped to reactions using GPR associations. Reactions are scored based on whether there is direct genetic evidence for the enzymes involved in the reaction. The universal model is then carved to create an organism-specific model by solving a mixed integer linear programming (MILP) optimization problem that maximizes the presence of high-score reactions (those with genetic evidence) and minimizes the presence of low-score reactions (those without genetic evidence). The result is a “carved” organism-specific model. After generating the organism-specific model, there are options for post-reconstruction modifications, including ensemble generation of models based on random weighting of reactions without genetic evidence, addition of experimental constraints, and media-based gap-filling. The output of CarveMe is a simulation-ready GSM in SBML format, the community standard.

Reconstructor Reconstructor [24] is a Python-based tool for GSM construction from an annotated genome sequence that creates GSMs that are directly compatible with COBRApy (does not require the use of additional compatibility modules). Reconstructor GSMs are built using the ModelSEED namespace, allowing them to be used in conjunction with models created from a variety of other tools.

Reconstructor begins by taking a pre-annotated protein FASTA file and aligning it to the KEGG database using DIAMOND BLASTp to identify all homologous genes which are then mapped to reactions in the ModelSEED namespace. These gene-associated reactions are then added to a draft GSM. Reconstructor then uses a parsimonious FBA gap-filling approach to identify the set of non-gene-associated reactions that minimizes flux through the network, resulting in the most biologically parsimonious network. After pFBA-based gap-filling, a subsequent media-based gap-filling step can be performed to add additional media-specific transport reactions to the GSM. Reconstructor can take three types of input: (1) an annotated amino acid FASTA file, (2) the output of a DIAMOND BLASTp search, and (3) an existing SBML GSM for further media-based gap-filling, allowing for reconstructor to be integrated into computational pipelines in a variety of capacities. The result of reconstructor is a simulation-ready SBML file.

pyFBA pyFBA [25] is a Python-based open-source software package where functional annotations can be used to build GSMs ready for simulation that are backed by the ModelSEED biochemistry database. No specific annotation type is required for pyFBA (RAST, PROKKA, BG7, Blast2GO, BASys annotations are all valid), but it does require annotation to connect genes to enzymes to reactions for defining GPR rules.

The pyFBA algorithm begins by converting functional roles provided by the genome annotation information into reactions with the use of a biochemistry database. If using RAST annotations, the SEED database provides a connection between function, enzyme complexes, reactions, and compounds in a consistent namespace. pyFBA identifies ModelSEED reactions and compounds that map to the functional roles provided by the annotations. This list of gene-associated reactions and compounds is converted to a stoichiometric matrix, then unconstrained export or secretion reactions are defined and added to the stoichiometric matrix. This process results in a draft model that is ready for FBA simulation. If the results of the FBA simulation do not produce a growing model, the model can be gapfilled using a variety of methods: (1) a list of 109 reactions known to be in every model are first tried, (2) media-based exchange reactions are added, (3) add reactions that are proposed to complete a subsystem in the model, (4) add reactions that connect orphan compounds, and (5) add reactions that are known to be present based on annotations of closely related organisms. The result of the pyFBA iterative gapfilling process is a growing, simulation-ready, SBML GSM.

2.3.2.3 From Reaction Database Information

Raven Raven [26] is a MATLAB toolbox for GSM reconstruction, curation, constraint-based modeling, and simulation. Using Raven, GSMs of a variety of organisms, including bacteria, archaea, the human gut microbiome, eukaryotic microalgae, parasites, fungi, and human tissues, can be created. Raven uses either the MetaCyc database (which contains only experimentally verified pathways) or the KEGG database for GSM reconstruction. Raven can create GSMs (1) based on protein homology to an existing template GSM, or (2) de novo using reaction databases.

The first approach requires an existing high-quality GSM of an organism that is phylogenetically closely related to the organism you are reconstructing. Protein homology is inferred using a bidirectional BLASTp, and the results from the BLASTp are used to build the new draft GSM. Alternatively, de novo reconstructions can be built using either the KEGG or MetaCyc databases. KEGG-based reconstruction uses either KEGG-supplied annotations (over 5,000 genomes are available) or queries protein sequences for similarity to hidden Markov models trained on the genes in KEGG. If building a MetaCyc-based GSM, protein sequences are queried with BLASTp for homology to enzymes curated in MetaCyc. Regardless of the method, the draft model that results is further curated with a gap identification and gap-filling method to result in a high-quality network reconstruction that is simulation-ready.

AutoKEGGRec Automated generation of genome-scale metabolic draft reconstructions based on KEGG (AutoKEGGRec) [27] is a MATLAB-based tool that creates draft GSMs from KEGG organism IDs and integrates seamlessly with COBRA Toolbox v3. The draft GSM created by AutoKEGGRec is not intended to be fully functional. Rather, it is a starting point for further manual curation and simulations with other tools in the COBRA Toolbox.

AutoKEGGRec begins by providing a KEGG organism ID as input, which then queries the link between EC numbers and the corresponding genes from KEGG for each organism. Then, the linkage between reactions and EC numbers is retrieved. Every reaction in KEGG that is associated with the queried KEGG organism ID is retrieved and related to the corresponding genes in the target organism. At this point, each reaction, along with its annotation and the corresponding compound annotations, is downloaded from KEGG to be used in draft model reconstruction. The output of AutoKEGGRec is a list of KEGG reactions, associated GPR rules, and annotation annotation information, which in a MATLAB structure variable. This model can then be used with the COBRA Toolbox for gap-filling and curation efforts. Importantly, this model is not intended to be fully functional, but a first draft network reconstruction based on the KEGG database, which is created through a set of simple procedures.

rBioNet rBioNet [28] is a MATLAB package that implements QA/QC measures to generate high-quality biochemical network reconstructions that can be readily converted to COBRA Toolbox-compatible GSMs. The rBioNet pipeline consists of three parts: (1) a metabolite creator and corresponding database (MetDB), (2) a reaction creator with corresponding reaction database (RxnDB), and (3) a reconstruction creator.

Metabolites can be created in three ways: (1) manual addition of metabolite information, (2) loading of a tab-delimited file containing all information, and (3) loading metabolite information from other GSM reconstructions. Secondly, reactions can be added in the same three ways. Importantly, reactions can only contain metabolites contained in MetDB. Then, the user can create a reconstruction based on the reaction information provided in the RxnDB, and import metadata to the reconstruction if necessary. After creating the biochemical network reconstruction, the user can assign each reaction a gene association through GPRs. To accomplish this, the user must provide a tab-delimited file consisting of the organism's gene annotation information. Following GPR associations, the reconstruction can be benchmarked to find dead-end metabolites, and finally exported in a variety of formats, including SBML, a spreadsheet, or a data structure compatible with COBRA Toolbox. Importantly, rBioNet generatesi8u a biochemical network reconstruction, not a model. The reconstruction can be constrained using the COBRA Toolbox to generate a condition-specific, simulation-ready model.

FAME Flux analysis and modeling environment (FAME) [29] is a web-based one-stop-shop stoichiometric modeling tool that incorporates creation, editing, running, analysis/visualization into a user-friendly interface. While FAME is no longer maintained as a functioning tool, certain aspects of this tool are worth discussing to inspire the next generation of modern/functioning tools with similar characteristics.

In the FAME workflow, the user can either generate their own model based on KEGG information or upload an existing model. When generating a new model, the user can select a subset of pathways from KEGG to avoid, including unnecessary reactions that may be present in existing GEMS. FAME also stores KEGG ID information to find more information from KEGG if the need arises during the generation process. After model loading or generation, FAME has incorporated tools to edit flux bounds, edit reactions, recognize orphan metabolites, and assign reactions to compartments. Once the model is curated, FAME also has built-in optimization and analysis tools, including FBA and flux variability analysis (FVA), which are supported by PySCeS-CBM [39]. Additionally, the gene association workbench allows the user to simulate knockout mutants by taking advantage of the gene association information encoded in the model metadata. Finally, FAME incorporates a pathway visualization module to more deeply explore the biochemistry involved in the model. One of the most attractive features of FAME is the web-based point-and-click interface, which makes GSM creation and analysis more accessible to a wider range of users with both computational and non-computational scientific backgrounds.

MicrobesFlux MicrobesFlux [30] is a web-based platform for semiautomatic generation of GSMs for annotated microorganisms in the KEGG database. MicrobesFlux can download the enzymatic reactions, metabolites, and metabolic networks associated with ∼1,200 unique species from the KEGG database and convert the metabolic network information into a draft GSM. The draft model can be converted to a constraint-based flux model to predict carbon fluxes in microbial metabolism, and can ultimately be exported in SBML format. Importantly, MicrobesFlux is an installation-free platform that enables accessibility of metabolic network modeling to biologists without existing programming knowledge to develop models for organisms in the KEGG database.

The MicrobesFlux pipeline is dependent on the KGML (organism-specific metabolic networks) and KEGG LIGAND (enzymatic reactions and metabolites) databases for model generation. To generate a functional GSM, organism-specific metabolic networks are first downloaded from KEGG, which can then be formulated as an FBA model for simulation. MicrobesFlux also provides a suite of tools for model customization and gap-filling; however, it is important to note that the GSMs created with MicrobesFlux are still considered draft models. After GSM customization, constraint-based flux analysis is performed using optimization solvers, and the resulting flux distributions and model are recorded in SBML format, which is provided to the user. Overall, MicrobesFlux can perform three major tasks: (1) high-throughput metabolic model generation, (2) customized metabolic model drafting, and (3) constraint-based flux analysis in steady and dynamic states.

2.3.2.4 Based on Existing GSMs

MetaDraft MetaDraft [31] is a downloadable Python-based software with a graphical user interface (GUI) that creates a GSM based upon a previously manually curated model. MetaDraft has an extensive user interface that allows for informed model curation through visualization of gene BLAST scores, reactions, and metabolites, which can be edited and removed from the reconstruction.

MetaDraft takes a protein sequence in the form of a FASTA or GenBank file as input. MetaDraft works by comparing the protein input to a list of template models curated from the BiGG database. The user can select a set of template models, which will then form the basis of the metaproteome. Then, the user can blast their input protein sequence against the metaproteome created by the set of chosen template models. The BLAST results can then be viewed to select gene matches from the metaproteome that the user would like to include in their reconstruction based on score values. Each gene that is selected has an existing GPR association, and the user can view and edit the gene-associated reactions for further model curation. The reconstruction can then be converted and exported in SBML format for further analysis and simulation with other tools.

GEMSiRV GEMSiRV [32] is a freely available, downloadable software platform for genome-scale metabolic simulation, reconstruction, and visualization. GEMSiRV comes with a repository of existing metabolic models, reference databases, metabolic maps, and analysis toolboxes, which can be used as the starting point for network construction and simulation. GEMSiRV can run on local computers/servers without relying on a web-based interface. Importantly, GEMSiRV can also import existing models for further curation and gap-filling, and can incorporate experimental data for model contextualization.

GEMSiRV consists of three main modules: (1) network reconstruction, (2) simulation, and (3) visualization. A new GSM can be built using existing GSMs of closely related species as a reference. Given a user-defined list of orthologous genes, GEMSiRV will extract corresponding reactions that conform to the gene-protein reaction associations defined in the reference model. Building a GSM based on an existing model helps reduce the effort required for manual model construction. After construction of the draft GSM, GEMSiRV has built-in simulation modules which users can use for biological hypothesis generation, including dead-end metabolite identification, objective optimization, FVA [40], robustness analysis, gene/reaction essentiality analysis, and gene deletion analysis. Finally, the visualization module allows for editing and visualizing the metabolic networks of interest based on KEGG pathways.

SuBliMinaL The SuBliMinaL [33] toolbox helps facilitate the GSM reconstruction process by providing independent modules to support common reconstruction tasks like generating a draft reconstruction, mass/charge balancing reactions, adding transport reactions, a biomass function, and converting to the proper format for analysis with third-party tools. The modules in SuBliMinaL can be chained to create a complete reconstruction pipeline or just be used to modify an existing model in SBML format.

Initial pathways for a given organism are extracted from KEGG and MetaCyc using the KEGG-extract and MetaCyc-extract modules. These pathways are then converted into SBML draft models, which can be further modified and curated. Alternatively, an existing model can be loaded into the software and modified through various modules. Taking the organism-specific pathways, SuBLiMinaL performs an annotation step, which cross-references model components with databases such as GO [41, 42], ChEBI [43], and UniProt [44], updating the model for downstream processing. SuBLiMinaL also supports merging KEGG- and MetaCyc-based models to create one consolidated model. There is also a protonate module that predicts metabolite pKa and charge states, subsequently updating these in the model. The Balance module automates the process of mass and charge balancing of reactions through a mixed integer linear programming approach. Since SuBliMinaL generates non-compartmentalized reconstructions, the compartmentalized module predicts the compartment where metabolites reside based upon protein localization information from UniProt. The transport reaction module adds import reactions to the model to allow the uptake of metabolites from the growth medium. Finally, the biomass module assigns a biomass reaction to the reconstruction, and performs reformatting to the model that allows FBA simulations with the COBRA Toolbox. The result of the pipeline is a simulation-ready GSM that can be used for biological hypothesis generation.

2.3.2.5 GSM Modification and Visualization Tools

PathwayTools PathwayTools [34] is a software environment designed for managing, analyzing, simulating, and visualizing integrated genome, pathway, and regulatory data collections. PathwayTools supports the creation and curation of organism-specific databases, including pathway-genome databases (PGDBs), which include information on genes, proteins, as well as metabolic and regulatory networks. PathwayTools includes a MetaFlux module, which allows for the construction and execution of steady-state metabolic flux models. MetaFlux simulates gene and reaction knockouts, which allows users to explore metabolic dynamics and dependencies within an organism. PathwayTools is also equipped with an API tool for executing more complex queries and data mining, which allows users to execute more custom analyses. One of the most important aspects of the PathwayTools program is the ability for users to visualize entire networks through cellular overview diagrams, and it even allows for mapping gene expression data or other experimental data onto the network. The ability of PathwayTools to integrate genomic, chemical, and regulatory information makes it a powerful tool for enriched metabolic modeling and visualization.

AuReMe AuReMe (Automatic Reconstruction of Metabolic Models) [35] is a pipeline tool and workflow controller that supports flexible reconstruction and customization of GSMs by integrating a suite of existing academic-grade tools. While AuReMe does not generate models, it enables users to compile tools into customizable pipelines tailored to different data sources and project requirements. Importantly, AuReMe maintains a complete record of methods used and metadata for pipeline reproducibility. This tool supports key GSM creation practices like annotation, gap-filling, manual curation, and various model analysis and simulation methods, making AuReMe adaptable for automated and manual modeling approaches. AuReMe works with prominent metabolic databases like BiGG, ModelSEED, and MetaCyc, and can also access KEGG if the user has a license available. Additionally, AuReMe offers broad input flexibility, accepting genome GenBank files, protein sequence FASTA files, metabolic models in SBML format, pathway/genome databases, gene expression data, growth media composition, metabolic targets, biomass components, and databases of reactions and metabolites in CSV format. AuReMe's comprehensive integration and export functionality, which includes exporting models in SBML format for compatibility with the COBRA toolbox, allows users to construct detailed, transparent, and easily shareable metabolic models tailored to diverse research needs.

MEMOSys MEMOSys (metabolic model research and development system) [36] is a comprehensive, web-based platform that facilitates the management, storage, and development of GSMs. MEMOSys is designed to enhance model modification workflows rather than generating models from scratch, making it ideal for users who work with evolving or derivative metabolic models. It provides a robust database for GEMs, enabling users to create hierarchical model structures where changes can propagate through related models, allowing for efficient updating and streamlined version control across model generationsOne major feature of MEMOSys is its capability to annotate model components, including reactions, metabolites, genes, and cellular compartments, using the minimum information required in the annotation of biochemical models (MIRIAM) standard [17]. This integration includes links to external databases, enhancing model utility by allowing researchers to leverage external biochemical, genetic, and regulatory information. The database also supports metadata extraction from SBML files, making it easier to incorporate and store detailed annotations.

MEMOSys currently hosts 20 publicly available GSMs, which can be exported in standardized formats for further analysis with external tools. The platform's recent updates have expanded compatibility, allowing installation on Linux, Mac, and Windows operating systems, and it is now available as a fully configured virtual machine image, reducing setup complexity for users. This virtual image configuration not only simplifies deployment but also makes MEMOSys more user-friendly, offering researchers a ready-to-use environment for constructing, modifying, and managing metabolic models based on existing GSMs.

MetExplore MetExplore [37] is a collaborative, web-based application that supports the curation, annotation, visualization, and sharing of draft metabolic models. Designed to enhance previously reconstructed models, MetExplore provides users with advanced tools for refining and annotating metabolic networks, improving their accuracy and utility for downstream analysis. Researchers can perform key analytical functions directly within the platformincluding FBA, FVA, and assessments of gene and reaction essentiality, which facilitate deeper exploration of metabolic dependencies and bottlenecks. MetExplore also offers a comprehensive visualization system, enabling users to create graphical representations of selected subnetworks and to visualize GPR relationships within the network. This visual feature is particularly useful for mapping out specific areas of interest and understanding the functional roles of genes and reactions in the model. By integrating curation, annotation, analysis, and visualization capabilities in a single platform, MetExplore supports collaborative metabolic model refinement, making it an invaluable tool for researchers aiming to share, improve, and explore draft metabolic models collaboratively.

Table of 20 computational tools that can be used for automated genome-scale metabolic network reconstruction and further analysis, curation, or pathway visualization. Strengths and weaknesses of each tool are outlined in the main text. Tools are listed in the table in the order that they appear in the text.

2.4 Applications of Automatically-Generated GSM Collections

Automated GSM tools enable easy, accessible reconstruction of metabolic networks by drastically reducing the time required for reconstruction and eliminating the need for extensive manual curation. Beyond the ease-of-use, automated GSMs enable scientists to ask high-level questions and generate biological hypotheses about large groups of organisms (e.g. all pathogens, all members of the gut microbiome), which would be difficult to achieve with manually curated GSMs of individual organisms. For example, automated GSM methods can enable large-scale community modeling, allowing for predictions about interactions between community members. Recently, several large collections of automatically generated GSMs have been created and have since been used to address a variety of biological questions and pose biological hypotheses that could not have otherwise been addressed with individual manually curated GSMs.

2.4.1 AGORA1 – 773 GSMs

The AGORA collection [4] consists of 773 automatically generated GSMs of human gut bacteria, representing 205 genera and 605 species. This collection of GSMs was created with the purpose of inferring the metabolic repertoire of the whole human gut microbiome. This collection of automatically generated GSMs was one of the first, created in 2016. Since then, the AGORA collection has been a keystone resource in the metabolic network modeling community.

The AGORA resource has been used in many studies that address biological questions related to the microbiome and gut health. One interesting application used GSMs from the AGORA collection to identify metabolic functions of gut microbes associated with efficacy of tumor necrosis factor agonists in patients with irritable bowel disease. The 773 GSMs in the AGORA database were used to predict metabolic biochemical interactions between species in the human gut microbiome of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and rheumatic diseases compared to healthy controls. Using the GSMs, they determined that antagonistic interactions in the gut microbiome were reduced at the beginning of IBD treatment and restored toward the end of treatment. Furthermore, increased competition among species was observed in inflammatory conditions, suggesting that the gut microbiome community is less stable in an inflammatory state. The results of this study were partially validated with clinical data, demonstrating the use of the AGORA resource for making biologically meaningful computational predictions [45].

Another study used the AGORA collection to identify metabolic functions in the gut microbiome associated with Parkinson's disease. 243 GSMs from the AGORA database were selected based upon the species presence in stool samples of Parkinson's patients and healthy controls. Using the GSMs and community modeling techniques, they identified altered metabolite secretion potentials in Parkinson's disease patients. Specifically, they observed an age-dependent association with Parkinson's disease patients and Cysteine-Glycine production. Although the correlation was not particularly strong, this study represents a step toward a systems-biology approach to identifying the interplay between the gut microbiome and neurological disorders [46].

2.4.2 EMBL GEMs – 5,587 GSMs

The EMBL GEMs (genome-scale models) collectionconsists of 5,587 models of bacterial metabolism created with the CarveMe tool [7]. The GSMs in this collection represent the metabolic diversity across bacterial life at the strain level. At the time of its creation (2017), this was the largest collection of GSMs. Since 2017, the EMBL collection has been used to explore a variety of biological topics, two of which we discuss below.

The CarveMe-generated EMBL GEMs have been previously used in community metabolic modeling applications. A study published in 2024 [47] used 331 EMBL GEMs of gut bacteria to identify competitive, neutral, and mutualistic interactions within the gut microbiome community and between the microbiome and intestinal epithelial cells. Using a multi-objective optimization approach, they demonstrated that two organisms in nutritional co-limitation can attain better fitness together than alone by taking advantage of mutualistic interactions. Additionally, they demonstrated that diet plays an important role in modulating this mutualistic interaction, emphasizing the implication of diet composition in the function of the gut microbiome.

The EMBL GEM collection has also been used in another study to gain a deeper understanding of tryptophan metabolism across members of the gut microbiome. In this study, all 5,587 GSMs in the EMBL collection were used to develop a comprehensive database and analytics platform that is dedicated to tryptophan metabolism within a host context by using metabolism information from the EMBL GSMs. The database of tryptophan metabolism information, TrpNet, contains data on tryptophan metabolism involving 130 reactions, 108 metabolites, and 91 enzymes across 1,246 human gut bacterial species and 88 mouse gut bacterial species [48].

2.4.3 MetaGEM – 447 GSMs

During the validation of the MetaGEM tool (3.2.1.3), the authors generated a collection of 447 metagenome-based GSMs that are available on a public Zenodo repository. These 477 GSMs were created based on metagenome shotgun samples from five separate previously published metagenomic studies. While the MetaGEM tool has been used by many in the field, the GSM collection is relatively underutilized. Nonetheless, the creators of MetaGEM used their collection of GSMs to model human gut communities to validate their pipeline.

In this validation study, the collection of GSMs was used to investigate potential microbial metabolic interactions in the gut microbiome of healthy individuals and individuals with type 2 diabetes. They identified 22 compound exchanges that were significantly different between disease groups. Furthermore, they identified 27 donor microbes and 27 receiver microbes that had had significantly different cross-feeding interactions than the rest of the community members in diabetes vs healthy control patients (such as Bifidobacterium, Faecalibacterium, Roseburia, and Ruminococcus species). These results are consistent with some previous experimental results, suggesting that this collection of microbes was able to discern metabolic differences in diabetes and healthy control microbiomes. Moreover, by directly modeling community-level microbiomes, they identified potential interaction differences in type 2 diabetes microbiomes independent of abundance estimates, emphasizing the need for models that simulate functions of the microbiome [8].

2.4.4 AGORA2–7,302 GSMs

The AGORA2 collectionis an expanded version of the AGORA resource, containing 7,302 GSMs of human gut microorganisms, including 1,738 species and 25 phyla. This AGORA2 collection significantly expands upon the number of models present in the original AGORA collection. This collection of bacterial GSMs has been used in a variety of studies to address biological questions related to the gut microbiome, the lung microbiome, the Atlantic salmon gut microbiome, obesity, colorectal cancer, and food microbiology, among others.

As an example, one study published in 2023 used the A. fumigatus strains present in the AGORA2 database to gain a better understanding of their growth dependencies in the lung microbiome. More specifically, they used the AGORA2 GSMs to identify core and unique reactions across the A. fumigatus genome, identify reactions that have differential metabolic activity between environmental and clinical strain-specific GSMs, and corroborate experimental validation data. Using the GSMs, the authors ultimately determined that aromatic amino acids provided by other lung bacteria might have beneficial growth implications for A. fumigatus in the context of cystic fibrosis. Additionally, they determined that there are 53 reactions that have significant flux changes in cystic fibrosis conditions, and several of these reactions are related to the shikimate pathway. Together, these results suggest that aromatic amino acids are possibly important for fungal colonization and have implications in the severity of cystic fibrosis lung disease [13].

2.4.5 PATHGENN – 914 GSMs

The PATHGENN collectioncontains 914 GSMs of all known human bacterial pathogens with high-quality genome sequences, including 345 species and 9 phyla. This collection was created using the Reconstructor tool and is currently the only publicly available collection of pathogenic GSMs. The PATHGENN collection was used to identify uniquely targetable genes in bacterial species sharing a physiological niche. Beyond this application, the PATHGENN collection has the potential to be a valuable resource in the future for antimicrobial identification, computational simulation of pathogens that are difficult to grow in vitro, and pathogen pangenome analysis [7].

2.5 Future Directions for the Field of Automated GSM Development

Automated GSM tools have been valuable for fast generation of GSMs of thousands of bacterial species, enabling rapid biological hypothesis generation and metabolic simulations. While GSM construction has come a long way since the manual creation of the H. influenzae GSM in 1999, there is still room for improvement. Current automated GSM methods enable rapid creation of GSMs but do not always produce GSMs that are high-quality, simulation-ready, compatible with COBRA-based analysis tools, or are user-friendly. Because of these shortcomings, there is an increasing interest in making these automated tools generate higher-quality GSMs by integrating machine learning techniques into model generation, incorporating an iterative curation process, and improving maintenance of tools, standardization of GSM collections, and quality assurance methods.

Integration of machine learning techniques into automated GSM methods could allow for higher-quality automated GSM reconstruction. Most often, machine learning has been integrated into GSM analysis tools for metabolic flux phenotype predictions after the generation of the models. However, few studies have worked to integrate machine learning methods into the GSM creation step. One study has used unsupervised machine learning, like PCA, on metabolomics data to identify key metabolites that can be used as constraints for GSM construction [49]. In the future, there could be an opportunity to use deep learning methods to integrate multi-omic data into GSMs in an automated manner to increase the biological relevance and quality of generated GSMs. However, this idea has not been incorporated into any existing automated GSM development tools.

Another way to improve the quality of automatically generated GSMs is by using iterative model curation processes through automated experimental validation. Carbon-source utilization experiments using Biolog plates have been one way to corroborate computational model predictions with in vitro growth data. While this approach provides valuable information for model curation, it is not an automated process. A recently developed approach uses AI systems for performing autonomous experiments to more comprehensively map microbial metabolism. This method enables high-throughput experimental data collection through AI-driven experiments [50]. This method could be used to develop an experimentally driven approach for automatically generating high-quality, experimentally validated, physiologically relevant GSMs. Integrating model curation through experimentation into automated GSM tools could be the key to generating the next generation of high-quality models of metabolism.

While many tools for automated GSM development have been created, some of these tools are poorly maintained and currently nonfunctional. Furthermore, not all automated GSM tools create models with the same output file format, often requiring additional compatibility modules to use analysis tools like COBRA Toolbox or COBRApy. These points underscore the need for community standards [51]. The community standards for quality assurance including MEMOTE and FROG have been invaluable for model benchmarking allowing researchers to assess the quality of the models they are generating with automated GSM methods. Developing additional standards within or beyond MEMOTE and FROG for tool maintenance and standard GSM output file formats would allow researchers to have access to a wider variety of functional tools and be able to ensure that the models they are generating are simulation-ready models.

2.6 Conclusion

The first GSM (H. influenzae) was created manually in 1999. Since then, thousands of bacterial and eukaryotic GSMs have been created both manually and with automated GSM tools. Automated GSM creation tools have proven to be invaluable for generating large, high-quality collections of GSMs rapidly, which can then be used for biological hypothesis generation or further in silico analysis. The integration of machine learning methods into automated GSM methods, iterative model curation processes like AI-driven automated experimentation, and community standards for tool maintenance and model format will allow these methods to become more accurate and more powerful.
