3
Machine-Guided Approaches for Synthetic Biology Part Design

Marc Amil

1King's College London, Randall Centre for Cell & Molecular Biophysics, New Hunt's House, Guy's Campus, SE1 1UL, London, UK
2Chalmers University of Technology, Department of Biology and Biological Engineering, Kemivägen 10, SE-412 96, Gothenburg, Sweden
3Vilnius University, Institute of Biotechnology, Life Sciences Centre, Sauletekio al. 7, LT10257, Vilnius, Lithuania

3.1 Introduction

Synthetic biology aims to engineer biological organisms by designing and combining genetic parts to create complex systems that are used for diverse biotechnological applications [1], including the production of biofuels [2, 3], pharmaceuticals [4], and industrial chemicals [5]. Central to synthetic biology is the concept of standardized genetic parts – DNA sequences that encode defined biological functions. While Chapters 1 and 2 have demonstrated ways to extract genome-scale metabolic functions from these DNA sequences, this chapter seeks to look at the functional parts of the DNA itself. These parts include promoters that initiate transcription, ribosome binding sites (RBSs) that facilitate translation initiation, coding sequences that determine transcription rate, protein structure and function, terminators that signal transcription termination, and enhancers that regulate RNA transcription. For instance, combining a promoter, a coding sequence, and a terminator yields a gene expression cassette. These modular components can be further assembled into higher-order genetic biological circuits to perform complex tasks within engineered organisms like oscillators or toggle switches [6, 7]. A well-known example is the genetic toggle switch, which uses two repressible promoters (such as Ptrc-2 and PLtetO-1) and their matching repressor genes (lacI and tetR), each blocking the other's activity. This setup allows cells to stably switch between two states ON (expressing GFP) and OFF (not expressing GFP) – and has been used to create a memory device that records exposure to a chemical such as isopropyl-beta-d-1-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG), which temporarily inactivates lacI, flipping the switch from one state to the other [7]. Resources such as the iGEM Registry of Standard Biological Parts [8] and SynBioHub [9] have facilitated this process by curating extensive libraries of characterized genetic parts, promoting standardization and reuse.

Access to high-quality, diverse libraries of functional genetic elements – such as promoters, enhancers, and terminators – is essential for building robust and tunable genetic systems. One common strategy to generate such diversity involves mutagenesis-based methods, including error-prone PCR and saturation mutagenesis [10–13]. These approaches introduce mutations that are subsequently screened using selection methods, forming the basis of the iterative process known as directed evolution [14, 15]. Directed evolution mimics natural selection in the laboratory by applying repeated cycles of diversification, expression, and selection to enrich for improved variants, without requiring prior knowledge of beneficial mutations [16, 17]. While highly effective, conventional directed evolution approaches remain time-intensive, requiring multiple rounds of screening [18]. Because mutations are introduced at random, a vast majority of variants are either nonfunctional or fail to meet design specifications, needing extensive screening efforts to isolate rare beneficial mutations. For example, when mutating proteins, up to 70% of random single amino-acid substitutions typically result in a decline of protein activity, out of which 50% are completely deleterious to protein function [19–21]. In E. coli, replacing a native promoter with random ∼100 bp sequences showed that only ∼10% of random sequences could drive measurable transcription, whereas ∼90% produced no expression [22]. Similarly, random DNA can lead to active gene expression [23], but the sheer size of the sequence space presents a major challenge, requiring screening hundreds of millions of DNA constructs. For example, a 100 bp promoter has ∼1.6 × 1060 possible variants, which is comparable to the number of atoms in the observable universe [24], making exhaustive screening impractical. When the goal is to improve promoter-driven expression, modeling the random mutation process shows that fewer than 0.5% of variants lead to the desired outcome [25]. Additionally, because each evolutionary step builds upon the last, the process is inherently path-dependent, meaning that each mutation selected in one round influences which future mutations are possible or likely to succeed. If an early mutation provides a small benefit but blocks access to a much better solution (due to needing to go through intermediate, less-fit variants), the process may miss out on reaching the best possible outcome. While experimental strategies for directed evolution are rapidly advancing [26] and remain a go-to method for biological sequence engineering, they have been extensively reviewed elsewhere [27]. This chapter instead focuses on emerging data-driven approaches employing deep neural networks for DNA sequence design.

To reduce experimental burden and guide design efforts more effectively, computational tools have been developed to simulate genetic part performance in silico. These include tools such as the RBS Calculator [28, 29], RBS Designer [30], UTR Designer [31], and EMOPEC [32]. By modeling molecular interactions such as ribosome–mRNA binding, mRNA secondary structure, and thermodynamic properties, these algorithms estimate translation initiation rates and thus aim to predict gene expression levels. For instance, the RBS Calculator [28] uses a thermodynamic model of bacterial translation initiation to predict the Gibbs free energy change associated with ribosome binding, thereby estimating the relative translation initiation rate of a given mRNA sequence. It supports both reverse engineering – predicting initiation rates from existing sequences – and forward engineering – designing synthetic RBSs to achieve user-specified expression levels, with predictions spanning over five orders of magnitude. However, despite its sophistication, the RBS Calculator is primarily tailored for Escherichia coli and assumes equilibrium thermodynamics, which may not hold for highly structured RNAs or in non-model organisms. Additionally, it does not account for other regulatory elements such as RNA-binding proteins. Consequently, genetic parts designed with these tools may exhibit unpredictable behavior across diverse hosts or environmental conditions, limiting their portability and predictive power.

Despite progress in computational tools for rational sequence design, conventional statistical and mechanistic models remain limited due to incomplete understanding of molecular mechanisms, host-specific assumptions, and poor generalizability across diverse biological contexts [33]. As a result, previous generation computational methods failed to replace traditional experimental approaches involving large-scale screening, which remain the standard in biological parts engineering. On the other hand, over the past decade, our ability to read biology has dramatically improved. Advances in single-cell sequencing and high-resolution profiling of gene expression and chromatin accessibility across species, tissues, and cell types have generated vast datasets [34–37]. This wealth of information, combined with fast-paced developments in machine learning and progress in artificial intelligence (AI) has enabled the modeling of nonlinear complex sequence-to-expression relationships, to design enhancers [38], tune promoters [39–41], design entire genes [25, 42], control tissue specific expression [43, 44], and even the design of synthetic regulatory DNA tailored to specific human cell types [45, 46].

Mechanism-agnostic, AI-driven approaches are transforming sequence design – from trial-and-error screening to a predictive, programmable engineering discipline. Leveraging large-scale biological datasets, deep neural networks can learn subtle sequence–function relationships, enabling the design of regulatory DNA elements for gene expression control without solely relying on exhaustive experimental screening. These advances have given rise to model-guided sequence design – a framework in which trained predictors assess the functional fitness of candidate sequences (e.g. expression strength or cell-type specificity) and help iteratively guide the design of sequences with greater functionality. In the following section, we introduce neural network-based frameworks for predictive and generative sequence design. We discuss how commonly used architectures, such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs) [47, 48], are employed to interpret DNA functionality and extract regulatory features like sequence motifs [49]. We also highlight the integration of generative deep learning (DL) models, such as generative adversarial networks (GANs) [50, 51], diffusion models [52, 53], and transformer-based language models [54], which can generate novel, functional regulatory sequences by learning directly from existing data. These data-driven strategies reduce reliance on large-scale experimental approaches like random mutagenesis and directed evolution, marking a significant shift toward programmable and predictive design of biological parts.

3.2 Model-Guided Sequence Design Using Deep Learning

In the model-guided sequence design framework, candidate DNA sequences are generated and evaluated to identify optimal designs for specific biological functions, such as maximizing protein expression. This framework typically integrates two neural network-based components: generative models, which produce novel sequences, and predictive models, which assess the functional potential of each design (Figure 3.1d).

The predictive model acts as an oracle, guiding the generative model by scoring sequences based on desired biological outcomes. Predictive supervised models operate in two modes: (i) classification, which assigns discrete labels (e.g. transcription factor binding: yes/no), and (ii) regression, which predicts continuous variables such as gene expression levels [42, 55, 56] or translational efficiency metrics like mean ribosome load (MRL) [57]. CNNs are commonly used for regression tasks due to their effective ability to learn local sequence features relevant to biological function.

On the generative side, recent advances have demonstrated the use of DL architectures, including GANs, diffusion models, and transformer-based language models (e.g. Generalized Pre-trained Transformers, GPTs), to sample biologically plausible and diverse DNA sequences. Unlike random mutagenesis approaches that often yield nonfunctional or biologically implausible variants, these models learn from functional sequence distributions and improve design efficiency, thereby reducing experimental screening burdens (Figure 3.1c). While there are many other generative models used in genomics research, such as variational autoencoders [58, 59], here, we explicitly focus on models that have been experimentally applied to DNA part design.

3.2.1 Predictive Models for DNA Function: CNNs in Regulatory Sequence Analysis

Decoding the cis-regulatory code – the sequence rules that govern gene expression – remains one of the central challenges in genomics. With the rise of large-scale functional genomics datasets, machine learning models, particularly DL architectures, have emerged as powerful tools to decode these regulatory elements directly from DNA sequence. Among these, CNNs have become foundational for predicting key regulatory phenomena such as transcription factor binding [48, 60], chromatin accessibility [61], gene expression [55, 56], and even 3D genome architecture [62, 63]. CNN-based models not only match or exceed prior methods in predictive power but also offer interpretable insights into the sequence motifs and interactions underlying gene regulation [49]. Notably, CNNs have been extended to model outputs from massively parallel reporter assays (MPRA), providing a direct link between sequence and regulatory activity, allowing the design of novel synthetic regulatory elements [64, 65]. In this chapter, we will focus specifically on the application of CNNs to model gene expression to predict quantitative metrics such as transcripts per million (TPM) from regulatory DNA sequences.

3.2.1.1 Data Considerations for Supervised Learning on Genomic Sequences

DL is inherently both data-centric and algorithm-centric – successful outcomes rely not only on model architecture but also on careful dataset preparation. All supervised learning models share a common framework: a dataset is assembled from input variables, such as genomic DNA sequences or sequences derived from MPRAs, and paired with target gene expression values, often measured using RNA-seq data (e.g. TPM values).

When using genomic data, model inputs typically consist of regulatory DNA sequences associated with each gene – such as enhancers, promoters, and untranslated regions (UTRs). The dataset is usually split into training (80–90%), validation (5–10%), and test (5–10%) sets (Figure 3.1a,b). The training set is used to learn model parameters, while the validation set monitors performance during training (e.g. for hyperparameter tuning). The test set is strictly reserved for final evaluation and must not be exposed to the model during training or validation to ensure an unbiased assessment of generalization.

While we do not cover general statistical and machine learning principles or optimization strategies here (see recommended literature [66–68] as well as other chapters as other models relate to different sectors of understanding biological function), we emphasize several data-specific considerations that are crucial when working with biological sequence data (especially for the characterization of parts) to avoid misleading results:

  1. Bias in the Target Variable

    Expression measurements like TPM are influenced by gene length. A naive model may appear to perform well by simply learning gene length rather than true regulatory determinants. To avoid this, it is common to regress out gene length from TPM values using linear models prior to training.

  2. Bias in Input Sequences

    RNA-seq and other sequencing technologies may introduce GC-content bias due to amplification steps [69]. These biases must be corrected using standard normalization protocols to avoid training the model on technical artifacts [70].

  3. Distribution Consistency

    The training, validation, and test sets should follow similar distributions. Otherwise, performance on the test set may not reflect real-world generalization.

  4. Sequence Redundancy and Data Leakage

    Data leakage happens when the data used to train a machine learning algorithm happens to have the information you are trying to predict. A frequent pitfall in genomics is sequence redundancy: similar or identical sequences appearing in multiple data splits. This leads to data leakage, where the model “cheats” by memorizing rather than learning generalizable features. To mitigate this, sequences should be clustered by identity (e.g. 80–90%) and split in a way that prevents similar sequences from crossing between training, validation, and test sets.

  5. Data Transformation Leakage

    Preprocessing steps such as scaling, normalization, and imputation must be fit only on the training data and applied separately to validation and test sets. Applying transformations globally (i.e. using information from the full dataset) introduces data leakage and inflates performance metrics [71].

By adhering to these practices, one ensures that neural networks trained on DNA sequence data generalize robustly and are evaluated fairly, avoiding artifacts that could confound biological interpretation [72].

3.2.1.2 Primer on Convolutional Neural Networks for Supervised Genomic Sequence Modeling

Once the dataset has been properly curated, the next step is to train the supervised predictive model. The process of training a CNN, also summarized in Figure 3.2, begins with a forward pass, where the information flows from the input DNA sequence through all the model layers to output a prediction value. Prior to training, each nucleotide in a DNA sequence is converted into a numeric, machine-readable one-hot vector format. For instance, A is encoded as [1, 0, 0, 0], C as [0, 1, 0, 0], G as [0, 0, 1, 0], and T as [0, 0, 0, 1]. As a result, a sequence such as ATATAACG is represented as an 8-by-4 binary matrix, where each row corresponds to a nucleotide and each column to a channel in the input tensor (Figure 3.2a). This matrix is then passed through a convolutional layer composed of learnable filters or kernels (Figure 3.2b). These filters act as pattern detectors, scanning across k-mer subsequences to compute dot products between their internal weights and the corresponding one-hot encoded window. In the example in Figure 3.2, the CNN applies a single 3×4 kernel across the DNA sequence. Each kernel position produces a scalar output. These outputs reflect early representations of biologically significant features, where larger values represent more significant features – such as transcription factor binding sites (TFBS) or splicing enhancers. To introduce nonlinearity, a Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU)) [73] activation function is applied. ReLU retains all positive values and replaces negative activations with zero, effectively filtering out weak or irrelevant signals and allowing the network to focus on salient motifs. The result is a refined activation map, which is then flattened into a one-dimensional vector (the activation vector) to prepare it for downstream processing. Next, this vector is passed into a fully connected (dense) layer (Figure 3.2c), which integrates localized sequence features into a global representation. Specifically, each neuron in the dense layer multiplies each value from the activation vector by the corresponding weight, sums these products, and adds a bias term. For example, using the values shown in Figure 3.2c, the calculation is:

By combining information from all positions in this way, each neuron learns how different local patterns – such as motifs detected at various positions – collectively influence the final prediction. This approach allows the CNN to capture sophisticated syntactic logics and represent them as a scalar output, which often corresponds to a biologically relevant score such as a predicted gene expression level or the probability that a sequence has regulatory activity. This output is compared to the true, known target value using a loss function – in this case, mean squared error (MSE). For example, if the true label is 1.2 and the model predicts 0.76, the squared error is 0.1936 (Figure 3.2d).

In the second stage of CNN training, or backpropagation, the model adjusts its internal parameters to minimize the loss (Figure 3.2e). Backpropagation starts from the computed loss and works backward through the network, calculating how each weight in the convolutional and fully connected layers influences the final prediction. Specifically, the network computes gradients – mathematical values indicating the direction and magnitude by which each neuron's weight should change to minimize the loss function. Using gradient descent, the CNN updates these weights incrementally to improve its predictions. Over multiple iterations, the network fine-tunes itself, becoming progressively better at recognizing biologically meaningful patterns, thereby enhancing its predictive accuracy and interpretability.

CNNs have been successfully applied to predict the levels of mRNA expression from DNA sequence alone [55]. Using a dataset of over 20,000 RNA-seq experiments across seven species, Zrimec et al. [42] trained a model that achieved a predictive score of R2 = 0.82 in S. cerevisiae. This paper demonstrates that gene regulatory structure alone encodes a substantial portion of expression variability. Crucially, this model identified over 2,000 regulatory motifs, including both known TFBS and novel sequence elements distributed across promoters, UTRs, and terminators. The model also uncovered rules of co-occurring motifs – specific combinations of motifs modulating expression changes spanning over three orders of magnitude. These findings highlight the potential of CNNs to extract biologically meaningful patterns and motif interactions from sequence alone, thanks to their ability to integrate local motif signals to infer global expression outcomes.

3.2.2 Generative Sequence Modeling

After discussing the predictive component of the model-guided sequence design framework using CNNs, we now turn to the generative component, which typically involves designing sequences using Generative AI (GenAI). GenAI methods have become powerful tools for designing synthetic biological parts, with growing applications across genomics. The rise of GenAI has been fueled by tools such as ChatGPT and DALL·E, which can generate human-like text and realistic images based on simple prompts tailored to the user's needs. These same underlying technologies are proving powerful in biology, as DNA and proteins can be represented as text – DNA with bases “A,” “C,” “T,” and “G,” and proteins being represented as amino acid letters. This representation allows GenAI models to generate functional biological sequences in much the same way as they are able to generate language or art. Because of their ability to produce novel sequences with desired properties, GenAI models are increasingly being used to generate DNA, RNA, and protein sequences [74–77] with specific functional properties, from the design of optimized gene regulatory elements to functional promoters. For instance, PromoGen [78], a GPT-2-based model, enables the de novo design of prokaryotic promoters. Pretrained on over 120,000 promoter sequences from 27 organisms, PromoGen can be fine-tuned for species-specific tasks, capturing critical regulatory motifs such as the conserved −10 and −35 elements. It generates promoter sequences and has demonstrated strong performance in Bacillus subtilis, where over 80% of its predicted promoters were experimentally validated as active – some surpassing the strength of native promoters. Beyond regulatory elements, generative AI is also advancing codon optimization, traditionally performed using simple frequency tables that overlooked sequence context and regulatory features. Transformer-based models like CodonTransformer [79] provide a context-aware, host-specific approach, translating amino acid tokens (e.g. [M_UNK], [A_UNK]) into optimized codon tokens (e.g. [M_ATG], [A_GCC]) while maintaining GC balance and avoiding inhibitory motifs. Trained on over one million genes from 164 species, CodonTransformer allows the generation of a complete coding DNA sequence optimized for a chosen species. These models allow a more context-aware codon selection, enabling precise, high-yield expression for synthetic biology applications across diverse species.

Importantly, GenAI application extends well beyond individual DNA parts to the generation of entire molecular systems and even whole genomes. Evo [80], a multimodal genomic foundation model, exemplifies this broader potential by generating not only discrete elements like promoters or coding sequences but also complex functional assemblies such as CRISPR-Cas protein-RNA complexes and IS200/IS605 transposon systems. Evo is even capable of producing plausible megabase-scale genome sequences with coherent gene architecture, appropriate coding density, and operon-like structures at single-nucleotide resolution. This represents a transformative shift from designing isolated components to modeling and engineering genome-wide systems, positioning GenAI as a key enabler for constructing biological functions across synthetic biology systems. In the following sections, we explore how GenAI models can be applied to DNA to design novel biological parts.

3.2.2.1 Data Preparation for Unsupervised Learning

Successful generative modeling of biological sequences – using approaches such as GANs, diffusion models, or transformer-based language models – relies heavily on rigorous dataset preparation. Unlike supervised learning, where models are trained on labeled datasets to map input sequences (e.g. promoters) to outputs (e.g. gene expression levels), unsupervised generative models learn statistical patterns directly from unlabeled sequence data, typically directly using the raw genome FASTA file. Although labels are not required, data preparation remains essential – much like in CNNs – and involves removing redundancy, data leakage, and cleaning the sequence data. First, raw genomic DNA sequences must undergo quality control to eliminate sequencing errors and ambiguous nucleotides (e.g. “N” characters), which can impair learning. Another challenge in generative modeling is gene length variability, especially when models require fixed-length inputs. This is addressed by standardizing sequence lengths through trimming or padding. Padding typically involves appending neutral tokens (e.g. “N” characters) to shorter sequences to ensure uniform input lengths. For instance, if a model requires 512-base inputs, a 430-base sequence would be padded with 82 bases. Finally, to avoid training bias, datasets may be balanced by upsampling underrepresented sequence classes or downsampling overrepresented ones. In summary, careful data preparation is essential for unsupervised learning, enabling generative models to produce biologically plausible, diverse, and functional sequences.

3.2.2.2 GANs for the Design of Biological Sequences

GANs [50] are generative DL approaches for designing biologically meaningful DNA sequences by modeling the distribution of real genomic elements. A GAN is composed of two neural networks: the Generator (G), which is trained to generate realistic synthetic DNA sequences, and the Discriminator (D), which evaluates whether a given sequence is real or artificially generated. As shown in Figure 3.3a, the process of training a GAN begins with sampling a random latent vector . This vector is then passed into the Generator, where it undergoes a linear transformation (logits = wz + b) to produce raw scores or logits that are reshaped into a position-by-nucleotide matrix representing a synthetic DNA sequence. A softmax activation function is then applied across each row of this matrix – where each row represents a position-specific distribution over A, C, G, and T – to convert the logits into probabilities over the four DNA bases, and the resulting probability matrix is passed directly to the Discriminator. The Generator and Discriminator are trained in an adversarial loop: the Discriminator updates its weights to better learn to distinguish real from generated sequences, while the Generator adjusts its parameters to produce outputs that are increasingly difficult for the Discriminator to detect. This dynamic is visualized in Figure 3.3a, right panel, where the light grey distribution representing synthetic sequences gradually shifts to align with the dark gray distribution of real sequences. After applying a gradient descent algorithm over many training iterations, the Generator progressively learns to synthesize sequences indistinguishable from natural biological sequences. During inference, an already trained GAN is used to synthesize a discrete DNA sequence for inspection or downstream use. At this stage, the position-by-nucleotide matrix returned by the Generator is first used to generate a nucleotide sequence by calculating the nucleotide with the highest probability at each position of the matrix. Then, this synthetic sequence is passed into the Discriminator, which assigns a score indicating the likelihood that the sequence is real. High scores suggest the sequence is from the true data distribution, while low scores indicate it is synthetic.

The iterative adversarial training of a GAN involves alternating optimization steps for the Generator and the Discriminator. First, the Discriminator is optimized to accurately distinguish real sequences from generated “fake” ones. Mathematically, this optimization step is performed by calculating the gradients of the Discriminator loss function (LD), defined as:

D(xreal) represents the predicted probability that an input sequence xreal drawn from the training dataset is real. D(G(z)) denotes the probability that a synthetic sequence – generated from a random latent vector z via the Generator – is classified as real. The first term logD(xreal) rewards the Discriminator for correctly identifying real sequences, while the second term log(1 − D(G(z)) rewards it for correctly identifying generated sequences as synthetic. Therefore, the Discriminator loss is minimized by giving a low probability to generated sequences that look random (e.g. “GGGGGGGGG”); if it mistakenly gives a high probability, the loss increases. Gradient descent updates the Discriminator's weights and aims to minimize LD, thus enhancing its accuracy in classifying “natural” sequences. Subsequently, the Generator is optimized using the gradients computed from its own loss function (LG), aimed at minimizing the ability of the Discriminator to recognize generated sequences as synthetic, or in other words, the Generator loss LG measures how well the Generator can fool the Discriminator:

Here, D(G(z)) represents the probability, as predicted by the Discriminator, that the sequence produced by the Generator G(z) is a real (or “natural”) biological sequence. The Generator is trained to maximize this probability, and this is achieved by minimizing the negative log probability shown above. Minimizing LG encourages the Generator to create synthetic sequences that the Discriminator cannot easily distinguish from real ones. For example, if the Generator produces a sequence such as “GCCACCATGG,” which resembles a natural Kozak consensus sequence, and the Discriminator assigns it a high probability of being real, the Generator receives a lower loss. Crucially, the ultimate goal of the Generator is to match the distribution of real biological sequences – not by generating a single ideal sequence, but by creating multiple synthetic sequences whose collective characteristics (e.g. motifs, nucleotide frequencies, and patterns) closely mimic those observed in the original data. Consider a toy example involving Kozak sequences such as “GCCACCATGG” and “GCCGCCATGG.” Initially, the Generator produces diverse random sequences with little biological relevance. Over multiple training iterations, as the Discriminator becomes better at distinguishing authentic sequences, the Generator receives precise feedback on how its outputs deviate from real sequences. Consequently, the Generator's parameter adjustments steer it toward producing sequences that share the same statistical properties as the real dataset.

An example of GANs being applied for DNA sequence generation is ExpressionGAN [25], an approach developed to design synthetic regulatory sequences with a predictable transcriptional output in S. cerevisiae. In this framework, the Generator is coupled with a predictive “oracle” model that accurately estimates the gene expression levels corresponding to each generated sequence. During optimization, the predictive model guides the Generator toward sequences achieving specific target expression levels. Notably, despite substantial sequence divergence from natural regulatory DNA (>33%), experimental validations confirmed that sequences generated by ExpressionGAN were functional in vivo. Strikingly, 57% of the synthetic regulatory sequences associated with high gene expression surpassed the expression levels corresponding to natural controls [25]. This demonstrates not only the capability of GAN-based models to navigate extensive regulatory sequence-expression landscapes but also their potential for surpassing the limitations of traditional mutagenesis approaches. Thus, ExpressionGAN exemplifies the power of GANs to innovate beyond existing biological constraints, enabling precise control over gene expression levels with significant implications for biotechnology and therapeutic applications.

3.2.2.3 Transformer-Based DNA Models

The introduction of the Transformers architecture in the landmark publication “Attention Is All You Need” [81] has revolutionized our ability to train genome-sized sequence models and thus interpret and generate text. The publication also introduced the self-attention mechanism, which allows the model to weigh the relevance of each word in a sentence, achieving a more efficient semantic and syntactic understanding. For example, in the sentence “She went to the bank to deposit money,” self-attention allows the model to interpret “bank” as a financial institution rather than the land alongside a river, based on the surrounding words. Importantly, by eliminating any recurrent or convolutional operations and relying solely on self-attention, Transformers are able to process all the positions in an input in parallel, which enables the use of larger models and faster training. Building on this foundational work, models like Generative Pretrained Transformer (GPT) [82] have also demonstrated exceptional performance in generating coherent, context-aware text across a wide range of applications. The success of attention-based models in natural language generative tasks has encouraged their application in other fields. In genomics, where DNA or RNA sequences can be treated as text made up of A, C, G, T, and U nucleotides, genomic language models (GLMs) have proven effective at capturing both local motifs and long-range dependencies. This capability makes them particularly well-suited for synthetic part design, where precise sequence generation and contextual understanding are critical.

Similar to convolution-based models, the training of a GLM requires converting raw DNA sequences into a numeric format. However, instead of applying one-hot encoding, GLMs rely on tokenization, a process that maps nucleotide letters to numerical representations or tokens (Figure 3.4). In the simplest approach, known as single-character tokenization, each nucleotide is treated as an individual token, similar to how characters are treated in a text corpus (e.g. “A” might be encoded as 1, “C” as 2, and so on). Additional tokens can also be introduced to inform and guide the GLM to design sequences with particular characteristics. For example, in the regLM framework [83], synthetic S. cerevisiae promoters were generated using a two-token prompt, <X><Y>, prepended to the DNA sequence. Each token represents the desired promoter activity in a specific growth medium, where <X> represents activity in a complex medium and <Y> represents the activity in a defined medium. Token values range from 0 (very low activity) to 4 (very high activity). For instance, the prompt <2><4> instructs the model to generate an S. cerevisiae promoter with medium activity in complex medium and very high activity in defined medium. Similarly, for human enhancer generation, regLM implemented a three-token prompt, <A><B><C>, where each token specifies enhancer activity in a particular human cell line: <A> for HepG2 (liver), <B> for K562 (erythroid leukemia), and <C> for SK-N-SH (neuroblastoma). These values range from 0 (inactive) to 3 (very active). For example, the prompt <0><3><1> directs the model to generate an enhancer that is inactive in HepG2, highly active in K562, and exhibits low activity in SK-N-SH. An example of how these prompts are structured is shown below:

Alternatively, k-mer tokenization segments the DNA into overlapping subsequences of length k using a sliding window approach. For example, the sequence “ATGCA” would yield the 3-mers “ATG”, “TGC,” and “GCA.” This method preserves local context and introduces a more biologically relevant vocabulary, capturing short motifs such as TFBS. However, k-mer tokenization also increases the vocabulary size exponentially with respect to k (e.g. 43 = 64 for 3-mers), which can impact memory and computational efficiency. The choice between single-nucleotide or k-mer tokenization depends on the model's design goals – whether to prioritize fine-grained base resolution or richer motif-level context.

GLM training typically begins with a pretraining phase, where the model is exposed to large amounts of unlabeled genomic data to learn general representations of DNA syntax. This phase allows the model to capture the underlying patterns and contextual information within the DNA without the need for explicit labels or annotations, enabling it to generalize across different downstream tasks, such as DNA parts' classification or generation. For pretraining, genomes from one or more organisms can be used. For instance, HyenaDNA [84] focuses specifically on human genomic data, enabling it to learn specialized representations tailored to the human genome. In contrast, models like DNABERT-2 [85] aggregate DNA sequences from multiple species – including bacteria, plants, and humans – encouraging broader generalizability across evolutionary contexts.

There are two main pretraining methods: masked language modeling (MLM) and autoregressive modeling (AR) (Figure 3.4 bottom right panel). In MLM, some nucleotides within a sequence are masked, and the model learns to predict the identity of the masked tokens using the unmasked context. In AR modeling, the model is trained to predict the next nucleotide of a sequence based solely on the previous tokens. The key difference between both approaches is that MLM training allows the models to learn bidirectional dependencies from both sides of the masked nucleotide, understanding how upstream and downstream nucleotides influence a given position. For example, if the sequence “ATA_CC” is provided, the model learns to infer that the masked token is likely a “G” given the neighboring nucleotides, using both ATA and CC. On the other hand, in AR training, given “ATAGC,” the model estimates the probability distribution over the next base, and selects the most likely candidate of the four nucleotides to extend the sequence.

An important innovation of Transformer-based models is the attention mechanism, illustrated in the lower left panel of Figure 3.4. Attention allows the model to selectively focus on certain parts of the input sequence by assigning importance scores, or attention weights, to each position when predicting nucleotides. Importantly, attention weights are context-dependent, meaning that the relevance assigned to each nucleotide can shift depending on the specific surrounding sequence. For instance, when modeling a promoter region, the model may assign high attention scores to a known regulatory motif such as the TATA box (“TATAAA”) in order to predict the transcription start site (TSS) downstream.

Transformer-based DNA language models are trained using cross-entropy loss as the objective function. Cross-entropy compares the predicted probability distribution over nucleotides to the actual correct nucleotide. A lower cross-entropy value means the model is assigning a higher probability to the correct answer. For MLM, the model only predicts the masked positions using full sequence context; for AR modeling, the model predicts each nucleotide from left to right using only previous positions. In both cases, cross-entropy is computed at each relevant position to guide learning. The loss for each setting can be defined as:

Here, N is the sequence length, and V is the vocabulary size (e.g. 4 for DNA: A, C, G, and T). The term yi,j is a one-hot vector where the correct nucleotide is marked with 1, and all others are 0. Since the loss multiplies each predicted log-probability by yi,j, only the correct class contributes (because 1 × log-probability is retained, and 0 × anything else is zero). For example, if the true nucleotide is A (one-hot label = [1,0,0,0]) and the model predicts [0.7,0.1,0.1,0.1], Loss =  −log (0.7) ≈ 0.36, indicating a confident prediction. In contrast, if the model assigns equal probability to all the nucleotides ([0.25,0.25,0.25,0.25]), Loss =  −log (0.25) ≈ 1.39, a higher value reflecting uncertainty and poor predictive capabilities.

Typically, MLM is predominantly used by Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT)-style models [86, 87], where the goal is to predict masked tokens within a sequence by leveraging context from both directions. This bidirectional approach enables BERT-based models to learn contextually rich representations, making them highly effective for downstream tasks such as regression and classification. When applied to DNA sequences, these BERT models often incorporate an additional regression or classification “head” – a small neural network layer placed on top of the pretrained Transformer – to translate the learned representations into specific predictions, such as enhancer activity levels or promoter classifications. In contrast, GPT [82] models adopt an AR approach, predicting nucleotides sequentially from left to right, thus allowing generative capabilities useful for synthesizing new DNA sequences. Consequently, GPT-style AR models are well-suited for tasks involving sequence generation, such as designing novel regulatory elements or generating optimized sequences with desired biological functions [46]. The first DNA-based large language model (LLM), DNABERT [87], was built upon a 12-layer BERT [88] architecture trained on sequences of 512 nucleotides derived from the human genome. Since then, several additional GLMs have emerged, notably Nucleotide Transformer [86] and DNABERT-2 [85]. While all these models use Transformer architectures, they differ considerably in their tokenization strategies. Despite their successes, Transformer models inherently face computational challenges due to their reliance on the self-attention mechanism, resulting in a quadratic computational complexity of O(n2), where n is the sequence length [81]. This is because self-attention computes pairwise interactions between all positions in the sequence, requiring the model to calculate an attention score for every possible token pair. The quadratic complexity can severely limit the scalability of Transformers, particularly for analyzing very long sequences such as whole chromosomes or performing inference across millions of nucleotides.

To address these scalability challenges, HyenaDNA [84] was introduced. HyenaDNA employs an AR next-token prediction approach at single-nucleotide resolution. Crucially, it scales sub-quadratically with sequence length, achieving a computational complexity of O(n log n). This results in an up to 160 times faster than quadratic Transformer models. The underlying Hyena architecture supports input sequences of up to one million nucleotides, significantly expanding the range of genomic contexts that can be effectively modeled. By integrating language modeling techniques with supervised sequence-to-function predictive models, HyenaDNA effectively generates realistic synthetic DNA sequences, demonstrated by creating functional yeast promoters and human cell-type-specific enhancers [83].

Building upon these advances, the Evo model [80], based on the StripedHyena architecture, has recently emerged as a versatile approach capable of both sequence generation and functional prediction across DNA, RNA, and proteins. Evo, trained using a large-scale dataset with 7 billion parameters and a context length of 8 kb and 131 kb, exhibits impressive performance. It surpasses specialized models in predicting fitness effects of mutations within diverse biological systems, including E. coli proteins, non-coding RNAs, and regulatory DNA sequences. A particularly noteworthy application of Evo is the generative design of synthetic CRISPR-Cas systems, such as Cas9, Cas12, and Cas13 proteins. Evo generates protein-RNA complexes that closely resemble their natural counterparts in both sequence composition and structural integrity. Moreover, Evo extends its generative capabilities to entire transposable elements, exemplified by the IS605 system, producing novel, functionally coherent coding sequences. Remarkably, Evo also enables generation of genome-scale sequences up to 650 kb, significantly expanding the scope of genomic modeling and opening new avenues for large-scale biological engineering.

3.2.2.4 Diffusion Models for the Design of Biological Sequences

Diffusion models have recently emerged as powerful generative architectures, offering an alternative to adversarial and attention-based frameworks for the generation of realistic synthetic regulatory elements [53, 89], long DNA sequences [90] and 5′-UTRs [91]. Unlike GANs, which generate sequences through adversarial training, diffusion models operate by learning to reverse a progressive noising process. As shown in Figure 3.3b, the generative process begins with a real DNA sequence, which is first one-hot encoded into a binary matrix. During the forward diffusion process, Gaussian noise is incrementally added to the one-hot encoded sequence across multiple timesteps, denoted by x0 → x1 → xt. As noise accumulates, the structured patterns of the sequence gradually degrade until the representation resembles pure noise. Mathematically, each noisy sequence xt is computed using a predefined noise schedule t, with added Gaussian noise ɛ∼N(0,1). This process simulates the loss of biological information, turning a highly structured sequence into a noisy, uninformative distribution where each nucleotide has an equal probability (e.g. ∼0.25 for A, C, G, T). This transformation is defined by the equation:

Here, αt is a predefined noise schedule that determines how much of the original signal is retained at each timestep, with values that gradually decrease from 1 at each timestep. The term preserves the structured information from the previous timestep, while injects Gaussian noise sampled from a standard normal distribution. Early in the process, the sequence remains mostly intact, but as t increases and αt shrinks, noise dominates and the sequence becomes increasingly degraded. This gradual corruption process creates the training data for the model, which learns to reverse the noise and recover biologically meaningful sequences during the generative phase.

The reverse diffusion process is where generation occurs. A neural network – often a U-Net or Transformer [92] – is trained to denoise these random sequences, gradually transforming noise back into a meaningful DNA sequence. The model receives a noisy input xt, along with the current timestep t, and learns to predict the noise that was added. The training objective is to minimize the difference between the predicted noise and the actual noise used in the forward process.

As shown in Figure 3.3b, denoising begins with a random sequence in which each base has an approximately uniform distribution. At each timestep, the network refines these probabilities, gradually restoring higher confidence in biologically plausible nucleotide choices (e.g. increasing the probability of G at a conserved position in a Kozak motif). Eventually, the model outputs a nearly one-hot encoded matrix, from which the most probable nucleotide is selected at each position to form the final DNA sequence. Notably, the generative process is stochastic, allowing for the creation of diverse but realistic sequences that follow learned biological patterns without replicating any specific sequence from the training data. This iterative refinement process can be thought of like sharpening a blurred image – each step reintroduces critical structural elements such as transcription factor motifs, GC content profiles, or positional constraints, leading to the emergence of high-fidelity synthetic DNA with meaningful biological features.

3.3 Sources of Sequence–Function Data for Deep Learning

The effective training of DL models that translate DNA sequences into functional predictions requires large, well-curated sequence-to-function datasets. These data provide the empirical “ground truth,” mapping specific nucleotide patterns to transcriptional outputs, chromatin conformation, or any other cellular state directly modulated by DNA sequences. Therefore, these datasets are indispensable for DL models to learn the complex context-dependent rules that govern gene regulation. In synthetic biology, transcriptional profiling datasets are especially valuable. Available datasets can be broadly divided into two types: native-context datasets derived from genome-wide assays performed in their original chromatin and regulatory context, and synthetic dataset generated by screening the activity of cloned DNA sequences into reporter constructs and introduced into cells via plasmids or genomic integration. In this section, we will describe representative native-context and synthetic datasets, and discuss how each has enabled the training of predictive models suitable for synthetic part design.

3.3.1 Native-Context Genome-Derived Datasets

Native datasets are derived from whole-genome sequences and analyzed in their original biological context. These datasets include raw genomic sequences as well as functional annotations that capture specific biochemical activities across cell types and conditions. Large collections of native-context datasets are publicly available through free-access resources (detailed further in Table 3.1), including ENCODE [37] (Encyclopedia of DNA Elements), GTEx [93] (Genotype-Tissue Expression), the Roadmap Epigenomics Consortium [94], FANTOM [95] (Functional Annotation of the Mammalian Genome), CATlas (Cis-elements Atlas), Expression Atlas [96] RegulonDB [97]. The combination of genomic annotations with whole-genome transcriptional activity datasets has been essential for training DL models that link DNA sequence features, such as the annotation of a promoter sequence, to transcriptional activity. For example, Xpresso is a CNN trained only on promoter sequences and sequence-derived features related to mRNA stability to predict steady-state gene expression levels in humans and mice [55]. To train Xpresso, the promoter sequence for each gene (e.g. the genomic region spanning from ∼7 kb upstream to ∼3.5 kb downstream of the TSS) was extracted and converted to a one-hot vector to feed the neural network. Each sequence was labeled with its corresponding gene expression level derived from bulk RNA-seq datasets from the Epigenomics Roadmap Consortium and ENCODE. Another CNN-based model, Basenji, predicts cell-type-specific RNA expression profiles using 131 kb genomic regions as inputs and Cap analysis of gene expression (CAGE) datasets as targets [61]. This model applies a dilated convolutional architecture to enable the use of large receptive fields, improving gene expression prediction by modeling long-range enhancer-promoter interactions. The same dataset was used to train Enformer [56] on 196 kb genomic regions. The architecture of Enformer combines convolutional blocks with Transformers to integrate information from longer-range interactions up to 100 kb, outperforming Basenji in gene expression prediction (Pearson's correlation 0.85 vs 0.81). A more recent advancement is Borzoi, a U-Net-style architecture combining convolutional and Transformer layers to predict RNA expression (Pearson's correlation of 0.87) from 524 kb genomic windows [98]. Borzoi was trained using over 10,000 human and mouse genomic assays, including CAGE datasets from the FANTOM5 Consortium as well as RNA-seq coverage tracks from ENCODE and GTEx. Using the same datasets, the authors trained Flashzoi, an enhanced version of Borzoi that incorporates rotary positional encoding to reduce training time while preserving or improving accuracy of several predictive tasks, including RNA coverage [99].

3.3.2 Synthetic Datasets

In addition to profiling natural genomic sequences, RNA-seq also serves a crucial role in evaluating the function of synthetically designed biological parts, particularly in combinations with MPRA. In MPRA experiments, large libraries of synthetic DNA sequences – typically encompassing promoter, enhancer, or 5′UTR elements – are cloned upstream of a reporter gene and introduced into cells. Upon transcription, each synthetic construct generates a unique mRNA tagged with a barcode, allowing sequence-specific quantification of expression levels. RNA-seq is then used to measure the relative abundance of each transcript, effectively linking sequence design to transcriptional output.

In a “classic” low-throughput setup, a synthetic dataset of transcriptional activity is created by cloning a set of candidate regulatory DNA sequences besides a reporter gene, such as luciferase [100]. These constructs are then delivered into cells through plasmid transfection or lentiviral integration, and reporter expression is quantified using luminescence-based readouts. The emergence of high-throughput RNA-sequencing, combined with affordable DNA synthesis and advances in laboratory automation, has enabled more efficient screening methods, including MPRA (Figure 3.5). This technique allows the simultaneous analysis of transcriptional activity of thousands to millions of candidate DNA sequences in a single experiment [101]. MPRA exists in several variants, including episomal MPRA, lenti-MPRA [102, 103] and STARR-seq [104], but all share a common framework: libraries of CREs are cloned alongside barcoded reporter genes. These libraries are then delivered into cells, and transcriptional activity is quantified in parallel using RNA sequencing. In barcode-based MPRAs, the RNA expression of the associated barcode serves as a proxy for activity, while in STARR-seq, the candidate sequence itself is transcribed and directly measured, eliminating the need for separate barcodes.

One prokaryote MPRA dataset was derived from metagenomic mining of bacterial regulatory sequences [105]. Over 29,000 165-bp regulatory sequences from 184 prokaryotic genomes were synthesized, barcoded, and cloned upstream of a GFP reporter in species-specific plasmids. These constructs were transformed into various bacterial hosts and assayed using RNA-seq and FACS-seq. The resulting dataset was used to train DeepSEED, a DL framework that learned the relationship between promoter sequence and activity and allowed the design of species-specific synthetic promoters [39]. The 2024 DREAM Random Promoter Challenge generated a FACS-based MPRA dataset consisting of over 6.7 million random 80-bp sequences cloned into a promoter context and expressed in S. cerevisiae. Fluorescence measurements and high-throughput sequencing quantifications enabled the training of a range of models to predict RNA expression from DNA sequence alone. The participating teams employed a variety of DL architectures, including CNNs, recurrent neural networks (RNNs), and Transformers, to achieve strong sequence-to-expression prediction performance [106]. In an earlier study, Cuperus et. al. assayed the activity of 500,000 50-nucleotide-long random 5′-UTRs in S. cerevisiae using a histidine-negative growth assay MPRA [107]. A CNN trained using this dataset predicted the effect of both random and native 5′ UTR on protein expression and guided the design of synthetic 5′ UTR by single nucleotide in silico evolution. The same group used an MPRA-based approach to quantify the activity of 280,000 random 5′ UTR in human cell lines [57]. The resulting dataset was used to train Optimus 5′-Prime, a CNN that predicts ribosome loading from 5′ UTR sequences. This model was successfully used in conjunction with a genetic algorithm to guide the design of novel 5′ UTRs with precise translational control. The same dataset supported the training of other 5′ UTR activity predictors, such as the CNN-based FramePool series [108], and the Transformer-based UTR-LM [109] and UTR-Insight [110]. MPRA has also been widely used to investigate distal regulatory elements, such as enhancers. For example, UMI-STAR-seq, a variant of STARR-seq, was used to generate high-resolution activity maps of developmental and housekeeping enhancers in Drosophila S2 cells [64]. This dataset was used to train DeepSTARR, a CNN based on Basset architecture [111], to identify novel enhancers and predict their activity. DeepSTARR was used to predict the activity of 1 billion random 249-bp DNA sequences that were not present in the Drosophila genome, and the experimental validation of 249 selected sequences showed a Pearson correlation of 0.62, demonstrating its predictive potential. Using an episomal MPRA dataset comprising 776,474 200-bp sequences assayed in K562, HepG2, and SK-N-SH human cell lines, Gosai et al [46] trained Malinois, another Basset-based CNN activity predictor. Combining Malinois with sequence design algorithms, they developed CODA (Computational Optimization of DNA Activity), a platform for designing novel cell-type-specific CREs. Importantly, these synthetic CREs were functionally validated in vitro using MPRAs and in vivo in physiologically related tissues in mice and zebrafish. The same dataset also supported the training of regLM, a workflow that combines HyenaDNA with an oracle-like regressor to generate synthetic cell-type-specific human enhancers [83]. A lentiMPRA approach was used to quantify the transcriptional activity of over 680,000 candidate CREs across three human cell types (HepG2, K562 and WTC11) [112]. The resulting dataset was used to benchmark the predictive potential of four models, with MPRALegNet achieving the highest performance (Pearson r ≈ 0.83).

Altogether, these examples show how sequence-to-function datasets can be leveraged to train DL models that map DNA sequence to regulatory activity. These approaches are transforming our ability to interpret regulatory codes, design optimized genetic parts, and predict the functional consequences of sequence variation. As experimental and computational technologies continue to evolve, integrating diverse datasets will be key to advancing synthetic biology – from gene circuit design to novel therapies development.

3.4 Evaluating Synthetic Biological Parts Using Motif Analysis and Deep Learning

Designing synthetic biological parts using DL requires not only the generation of plausible sequences but also rigorous evaluation based on biological functionality and context. To streamline assessment across the biological parts, a range of quantitative evaluation strategies has been established. These include distributional similarity metrics (e.g. Fréchet Inception Distance, k-mer correlation), motif syntax evaluations (e.g. spacing and co-occurrence of TFBS), and structural feature checks (e.g. Kozak sequence presence, GC content, or polyadenylation signals). Table 3.2 summarizes these key metrics, offering a compact reference for how synthetic sequences can be quantitatively assessed against natural counterparts, enabling principled design and iterative optimization of synthetic biological systems.

While Table 3.2 provides a structured starting point for evaluating generated sequences, it is important to recognize that the underlying regulatory grammar of DNA is inherently flexible and context-dependent, rather than governed by universally fixed rules. DL models have proven essential in uncovering these complex patterns, learning positional constraints, motif syntax, and higher-order interactions directly from sequence data. For instance, species-aware DNA language models trained on over 800 fungal genomes captured species-specific promoter features, including the preferred position of the TATA box (∼30 bp upstream of the TSS in S. pombe, 50–120 bp in S. cerevisiae) and long-range interactions such as TATA-INR spacing and RNA structural elements [113].

Crucially, DL models can also decode motif syntax – the arrangement, spacing, and combinations of regulatory motifs that influence function. A CNN trained on MPRA data of synthetic B-cell promoters learned that transcriptional activity peaks when the OCT motif lies within 45 bp of the core promoter, and identified synergistic combinations like CArG-box + Runx1 + Arid3a [114]. Similarly, the DeepSTARR model, trained on thousands of Drosophila enhancer sequences, found that only specific motif instances (e.g. a single GATA motif) drive activity, depending on local context and spacing. These examples show how DL not only captures biologically meaningful features but also formalizes a probabilistic, context-aware grammar of regulatory DNA [64].

3.5 Current Challenges of Generative Part Design

GenAI has proven its capacity to design tailored biological sequences, such as promoters and enhancers, with significant applications in biotechnology – from developing cell-type-specific regulatory elements for therapeutic use to engineering novel enzymes with enhanced catalytic efficiency for industrial purposes [83]. Despite these advancements, current LLMs are limited by their inability to capture long-range interactions in regulatory elements, mainly due to the quadratic complexity () of existing Transformer models. Emerging models, such as state-space models, like MAMBA [115], address this challenge by achieving linear complexity (), enabling the training and generation of chromosome-length sequences with reduced memory constraints. The integration of bi-directionality in the Caduceus model [116] can potentially be used for the generation of both upstream and downstream sequences, paving the way for de novo chromosome generation.

Another key limitation of LLMs lies in their susceptibility to hallucinations, that is, the generation of biologically implausible or nonfunctional sequences. This issue may stem from limited sequence diversity in training datasets, leading to model overfitting on prevalent patterns while failing to capture rare but functionally important sequence variations. Incomplete or inaccurate genome annotations further compound this problem, often resulting in unreliable outputs. Currently, these challenges remain largely unaddressed in the context of DNA sequence generation. To mitigate such limitations, strategies from natural language processing, such as Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF)) [117], could be adapted to the engineering of synthetic parts. RLHF fine-tunes models based on curated human feedback. In a biological setting, this could be experimental validation feedback, though this will come at significant computational and labor cost.

Despite rapid progress in using DL models to design biologically compatible synthetic DNA sequences, the vast majority of these sequences have not yet been experimentally validated. Current validation approaches often depend on computational metrics like k-mer similarity, which, while useful proxies, are insufficient to fully capture biological function or regulatory effectiveness. Bridging the gap between in silico predictions and experimental validation remains a major challenge in the field of generative part design.

3.6 Conclusion

GenAI marks a paradigm shift in synthetic biology, offering a streamlined alternative to the traditional design-build-test-learn cycle. By learning complex sequence–function relationships from large-scale datasets, these models can generate novel, realistic functional sequences with reduced experimental burden. As predictive and generative models continue to improve, we anticipate their integration will become central to the rational programmable design of synthetic elements across diverse organisms. By tailoring the synthesis of biological sequences to specific user needs, GenAI will drive innovation in the bioeconomy and expand the potential of the biotechnology industry.
