4
Machine Learning for Sequence-to-Function Approaches

Rana A. Barghout

1University of Toronto, Department of Chemical Engineering & Applied Chemistry, 200 College St, M5T 3E5, Toronto, ON, Canada
2Vector Institute for Artificial Intelligence, 108 College St, M5G 0C6, Toronto, ON, Canada

4.1 Introduction

Proteins, the molecular machines of life, derive their biochemical and cellular functions from linear sequences of amino acids. They can fold into dynamic three-dimensional structures, ranging from ordered to conformationally flexible states. This relationship can be described using a “language” analogy proposed by Bepler and Berger [1]: amino acids serve as a chemical “alphabet” that combines into structural elements (“words”), which when assembled into sentences, acquire a functional “meaning.” However, it's important to note that protein sequences differ fundamentally from human language: they operate through physical and chemical interactions rather than symbolic representation, and their “meaning” is governed by biophysical principles rather than semantic conventions. Deciphering how the sequence of a protein encodes its functional outcomes, known as the sequence-structure–function relationship, contributes to a wider comprehension of evolutionary biology.

The linear arrangement of amino acids in a protein sequence encodes the structural and functional properties with high efficiency [2]. Even minor perturbations to this sequence, such as single mutations, can alter their stability, highlighting the difficulty of inferring function solely from sequence information. Overcoming this challenge is essential for applications in disease research and biotechnology [3]. Inferring the function of a protein directly from its sequence would improve the understanding of genetic diseases [4] and identify novel drug targets [5]. It could also enable the design enzymes with enhanced capabilities for the synthesis of chemicals [6] and degradation of pollutants [7].

In recent years, modern sequencing technologies have produced an exponential growth of sequence data. As of 2025, the UniProt database contained over 253 million protein sequences [8], yet fewer than 0.3% had experimentally validated annotations of their function [9]. This is due to the labor-intensive and time-consuming nature of experimental assays, which are also prone to biases and have limited coverage across all proteins [10]. The gap between sequencing and functional annotation creates an urgent need for reliable computational methods that would enable the prediction of protein function from its sequence information.

Machine learning (ML) has enabled major breakthroughs in sequence-to-function mapping. Typically framed as a classification or regression task, ML models are trained on raw amino acid sequences (the input) to accurately predict functional characteristics (the output). Traditional ML approaches require the alignment of protein sequences or manual feature engineering; thus, they are limited in capturing the complex, high-dimensional relationships between a sequence and its corresponding function. In contrast, modern ML models can learn features and nonlinear patterns from large datasets, making them well-suited for protein sequence data. Deep learning (DL) models, using neural networks as building blocks for ML models, employ parameterized transformations of data to learn new representations of data that are optimized for the task at hand. The initial breakthroughs were driven by convolutional neural networks (CNNs), with the identification of sequence motifs, which correspond to catalytic sites or binding domains that drive protein function [11]. These models have also been combined with other architectures, such as recurrent neural networks (RNNs), to capture temporal relationships [12]. Most recent models incorporate transformer architectures [13], which can capture long-range dependencies and recognize amino acid sequences crucial to maintaining protein function throughout evolution.

As ML is increasingly applied to sequence-to-function problems, two key priorities are improving generalizability and integrating multi-omics data. Focusing on these aspects ensures that models remain not only accurate on benchmark datasets but also applicable across diverse biological contexts. A model is considered generalizable if it can make accurate predictions for unseen or diverse sequences beyond its training set. Many models have a significant drop in performance when faced with very dissimilar training data, as demonstrated in validation tasks with evolutionarily distant variants [14]. This highlights the challenge of extrapolating predictions to completely unseen sequence spaces. Methods such as self-supervised pretraining [15] and physics-informed architectures [16] help models move beyond memorization to context-aware predictions. Generalization capabilities go hand in hand with the integration of multi-omics data. Biological function is rarely determined solely by sequence; it emerges from a cascade of molecular interactions. Therefore, the training data for these models requires the integration of genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, and microbiomics [17]. By prioritizing both generalizability and multi-omics integration, sequence-to-function models can move from narrow, benchmark-specific successes to widely usable tools in research (Figure 4.1).

4.2 Current State of Sequence-to-Function Modeling

4.2.1 Protein Function Prediction: From BLAST to Language Models

Before the now-commonplace ML models were established, many different rule-based methods were proposed. Since 1997, methods such as the basic local alignment search tool (BLAST) and psi-BLAST [18] have been used to predict protein functions by homology by finding sequence similarities in established protein or DNA databases. More recent methods include DIAMOND [19] and HHblits [20], which significantly improve the search throughput for similar sequences.

Early 2000's ML models used algorithms such as k-nearest neighbor (KNN) and support vector machines (SVMs), considering function prediction as a classification problem [21, 22]. Since these ML methods rely on already well-established and annotated data that often comes from biasedly distributed data, they often fail at predicting out-of-distribution protein properties, or proteins with low sequence similarity to existing data.

While supervised learning has advanced protein functionality prediction, self-supervised learning has had a broader impact by exploiting vast unlabeled sequence datasets. Among those techniques, masked language modeling (MLM) has become a dominant strategy. In MLM, models are trained to reconstruct randomly masked amino acids in a sequence using surrounding context, allowing them to learn rich representations.

TAPE [13] was among the first to successfully train a protein language model (pLM) using MLM tasks, demonstrating that a transformer-based model could encode functionality-relevant information from protein sequences. ESM-1b and ESM-2 continuously expanded upon model depth while training on larger datasets, which offered improved performance in both structure and function predictions [23]. Beyond ESM, the ProtTrans suite introduced models like ProtBERT, which retains the bidirectional encoder representation from transformers (BERT)-based MLM approach, and ProtT5 that adapts the T5 encoder-decoder architecture to enable span-masking and enhanced flexibility in sequence representation [24]. In contrast to transformer models, CARP employs dilated CNNs, offering competitive performance with lower computational cost [25]. Adding pLM embeddings have been shown to improve a model's ability to map sequences to their corresponding functions through ablation studies [26, 27], underscoring the efficacy of ML-based self-supervised learning in advancing protein sequence-to-function prediction (Table 4.1).

4.2.2 Gene Ontology

In an effort to standardize the way proteins were described, the community created a vocabulary known as Gene Ontology (GO) in 2000 to provide a consistent way of annotating genes and products in different databases and research groups [28, 29]. GO covers three main aspects of gene/protein functionality: molecular function (MF), biological process (BP), and cellular component/location (CC/CL). The GO structure is hierarchical, with multiple other GO terms branching off from the three parent terms to fully encapsulate gene product functionality. This then provides the perfect groundwork for classification-type ML models to attempt and build GO “trees” for new, unannotated proteins.

In 2017, DeepGO used a CNN to better recognize patterns in sequential data and incorporated multimodal data sources to predict GO annotations [30]. DeepGOPlus [31] and Deep_CNN_LSTM_GO [32] build deeper networks and incorporate long short-term memory (LSTM), leading to predictive improvements and allowing larger sequence input enabling broader protein analysis. In 2021, DeepGraphGO [33] uses a structural GNN protein representation, enabling it to outperform DeepGoPlus when comparing predictions for BP and CC Ontologies. In 2023, DeepGO-SE [34] leveraged pLM embeddings from ESM-2 and allowed the model to generalize and predict GO terms for largely unseen proteins.

4.2.3 Enzyme Commission Numbers

Although GO remains the largest field for classification of sequences, other metrics have also been predicted from other ML/DL models. Within the microbial genome, enzymes constitute one of the most prevalent functional gene classes. Subsequently, their catalytic behavior and functionality are most often represented using an enzyme commission (EC) number. The EC number consists of four digits, representing the class, subclass, sub-subclass, and sub-sub-subclass of the enzyme.

Released in the same time frame as DeepGO, DEEPre [35] utilized raw enzyme sequence data to predict EC numbers. DEEPre uses both CNNs and RNNs, with RNNs extracting sequential, long-term interactions, and was capable of predicting the first three EC digits with a higher degree of accuracy than pre-existing ML models, such as EzyPred, SVM-Prot, COFACTOR, and EFICAz. In 2019, mlDEEPre was released, with additional capabilities to predict functionality for multifunctional enzymes instead of only monofunctional enzymes [36].

DeepEC [37], developed at the same time, consisted of three separate independent CNNs. Additionally, DeepEC implements homology analysis using DIAMOND for EC numbers that cannot be classified by the CNNs. In 2023, DeepECTransformer was released, using transformer layers in its neural network for prediction [38]. It covers more EC numbers compared to DeepEC, and employs a linear layer BERT architecture [39]. The improved architecture allows it to better predict enzymes with low sequence identities in the training set, relying less on the homology analysis than DeepEC utilized.

Finally, the CLEAN model (2023) reframed the EC problem from a multilabel classification to a contrastive learning framework [40]. It uses protein representations obtained from the ESM-1b pLM and a feed-forward neural network (FFNN). Using a distance-based prediction in its learning framework allows it to more accurately and reliably predict EC numbers, particularly for cases like understudied or mislabeled enzymes, outperforming traditional classification models to date. Many of these EC-based learning methods are further detailed in Chapter 5 of the book.

4.2.4 Enzyme Activity

Enzyme activity refers to an enzyme's ability to convert substrate into products. Enzyme activity is often represented by kinetic parameters such as rate of substrate conversion (kcat), substrate binding affinity (KM), and catalytic efficiency (kcat/KM). Accurately predicting these parameters is essential for various applications, including enzyme engineering, metabolic modeling, and drug development. Reliable predictions can accelerate the discovery of biocatalysts, optimize pathway design for synthetic biology, and reduce the need for costly and time-consuming experimental characterization.

Recent advances in kinetic parameter prediction have markedly improved kcat and KM estimates. In 2022, DLKcat aimed to make predictions using protein sequences and substrate representations but struggled with enzymes lacking close homologs [41]. In 2023, TurNuP set out to build a more generalizable kcat predictor by leveraging embeddings from pLMs for sequences and chemical fingerprints for substrates [42]. UniKP expanded this work by not only using pretrained embeddings from pLMs but also from chemical models [43]. With this new framework, UniKP was used to predict different kinds of kinetic parameters, such as KM (in addition to kcat), resulting in improved performance for all kinetic parameters. In 2024, CatPred utilized newer pretrained embeddings for sequences and substrates, an expanded dataset, and uncertainty predictions, resulting in better KM predictions [26]. We also recently developed CPI-Pred, a generalizable framework where pretrained models could be interchanged for sequence and substrate embeddings [27]. Interestingly, its best model performed on par with CatPred, suggesting that improvements in model architecture alone may no longer drive substantial gains in prediction accuracy. The key challenge is that future advances may depend more on the availability of higher-quality and more diverse datasets rather than further refinements to deep learning models themselves.

4.2.5 Protein Thermal Stability

Thermal stability refers to a protein's ability to maintain their spatial structures as temperature increases, and stability is critical for BPes. Proteins with low thermal stability tend to aggregate at physiological temperatures, leading to loss of activity, dysfunction, or the formation of toxic protein aggregates [44].

There are two main ways researchers are investigating the thermal stability of proteins. The first involves predicting the melting temperature (Tm) of a protein. Tm is the point at which 50% of the protein loses its native structure and is indicative of how stable a given protein is throughout a temperature range. In 2023, DeepSTABp was developed to predict Tm for a given protein sequence [44]. The model would extract sequence features and physical features from thermal proteome profiling datasets and run predictions to determine Tm. DeepSTABp was able to achieve state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance, beating out ProTstab2 on this regression task.

The second method treats thermal stability as a classification problem, but does so with a set of binary classification models due to dataset constraints. BertThermo was the first method that would consider whether or not a protein will remain stable above some threshold temperature (analogous to Tm) as a classification task [45]. This way, there are several binary classifiers where the threshold temperature remains static for each model. In 2024, TemProSta used a similar approach, leveraging a larger dataset, and outperformed all other comparable methods on standard benchmarks (iThermo, SAPPHIRE, SCMTPP, and ThermoPred) [46].

4.2.6 Protein Toxicity

Protein toxicity refers to the adverse effects that proteins or peptides can exert on biological systems, potentially leading to harmful physiological responses or even fatal outcomes. Using binary prediction methods to determine whether a protein is toxic is essential in developing protein-based therapeutics [47]. These methods help researchers identify and eliminate candidates that could cause harmful side effects, making the drug discovery process more efficient and ensuring patient safety.

Early toxicity prediction methods were largely template-based, employing sequence alignment tools like BLAST to compare unknown proteins to known toxic ones [48]. These approaches, while pioneering, were limited by the dependency on high-quality template sequences. To overcome this, researchers moved toward feature-based models that extracted compositional, evolutionary, and physicochemical attributes from protein sequences and utilized classical ML techniques. A notable model was ToxinPred [48], developed in 2013, which laid the groundwork for predicting peptide toxicity across various sources.

Recent advances have seen the adoption of alignment-free methods that leverage deep learning architectures such as RNNs, LSTMs, and transformers [47]. Specific models such as CSM-Toxin [48], ToxinPred 3.0 [47], and the more recent VISH-Pred [49] have harnessed the power of pLMs like ProteinBERT [50] and ESM-2 [51] to capture intricate sequence patterns and subtle structural nuances. These SOTA approaches have not only improved predictive accuracy but have also facilitated the creation of accessible web-based tools that integrate into practical workflows, ultimately enhancing the design of safer and more effective protein-based therapeutics.

4.2.7 Protein Solubility

Solubility refers to the proportion of a protein that remains dissolved in a solution and aggregated under physiological conditions. In protein expression, determining whether a protein will remain soluble or form aggregates is crucial for efficient production, which is more common in over-expressed proteins. Classifying proteins by solubility before production helps optimize selection, as insoluble aggregates can reduce yields, increase purification costs, and compromise function. In contrast, soluble proteins are easier to purify and use in downstream applications.

Although there are many model organisms for protein production, most efforts have focused on predicting protein solubility in Escherichia coli, as it is widely used in industry and has the most available data [52]. Preliminary methods were built to predict whether a protein is soluble (binary classification task) from its protein sequence through support vector machines and naive-bayes. [53]. PROSO was among the first ML models to manually curate expert features, such as grouping amino acids based on physicochemical properties, to improve predictive generalizability back in 2007. Since then, researchers have explored improved feature engineering and larger datasets. In 2021, NetSolP was an early adopter of pLMs, in the form of a fine-tuned ESM-1b model, to make these predictions and was able to achieve SOTA performance compared to other competitive models at the time [54]. In 2023, researchers identified that features like amino acid counts, transitions between adjacent amino acids, residue distribution along the sequence, and correlations between properties such as charge and hydrophobicity were particularly impactful [55]. This led to the development of the RPPSP model, which leveraged these features to outperform both NetSolP and earlier models. As interest grew in using pLM embeddings, the 2024 model PLM_Sol emerged as the best predictor by passing ProtT5 sequence embeddings through a bidirectional LSTM, and it remains the current SOTA at the time of writing [52].

4.3 Tool Kits and Benchmarks

4.3.1 Overview of Open-Source Tools

Datasets and Databases Large-scale datasets have been utilized extensively over the past decade for a multitude of functional prediction ML tasks. For proteins, UniProt [8] is the most well-known and used database. It contains information on protein sequences, their native host organism, and supplementary data such as 3D structures from the PDB database [58] and/or predictive models such as AlphaFold [59]. UniProt often also hosts other protein functional tags, such as kinetic information, GO, and PPI links, to external databases like STRING [60]. In the enzyme space, BRENDA [61] plays an essential role in providing functional enzymatic information. Many other datasets and databases, as listed in Table 4.2, have also been frequently used in sequence-to-function prediction pipelines.

Precursor Models Outside of existing databases and datasets, different types of modeling frameworks have also served as essential tool kits for sequence-to-function ML prediction pipelines. These frameworks include ML-based methods (AlphaFold [59], Chai-1 [9]), ESM-2 [51], etc.), as well as non-ML-based methods (molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, quantum-based methods, computational bio methods such as BLAST [18], etc.).

Early protein function prediction relied on sequence homology and domain architecture without the incorporation of any traditional ML methods, as previously discussed in the current state section. BLAST remains a foundational method for identifying homologous sequences through pairwise alignment. Hidden Markov models (HMMs) [75] advanced this through probabilistic profile matching in tools like Pfam [63] and InterProScan [76]. These methods established the paradigm of transferring functional annotations from characterized homologs, achieving moderate accuracy but limited by evolutionary divergence. Outside of these sequence similarity-based methods, sequence-to-function pipelines have also utilized MD simulations to provide physicochemical insights, which can be critical for understanding protein functions like allosteric regulations [77]. Furthermore, density functional theory and quantum mechanical methods can be used as precursor tools in sequence-to-function pipelines as they address electronic effects, which are crucial for metalloenzyme active sites [78].

As for ML-based methods, there are three types of models that typically play a precursor role in these sequence-to-function prediction pipelines. The first class of ML models is one that focuses on predicting protein structures, such as AlphaFold [59] and Chai-1 [79]. Researchers in this field will often dismiss the use of sequence-only function prediction models when comparing their performance against structure-based function models, where they've shown superior performance on monomer, PPI, and antibody–antigen CASP15 tasks [80]. Regardless, sequence-only models provide a big advantage in their lighter computational loads, extensive experimental data availability, and ability to model intrinsically disordered regions. The second class of ML models is pLMs, such as ESM-2 [51], ProtT5 [81], and ProteinBERT [50]. These models utilize different training objectives (masked language modeling, bidirectional sequence reconstruction, GO term prediction) to “learn the protein language,” and therefore be able to output embeddings from protein sequences that can be utilized for downstream sequence-to-function prediction tasks. The third class of models is auto-regressive sequence design models, like ProtGPT2 [2] and ProGEN [82], that often serve as a generative surrogate for producing novel sequences that can be treated as synthetic data in these sequence-to-function pipelines [83, 84]. It is worth noting that there are also genomic language models, such as HyenaDNA [85], Evo [86], and gLM2 [87], that have been utilized for protein prediction tasks, although we won't be focusing on that in this chapter.

4.3.2 Importance of Standardized Benchmarks

Standardized benchmarks are crucial for the objective evaluation and comparison of computational methods. While there has been significant progress in the development of these benchmarking datasets (as listed in Table 4.2), studies focusing on benchmarking different models and methods on a wide variety of protein tasks still remain a challenge. This is often due to the lack of open-source models and data, or perhaps a lack of consolidation amongst researchers in this field. In terms of assessment protocols, the field has converged on a few different performance metrics. For classification tasks, Fmax, the harmonic mean of precision and recall at optimal threshold; AUPR, area under precision-recall curve accounting for class imbalance; and Smin, semantic distance metric for prediction completeness. For regression tasks, the R2 coefficient of determination, which quantifies the degree of any linear correlation between 2 datasets; Pearson's r, a correlation coefficient that measures the linear correlation between 2 datasets; Spearman's ρ, a correlation coefficient that measures the strength of association between 2 datasets. That being said, it is also important to consider domain-specific evaluation metrics that might be useful for different biological scenarios. For example, CatPred [26] introduces the p1,mag metric, which describes the percent of predictions within one order of magnitude error for prediction of different kinetic parameters. Outside of benchmarking studies and evaluation metrics, it's also crucial to consider data splits. Proteins are really complex when it comes to feature extraction and input space; therefore, we find that models tend to be able to learn and predict things well when they've learned information from sequences that are similar to sequences they've seen during training. A recurring issue with protein datasets is their biased/uneven distribution, where they have very sparse annotations for certain protein classes. It's important to benchmark any sequence-to-function model on a wide variety of sequence-similarity-based splits, which is often done through tools like CDHIT [88] or MMSeqs2 [89] (see 4.2 for datasets with preset splits).

4.4 Emerging ML Methods

ML methods for protein sequence-to-function prediction have rapidly evolved. Increasingly sophisticated approaches have been adopted to overcome different limitations in sequence-to-function learning. Emerging strategies leverage diverse methodologies. Sections below summarize key recent developments in some promising areas.

4.4.1 Contrastive Learning

Contrastive learning utilizes self-supervised strategies to generate robust protein representations by aligning diverse data types, such as sequence embeddings and structural embeddings. This approach significantly enhances generalization, particularly in data-scarce scenarios. An exemplar of contrastive learning's efficacy is the CLEAN model [90], which substantially improves enzyme function prediction. CLEAN excels in annotating understudied enzymes and accurately identifying promiscuous enzymes with multiple EC numbers. It consistently outperforms conventional methods like BLASTp [91], especially in distinguishing closely related enzyme functions and discovering novel enzymatic activities. Experimental validations have demonstrated CLEAN's robustness and reliability in assigning functional annotations to previously uncharacterized enzymes, establishing its value for genomics, synthetic biology, and biocatalysis research.

4.4.2 Meta Learning

Meta learning is a subcategory of ML that trains artificial intelligence (AI) models to understand and adapt to new tasks autonomously. Unlike conventional supervised learning, where models are trained to solve a specific task using a defined training dataset, meta learning involves multiple tasks, each with its own dataset. Models trained via meta learning generalize across tasks. This allows rapid adaptation to novel scenarios with minimal data. The meta learning process consists of two main stages: (1) meta training, where models are exposed to various tasks to discover common patterns and generalizable knowledge, and (2) meta testing, where models are evaluated on new, unseen tasks to assess their adaptive performance. A recent advancement in this area is DeepPFP [92], a multitask-aware model specifically designed for protein function prediction. DeepPFP combines model-agnostic meta-learning (MAML) [93] with ESM-1b to effectively capture universal sequence-function relationships. MAML optimizes a model's initial parameters so that the model can rapidly adapt to new tasks after only a few gradient update steps. ESM, on the other hand, leverages evolutionary information embedded within protein sequences, capturing deep contextual relationships crucial for accurate function prediction. By integrating meta-learning strategies like MAML with powerful sequence representations from ESM, DeepPFP achieves enhanced generalization across diverse enzyme function prediction tasks. Consequently, DeepPFP excels in few-shot learning scenarios, surpassing traditional deep learning models. Evaluations on multiple deep mutational scanning (DMS) datasets highlight its capability to significantly improve predictive performance, especially when sequence similarity alone fails to accurately predict protein functions. This approach effectively addresses the long-tail distribution challenge common in protein function prediction, enabling accurate identification of rare functional variants.

4.5 Case Studies

4.5.1 Prediction of Enzyme Activity and Substrate Specificity

Enzyme activity prediction has been a long-standing functional prediction task. While many models have recently emerged with the goal of predicting enzyme activity, the field has not yet achieved a comprehensive solution that meets key benchmarks, including extrapolating for enzymes outside of the available datasets. Predicting the rate at which enzymes speed up a reaction is arguably the most important prediction task for an enzyme, given that the majority of enzymes function as biological catalysts. Activity prediction can be described through several functional parameters, but the most common term used to describe it is the enzyme turnover number (kcat). These values are essential for understanding kinetic behaviors in the metabolism on a genome-scale for different organisms and also often serve as tunable parameters when looking at enzyme engineering. Several ML models have emerged over the past five years for predicting kcat values. Although kcat values are one of the most important and commonly used functional descriptors for enzyme assays, ML models that have surfaced over the past five years still struggle to accurately predict these values. One of the works pioneering the kcat prediction task in the ML space is from Heckmann et al. [94]. Heckmann et al. [94] utilized several traditional ML methods to predict enzyme turnover numbers from input fluxomics and proteomics data, including an elastic net, random forest, and an FFNN outputting predictions in an ensembled format. Following the publication of this work, several research groups worked on developing deep learning models for predicting kcat values, as previously mentioned in Section 4.2.4. Although these models utilize protein-compound inputs to predict enzyme turnover numbers, they serve as great examples for enhancing our understanding of protein property prediction. Next, we explore an example of how these pipelines work.

4.5.1.1 Predicting kcat Using CPI-Pred

CPI-Pred, or Compound-Protein Interaction Predictor, is a deep learning framework for inferring kinetic parameters such as kcat, as well as other compound-protein interaction functional descriptors. CPI-Pred takes in two inputs (protein sequence and compound SMILES) and predicts one value (kcat). For the context of this chapter, we can hone in on the sequence side of CPI-Pred. In the computational biology space, proteins typically follow IUPAC nomenclature before they are processed in any downstream process. For a computer to actually understand and process this protein language, it must be able to translate the amino acids into numbers. This is done in a step called tokenization; a protein sequence (e.g. “GCTVE”) is converted to numbers by assigning each amino acid a token ID (i.e. “2, 11, 7, 23, 25”). In many of these DL pipelines, pLMs (see Section 1.3.1) are utilized to “featurize” protein sequences of the dataset of interest from a much larger protein dataset (i.e. ESM-2 was trained on 650-million protein sequences). The tokenized protein sequences are passed to the selected pLM and a protein embedding is outputted from the model. In the case of CPI-Pred, the ESM-2 model is identified as the best-performing pLM in the pipeline, although many others were tested. From ESM-2, the protein embedding is outputted with dimension DL × DE, with DL being the protein sequence's length (number of amino acid residues) and DE being the pLM's embedding dimension; for ESM-2, it ranges from 320 all the way up to 5,120. Often, for protein functional prediction tasks, the proteins of interest don't come in datasets with consistent sequence lengths, meaning that DL = max(Dl,i), or the maximum length out of all of the proteins in our dataset (or batch). Due to the large dimensions, processing these pLM embeddings is a tedious and computationally expensive task. Therefore, different models, including CPI-Pred, have explored different methods of pooling that information in an efficient manner that tries to preserve as much learned residue-specific information as possible. CPI-Pred utilizes three different methods for this task: convolutional 1D pooling, self-attention-based pooling, and LSTM variational encoding pooling (Figure 4.2). Following these protein pooling steps, we are left with a fixed-dimension vector that can then be passed to a multilayer perceptron (MLP) for further processing and prediction.

4.6 Challenges in Sequence-to-Function Mapping

ML approaches show promise in protein engineering by efficiently exploring vast sequence spaces, but face challenges due to complexity and functional sequence sparsity [95, 96]. Protein designs often fail when transitioning from specific assays to biological applications, highlighting the need for better alignment between screening methods and intended outcomes [97–100]. Consequently, candidates from early screening frequently fail in rigorous validation [101–104], while certain protein classes lack suitable high-throughput assays altogether [6, 105–110].

4.6.1 Sparse Experimental Data

High-Dimensional Space and Limited Labels Protein engineering is challenged by vast sequence dimensionality coupled with limited functional annotations (Figure 4.3). Despite high-throughput screening capabilities, obtaining quality labeled datasets requires substantial resources [61, 111–114]. Recent approaches like low-N protein engineering [83] attempt to address this by using ML models such as eUniRep to predict functionality from minimal experimental data, enabling in silico screening of millions of sequences.

Imbalanced Datasets and Rare Enzymatic Activities Class imbalance, particularly under-representation of rare enzyme functions, further limits ML performance. This challenge intensifies with high-dimensional sequence embedding methods (Figure 4.3a). Whether developing therapeutic [115, 116], agricultural [117], or industrial proteins [118, 119], researchers face trade-offs between detailed evaluation and broader exploration. While extensive sequence and structure databases exist, functional annotation remains challenging due to diverse catalytic properties and experimental conditions [112]. Most databases weren't designed for ML applications, leading to inconsistencies, missing values, and conflicting annotations [120, 121]. Standardizing formats and adopting FAIR principles [122] and STRENDA guidelines [123] can enhance data quality, while oversampling rare classes or optimizing loss functions helps mitigate bias toward overrepresented categories [112].

4.6.2 Interpretability

The utility of sequence-to-function predictions depends on their biological insights, yet deep learning models often function as “black boxes.” Despite pLMs' success in predicting protein structures and functions, their lack of interpretability limits their application in critical domains like drug discovery, where understanding how sequence changes affect function is essential. While some models allow conditional generation by tagging protein features [82, 124, 125], they don't clarify which features influence specific predictions. The concept bottleneck pLM (CB-pLM) improves interpretability by introducing functional tags as biologically meaningful concepts [84]. Each bottleneck neuron corresponds to a specific attribute, enabling sequence generation aligned with desired properties while facilitating interpretation by mapping concepts to outputs. Other approaches include AlphaFold's structure predictions [59] and deep representation learning that generates biologically meaningful embeddings [126].

4.7 Conclusion and Future Directions

This chapter has examined the evolving landscape of ML approaches for protein sequence-to-function prediction, focusing on recent advances in predicting functional annotations (e.g. GO terms, EC numbers, enzyme activity, stability, toxicity, and solubility) directly from amino acid sequences. Key models exemplify how deep learning architectures leverage vast sequence datasets to bridge the annotation gap with the help of pLMs. These models address critical challenges, such as generalizing to evolutionarily distant proteins and integrating multimodal data (e.g. structural, kinetic, and multiomics insights), while highlighting persistent limitations like sparse experimental data, dataset biases, and computational costs. By connecting sequence patterns to functional outcomes, these tools accelerate discoveries in disease mechanisms, drug target identification, and enzyme engineering, though their reliability remains constrained by the quality and diversity of training data.

The progress in ML-driven function prediction underscores its significance in advancing both basic research and applied biotechnology. However, the field must prioritize strategies to enhance model interpretability, incorporate physicochemical constraints, and expand beyond homology-dependent predictions to fully realize its potential. While current models excel in narrow tasks, their broader utility depends on reconciling high-dimensional sequence data with underrepresented functional classes and dynamic biological contexts. These limitations set the stage for emerging methodologies, such as meta-learning and physics-informed architectures, which aim to unify sequence, structure, and environmental variables into predictive frameworks.
