5.1 Introduction

Enzymes play a crucial role in maintaining cellular physiological processes, effectively catalyzing metabolic reactions for operating energy metabolism, biosynthesis, and homeostasis. Thus, to thoroughly understand cell metabolism, it is essential to identify which proteins are enzymes and analyze their specific functions. While whole-genome sequencing technologies have significantly enhanced our capacity to elucidate the genetic underpinnings of metabolism by identifying putative enzyme-coding genes, the precise functional annotation of these genes has remained a persistent challenge. Traditional experimental approaches demand substantial time, labor, and cost, limiting high-throughput analysis. Consequently, many enzyme-encoding genes have been sequenced but remain functionally uncharacterized.

The development of computational enzyme function classification has complemented the limitations of traditional experimental approaches. These computational methods have enabled enzyme function prediction to transition from a localized scale to a genome-wide analysis, significantly expanding its scope and applicability. As described in Chapter 4, among the earliest computational strategies for enzyme function prediction are methods based on sequence homology. These homology-based approaches compare unknown sequences against well-characterized enzymes to identify regions of similarity, where similar sequences often suggest analogous biological functions. The effectiveness of these methods is widely acknowledged. However, they rely heavily on previous knowledge, and there are many cases where sequence similarity does not necessarily correspond to functional similarity. Thus, the importance of leveraging the intrinsic properties in enzyme sequences or structures for functional prediction has become increasingly emphasized. The emergence of artificial intelligence has facilitated accurate function prediction by learning and capturing the complex relationships between enzyme features and their functions [1, 2]. In this chapter, we review recent advancements in enzyme function prediction using computational approaches, encompassing conventional methods to advanced deep learning models. We focus on providing a comprehensive analysis of the field, emphasizing fundamental principles and methodological developments. Finally, we discuss ongoing challenges and future directions for further developing artificial intelligence-based enzyme functional annotation.

5.2 Conventional Computational Approaches for Predicting Enzyme Function

To predict whether an unknown protein functions as an enzyme and to determine its catalytic activity, the most fundamental and widely adopted computational approach involves transferring knowledge from already characterized enzymes to uncharacterized proteins by analyzing the similarities between them. This strategy has been widely employed since the early stages of computer-based enzyme characterization [3]. From an evolutionary perspective, proteins with high sequence similarity are presumed to have evolved from a common ancestor, thereby conserving their functions [4, 5].

As protein sequence availability increases with advances in whole genome sequencing technology, amino acid sequences and biochemical features derived from these sequences have become the main resources for enzyme functional classification. The basic local alignment search tool (BLAST) has been considered the gold standard tool for biological sequence similarity analysis [6]. It heuristically measures the local similarity for a pair of biological sequences, rapidly identifying sequences that are similar to a query from the large size of biological databases. Enzyme functions can be assigned to query proteins with statistically significant matches, making BLAST one of the most extensively utilized tools in protein and enzyme function prediction [7–10].

Although BLAST enables effective searching of protein sequences with global sequence similarity, it is challenging to detect sequences of remote homology that might affect enzyme functions. To address this limitation, position-specific iterated BLAST (PSI-BLAST) [11], a protein sequence search method that utilizes a position-specific score matrix (PSSM), was developed. PSI-BLAST iteratively performs sequence alignment to update PSSM, which is used for the next round of iteration, enabling it to better detect distant homologs and transfer knowledge of enzyme functions to the query protein. For example, ModFun successfully predicted the function of CYP7 – a peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerase – by utilizing PSI-BLAST and protein–protein interaction data, which was not predicted by performing BLAST alone [8].

Advances in bioinformatics have further enabled enzyme function analysis at the fine-grained level of functional domains, expanding beyond sequence-level analysis. Profile-HMM is a hidden Markov model that represents the position-specific frequencies of the amino acids and their probabilities of state transitions (i.e. match, deletion, and insertion) derived from a multiple sequence alignment (MSA) of a set of proteins [12]. This approach enabled the accurate recognition of conserved sequences or functional domains that are undetectable through conventional sequence alignments [13, 14]. Profiles derived from enzyme families with the same function provide functional motifs, domains, and families that characterize the enzyme functions. Aligning a query protein to these profiles facilitates the identification and analysis of its enzyme functions [14–16]. Thus, sequence similarity-based approaches have progressed from simple global sequence alignment to the precise detection of functional domains linked to enzyme activity through locally conserved sequences, enabling computer-aided high-throughput enzyme function prediction.

5.3 Prediction of Enzyme Functions Using Machine Learning

The homology-based approach contributed to shifting the trend in enzyme function prediction from experimental to in silico approaches. However, the diversity of evolutionary processes often significantly reduces their effectiveness [17]. An example is convergent evolution, which allows proteins to have similar functions despite low sequence similarity [18]. Another example is divergent evolution, which induces proteins to acquire different functions even with high sequence similarity [19]. Therefore, there has been a high demand for a new prediction methodology that does not rely on similarity. Machine learning, which learns the intrinsic features of data to make predictions, has addressed this need in enzyme function prediction quite effectively [20].

Two critical factors must be considered for the development of high-performance machine learning models. The first is feature extraction, which involves determining meaningful properties to extract from the raw data and how to preprocess them into a machine-readable format. Even when utilizing the same raw dataset and model architecture, model performance can vary substantially depending on the selection and processing of features for training. The second factor is the construction of machine learning models for effectively processing given features. Because various machine learning algorithms have distinct advantages and limitations, it is crucial to design models with a comprehensive consideration of the inherent properties of these algorithms and the training data. In this section, we explore different methods for extracting features from amino acid sequences and highlight machine learning algorithms frequently used for predicting enzyme functions.

5.3.1 Extraction of Enzyme Features from Amino Acid Sequences

The amino acid sequence is the fundamental determinant of enzyme characteristics, inherently encoding its chemical, structural, and evolutionary information. Enzyme features derived from amino acid sequences can be broadly categorized into direct and derived features. Directed features are defined as characteristics that can be immediately extracted from enzyme sequences based on statistical analyses of the physicochemical properties of amino acids (Figure 5.1a). In contrast, derived features are properties that require additional processing of raw sequence data to extract nonintuitive information such as higher-order structure, functional domains, and evolutionary profiles (Figure 5.1b).

Amino acid composition (AAC) is a direct feature that straightforwardly represents the entire physicochemical properties of enzymes by calculating the frequency of each amino acid sequence [21]. Due to its simplicity, it is widely used in the early stages of machine learning-based approaches [22–26]. For instance, AAC was used for training an enzyme function prediction model based on the k-nearest neighbor (kNN) algorithm [25]. Similarly, a support vector machine (SVM)-based model was designed to co-utilize AAC and physicochemical properties to classify enzyme functions [26]. However, AAC is insufficient to comprehensively reflect the detailed characteristics of a protein molecule.

To address this limitation, various physicochemical features derived from specific properties of each amino acid residue have been employed in enzyme function prediction [23, 24, 27–30]. Physicochemical properties are highly correlated with protein function, as they encompass critical information regarding molecular interactions and catalytic activity within the cellular environment. Several computational tools have been developed to extract and vectorize physicochemical properties from enzyme sequences based on statistical analysis. Representative examples are Pepstats, ProtParam, and PROFEAT [31–33]. Pepstats calculates molecular weight, isoelectric point, AAC, and the composition of aliphatic, aromatic, polar, nonpolar, charged, basic, and acidic residues [32]. ProtParam returns statistical values for negative and positive charge residues, and the count of each atom [31]. PROFEAT offers a comprehensive set of physicochemical features, including AAC, dipeptide composition, autocorrelation, and amino acid distribution patterns, calculating 1,447 descriptor values [33]. When integrated with machine learning models, these computed features are effective in classifying enzyme functions [28–30]. For example, ECPred leverages Pepstats to extract protein features, which are subsequently used to train an SVM for Enzyme Commission number (EC number) prediction [29]. However, both AAC and physicochemical features cannot provide the positional information of each amino acid in the enzyme sequence. The use of pseudo-amino acid composition (PseAAC), an extension of AAC that incorporates correlations between adjacent amino acids, has addressed this problem. Because physicochemical properties of amino acids were used for calculating these correlations, PseAAC can represent both physicochemical properties and local sequence order information of enzymes [34, 35].

Although direct features are straightforward to extract and interpret, relying solely on these features may be insufficient for accurately capturing the functional properties of enzymes. Derived features include nonintuitive information such as structural and evolutionary properties, in which additional preprocessing of amino acid sequences is necessary for extraction. For instance, the composition of structural and functional elements offers valuable insights into enzyme functionality, though additional computational processing is required and often complicated to extract from raw sequences. Secondary structure composition, which represents the local conformation of polypeptide backbones, can be extracted using computational tools such as STRIDE [36] and PSIPRED [37]. For example, secondary structure composition obtained from STRIDE is utilized to train SVM model to classify enzyme types, incorporating additional structural features (e.g. surface area, disulfide bonds, surface AAC) and physicochemical properties (e.g. AAC, cofactor types, metal ions) [27]. Functional domain composition quantifies the frequency of occurrence of specific domains within a protein sequence, utilizing information from protein domain databases such as Pfam and InterPro [38, 39]. Because functional domains are closely associated with the biological functions of proteins, this feature has been widely employed in enzyme function prediction [40–42]. For example, ECS is an SVM-based model trained on Pfam-based functional domain composition, successfully classifying protein sequences into six enzyme classes [40]. Each sequence was represented as a 2,657-dimensional binary vector corresponding to the presence or absence of functional domains from the Pfam database.

Evolutionary features, which were derived from conventional homology-based approaches, were also used to train machine learning models for accurate enzyme function prediction. For example, in ECPred, homology scores derived from a BLAST search were used to train the kNN module, predicting enzyme function based on the functional class of sequences that were highly scored [29]. Another example is EzyPred, in which PSSMs were used to provide detailed information related to evolutionarily conserved regions in protein sequences [43].

5.3.2 Machine Learning-Based Approaches Algorithms for Enzyme Function Prediction

Various machine learning algorithms process input data using distinct strategies. Therefore, selecting appropriate machine learning algorithms to effectively analyze the characteristics of given features is crucial. In enzyme function classification, the three most frequently used types of machine learning approaches are instance-based, boundary-based, and tree-based algorithms. Instance-based algorithms derive predictions directly from existing data without parameter optimization of explicit models. kNN is a representative example of this type, inferring the predominant enzyme functional class from the nearest neighbors within the corresponding feature space [44]. For instance, feature vectors derived from InterPro-based functional domain composition can be used to calculate the distance of each enzyme for kNN-based prediction [41]. In another example, feature vectors derived from PSSM were used to compute the distance of each protein sequence for predicting six enzyme classes of EC number (i.e. the first digit of EC numbers) with kNN [45]. Several advanced kNN algorithms have also been employed to better capture ambiguous relationships between biological features and labels. For instance, optimized evidence-theoretic kNN was used to consider the reliability of adjacent data affecting the decision-making process [43].

Instance-based approaches facilitate the straightforward identification of data points that significantly influence predictions. However, the need to store the full dataset and compute pairwise distances for each query leads to high computational costs, limiting its scalability for whole-genome scale analysis. Boundary-based approaches have addressed these limitations by defining specific regions in the feature space corresponding to each class [46]. SVM is a boundary-based algorithm that is most frequently used for enzyme functional classification [23, 24, 26, 27, 29, 30, 40]. For example, the classification of EC number and protein family was conducted with separate SVM models trained to identify each family, utilizing various physicochemical features extracted from protein sequences [23]. However, the effectiveness of both instance-based and boundary-based approaches is constrained by their sensitivity to feature distribution and the inherent challenges in interpreting their predictive outcomes. Tree-based approaches recursively split data according to well-defined criteria derived from feature attributes, enhancing the interpretability of predictions and offering robustness against variations in feature distribution [47]. However, relying on a single decision tree is prone to overfitting. Therefore, random forest [48], an ensemble tree-based method, was predominantly used for enzyme function prediction to improve generalization and predictive robustness [28, 42, 49, 50]. Multiple studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of random forest algorithms in the classification of enzyme functions. For example, PredictEFC, a random forest model for classification of seven EC classes trained on InterPro-based functional domain features, outperformed an SVM-based model on the same dataset [42]. EFPrf utilized random forests trained on CATH domain profiles derived from input protein sequences, exhibiting robust performance on proteins with low sequence identity relative to those in the training dataset. Analyzing feature importance scores facilitated the identification of specificity-determining residues that play a critical role in enzyme functionality, thereby improving the interpretability and reliability of predictions [50]. However, as the number of input features increases, tree-based approaches would become less effective in identifying important features, reducing their interpretability.

Since each machine learning approach has distinct advantages and limitations, integrating multiple algorithms could compensate for their respective shortcomings. Furthermore, it facilitates the systematic integration of diverse features into model prediction, further enhancing the performance of machine learning-based enzyme function prediction. For example, EFICAz2 employed a tree-based approach to integrate SVM with functionally discriminating residue detection modules, enabling the prediction of EC numbers using protein features derived from MSAs and the physicochemical properties of amino acids [51]. ECPred combined kNN and SVM-based modules to simultaneously utilize homology scores and physicochemical features of protein sequence, respectively [29].

The application of machine learning has enabled accurate enzyme function predictions even in cases with low sequence-function similarity, utilizing intrinsic properties of proteins. However, traditional machine learning models are typically designed to learn linear relationships or simple nonlinear patterns, making it challenging to capture the intricate and highly complex relationships inherent in biological data. The necessity of hand-crafted extraction of enzyme features is also a significant constraint in machine learning-based approaches. Although manually extracted features are based on an in-depth understanding of enzymology, they are often inefficient in reflecting the correlation between protein sequences and functions. Recent advancements in deep learning have addressed these limitations by enabling automatic feature learning, eliminating the need for manual feature extraction. Deep learning models facilitate inherently capturing hierarchical and complex relationships within biological data, leading to more accurate enzyme function predictions compared to traditional machine learning approaches.

5.4 Prediction of Enzyme Functions Using Deep Learning

Artificial neural networks (ANNs), developed by imitating the transmission of information between neurons via synapses in the human brain, serve as the fundamental algorithm underlying all deep neural networks [52]. For decades, ANNs have been employed to capture complex and nonlinear data patterns, enabling the analysis of nonlinear relationships between protein sequences and their functions [53, 54]. For instance, ANNs trained on sequence similarity to known domain groups can predict functional domain groups in input proteins, even for those with low sequence similarity, which was challenging for traditional BLAST searches [55]. Similarly, ProtFun was developed as an ensemble of ANNs to predict enzyme functional classes from various physicochemical properties, including hydrophobicity, number of charged residues, and secondary structures [56]. Although early use of ANNs was constrained to shallow network architectures due to limited computational capabilities, their emergence is highly significant as they form the foundation for all subsequent advanced deep neural networks.

In deep learning-based enzyme prediction models, EC numbers and GO terms are commonly used as target labels for model training. The EC number is one of the useful classification schemes for enzyme functions that assigns general functions of enzymes to specific digits [57]. The EC number consists of four digits separated by periods in a hierarchical system, with more detailed functional information toward the end of the EC number. The first digit is the enzyme class, assigned according to the primary reactions performed by the enzyme, classified as oxidoreductase (EC:1), transferase (EC:2), hydrolase (EC:3), lyase (EC:4), isomerase (EC:5), ligase (EC:6), and translocase (EC:7). The enzyme functions are further described by the second and third digits, known as subclass and sub-subclass, providing more detailed functional roles. The final digit indicates the type of substrates the enzyme reacts with. For example, EC:3.4.11.4 denotes a hydrolase that acts on peptide bonds, cleaving off the amino-terminal residue from polypeptides or proteins. Gene ontology (GO) terms, a gene functional classification system, also describe protein properties in terms of molecular function, cellular component, and biological process. Each category of GO terms represents molecular-level activities, cellular locations where these functions occur, and large-scale biological processes carried out by multiple molecular-level activities. By tagging multiple GO terms and linking them hierarchically, this system provides more detailed descriptions and complex relationships, structured as a directed acyclic graph.

With the breakthroughs in computing power, the development of novel neural network architectures, and the advent of big data, various deep neural network architectures have been developed to improve learning efficiency. Such neural networks have shown powerful performance in predicting enzyme functions. Basically, deep neural networks learn from amino acid sequences and/or features derived from sequences, identifying patterns inherent in an enzyme [1]. In this section, we discuss the recent advances in deep learning models used for predicting EC numbers and GO terms, focusing on their architecture for effectively processing enzyme data.

5.4.1 Convolutional Neural Network

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) were initially developed to learn patterns of image inputs by using channels and convolutional kernels, where kernels compress nearby pixels according to the kernel size [58]. These convolutional layers effectively capture local feature patterns through multiplication and summation between convolutional kernels and local regions of the input (Figure 5.2). These characteristics of CNNs can also be applied to learn local contexts of enzyme sequences, thereby enhancing performance in enzyme function prediction. By utilizing CNNs, various deep learning-based tools have been developed to predict EC numbers and/or GO terms [59–66]. A notable example is DeepEC, a model that predicts enzyme EC numbers using both CNN-based modules and a homology analysis module [63]. DeepEC operates in two steps: firstly, three CNN sub-modules predict whether the input sequence is an enzyme or not, the EC number up to the third digit, and the fourth digit in parallel. Then, if the EC numbers cannot be predicted consistently (i.e. the EC numbers predicted up to the third digit and the fourth digit are inconsistent), DeepEC assigns the EC number by employing homology analysis based on sequence similarity. Another example is ECPICK, which also utilizes three parallel convolutional layers alongside four hierarchical layers predicting each digit of the EC number, respectively [67]. The hierarchical layers perform two types of prediction: global prediction of all four digits at once from the last latent representation, and local prediction of each digit sequentially from the same level's latent representation. The final predicted probabilities are a weighted average of these two predictions.

Models for predicting GO terms as enzyme functions have also been developed using amino acid sequences with CNNs. For example, DeepGOPlus takes an amino acid sequence as input and embeds it into a one-hot encoded vector with dimensions of (21, 2000), representing the number of amino acid types and sequence length, respectively [65]. One-hot encoding simplifies information derived from the sequence without requiring complex calculations or learnable parameters in the embedding process. For input proteins longer than 2,000 amino acid residues, only the first 2,000 residues are retained, while shorter sequences are zero-padded in the one-hot encoded vectors. The one-hot encoded vector is then fed into 16 convolutional layers, followed by max-pooling layers and a fully connected layer, to predict the likelihood of each GO term. Convolutional layers are effective at extracting latent features from two-dimensional inputs like images due to their translational invariance, making them widely used in developing deep neural networks for GO term prediction from one-hot encoded vectors. Another model, ProteInfer, predicts both GO terms and EC numbers by employing dilated convolutional layers to identify a broader range of contexts with low computational cost and residual layers to ensure the stability of neural networks during training [66]. ProteInfer leverages these advantages to predict multi-label sequences (i.e. multifunctional enzymes) effectively.

5.4.2 Recurrent Neural Network

Unlike CNNs for capturing local patterns in images, recurrent neural networks (RNNs) were devised to process sequential data, such as natural language. RNNs read each token (e.g. words in natural language and amino acid residues in proteins) one at a time and retain information from previous tokens using internal memory. Inspired by the fact that, similar to natural language, the properties of proteins are predominantly specified by the order of amino acids, RNNs have been used to extract global contexts from protein sequences (Figure 5.3) [60, 64, 68–70]. For instance, DEEPre was developed by integrating CNNs with a subsequent long short-term memory (LSTM), a type of RNN [60]. DEEPre takes sequence-length-dependent features as input for CNNs to capture local contexts of enzyme sequences. The global representation is then derived from compressed convolutional features through LSTM. This global representation is concatenated with sequence-length-independent features to predict the EC number of the input sequence. DEEPre hierarchically predicts each digit of the EC number using a specifically trained submodel for each digit prediction. mlDEEPre, an extension of DEEPre, predicts multi-label enzymes by estimating the probability of all digits in EC numbers [61]. mlDEEPre performs a four-stage prediction: (1) determining if an input protein is an enzyme, (2) identifying enzyme promiscuity, (3) predicting the first digit of the EC number, and (4) predicting the full four-digit EC number.

RNNs are effective neural architectures for predicting not only EC numbers but also GO terms. For instance, UDSMProt, a model composed of LSTM that applies self-supervised pretraining, predicts both EC numbers and GO terms [68]. UDSMProt was first trained on an unlabeled protein sequence database, predicting next residue based on previous residues, allowing the model to learn general protein sequence contexts. Following such self-supervised pretraining, fully connected layers are added at the end of LSTM layers frozen with pretrained parameters and trained again on a labeled dataset to classify enzyme functions based on EC numbers and GO terms of the input sequences.

5.4.3 Transformer and Protein Language Models

While RNNs are valuable for processing sequential data, this architecture suffers from a fundamental drawback: initial information gradually fades as the sequence progresses through RNNs. However, the emergence of transformer architectures, designed to capture long-range dependencies between tokens in natural language, addresses this limitation by simultaneously identifying all relationships and influences among pairs of tokens [71]. Transformer architectures have also pushed the boundaries of protein science, drawing inspiration from the parallels between natural language and protein sequences. In proteins, transformer architectures are particularly effective for learning relationships between residues (Figure 5.4) [70, 72–81].

To utilize these strengths of transformer architectures with the tremendous amount of protein data deposited in various databases [82, 83], protein language models (pLMs) have emerged, mimicking BERT-like models pretrained with masked language modeling (Figure 5.1c) [84–96]. For example, ESM was constructed with 650 million parameters and trained on sequences in the UniRef50 database by applying masked language models to learn evolutionary relationships between residues (e.g. coevolution, contact, etc.) [85]. Recently, ESM has been updated to ESM3, which was trained on various aspects of proteins, such as sequence, structure, and other residue-level characteristics [96]. Another model, ProtT5, was designed as a pretrained pLM for downstream tasks, employing span masking to learn local contextual patterns by masking consecutive residue domains rather than single residues [87]. ProstT5, while maintaining the underlying architecture of ProtT5, incorporates structural information and supports bidirectional conversion (i.e. from structure to sequence features, or vice versa) using 3Di tokens, which encode structural characteristics of residues and facilitate sequence-structure transformations [95, 97]. Embeddings extracted from these pLMs serve as a robust foundation for downstream applications, effectively representing inherent patterns and characteristics. For instance, DeepECtransformer utilizes transformer layers and CNNs to predict EC numbers [72]. The transformer layers consist of two subsequent self-attention encoders from the ProtBERT model to embed the input amino acid sequences of enzymes into hidden representations [87]. The resulting hidden representation transformed through transformer layers is fed into two consecutive CNN layers, effectively learning local and global features of the input enzyme sequence. DIAMOND, a tool for a homology search algorithm, supplements DeepECtransformer in cases where neural networks fail to predict the EC number of an input enzyme, assigning EC numbers based on homologous enzymes [98]. Thanks to transformer layers, DeepECtransformer has demonstrated superior performance compared to previous EC number prediction tools.

The advent of transformer architectures and pLMs has also affected the prediction of GO terms as well as EC numbers. PFresGO, for instance, first uses protein sequences and GO term embeddings as inputs. The protein sequence is converted into two types of representations: features encoded from one-hot encoding of the input sequence and embeddings extracted from the encoder of the ProtT5 model [73, 87]. These representations are summed and fed into the multi-head cross-attention layer of a transformer along with GO term embeddings, learning which GO term is relatively more associated with each residue in the input sequence. Another example, PhiGnet, utilizes the ESM-1b model as the initial stage of neural networks to convert input enzyme sequences into hidden representations [85, 99]. The hidden representations are processed using two types of graph convolutional networks (GCNs): one captures evolutionary couplings representing relationships between pairwise residues at two covariant sites, and the other identifies residue communities as hierarchical interactions among residues. Based on these relationships (i.e. edges in the graph), corresponding features in the representations are updated and used to predict EC numbers and GO terms.

Similarly, protein structure information has been utilized for predicting GO terms, as a protein's three-dimensional structure often determines its roles in catalysis, molecular transport, and other functions. A recent study developed ESM-S, a pLM that incorporates structural information [81]. ESM-S builds upon ESM2, which was pretrained on sequence databases using masked language modeling (i.e. predicting masked tokens in a sequence) and further trained on a remote homology detection dataset to learn structural information. The learned representation from ESM-S has shown increased performance not only in GO term prediction but also in EC number prediction tasks, underscoring the importance of structural information for enzyme functional classification. PredGO combines representations learned from a pLM, protein-protein interaction networks, and three-dimensional structure information to predict GO terms, highlighting how exploiting heterogeneous data sources enhances the performance of GO term prediction [100]. To reflect structural information in predicting EC numbers, MAPred, a state-of-the-art model for EC number prediction, exploits ESM and ProstT5 as pretrained models to extract embeddings based on sequence and structure, respectively [80, 93, 95]. MAPred also employs cross-attention mechanisms to interlace sequence and 3Di representations for extracting global features, alongside convolutional layers using diverse kernel sizes for local feature extraction. Finally, MAPred concatenates global and local features, feeding them into multilayer perceptrons to predict digits of the EC number hierarchically.

Advances in machine learning training schemes have also transformed enzyme functional classification using deep learning. Supervised learning, a machine learning approach where a model is trained on labeled data to make predictions or classify new inputs, has been used for enzyme function prediction. However, the type of supervised model that predicts labels of the input itself has limitations when the sequence data used for training includes significant noise or the model encounters unseen labels during training. To complement this weakness, CLEAN was trained on EC numbers by using contrastive learning, which was devised to train the model to ensure that representations with the same EC number are more similar rather than focusing solely on inferring labels of the input itself [77]. This approach clusters enzymes with similar functional groups closely together in the latent space, while functionally distinct enzymes are spaced farther apart. Despite being composed entirely of simple neural networks, CLEAN has achieved superior performance.

5.4.4 Graph Neural Network

In line with the advancement in deep learning approaches, the development of AlphaFold and RoseTTAFold has pioneered protein structure prediction with high confidence, facilitating an exponential increase in the accumulation of protein structure data [101, 102]. With the increased accessibility of protein structure data, such as the AlphaFold DB, protein structure information has become instrumental in predicting EC numbers and GO terms, demonstrating significant potential [103]. Graph neural networks (GNNs) are well-suited deep learning architectures for processing protein structure data, capable of generating diverse, information-rich graphs based on how nodes (e.g. atoms or residues) and edges (e.g. spatial distance, sequential order, extrinsic/intrinsic distance, etc.) are defined (Figure 5.5) [92, 99, 100, 104–111]. For instance, GraphEC employs ProtTrans to extract protein embeddings and ESMFold to generate predicted three-dimensional protein structures from input sequences [87, 93, 111]. The nodes and edges are defined by residues and relationships between near residues, respectively. Using this GNN, the model predicts three types of outputs for the input enzyme: active sites, optimal pH, and EC number. For EC number prediction, the training of GraphEC-AS is preceded by the prediction of active sites of an input enzyme, whose trained parameters are used to emphasize which residues in the input sequence are more influential for EC number prediction. The hidden representation embedded by the GNN is compressed by using pooling based on weighted residues, predicting the EC number of the input enzyme. GraphEC also uses label diffusion to balance the prediction and labels derived from homologs of the input sequence. GraphEC has shown superior performance by utilizing evolutionary and structural information with suitable neural network architectures.

The increasing accessibility of three-dimensional protein structure data has also provided useful information for predicting GO terms. DeepFRI employs both sequence and structural information of enzymes to predict GO terms [106]. For this task, LSTMs are used to embed the sequence of an input enzyme, trained to predict the next amino acid based on preceding residues. Three-dimensional protein structures generate contact maps to identify spatially proximate residue pairs, forming protein graphs at the residue level based on these contact maps. GCN, a type of GNN, updates the features of each residue by reflecting features of neighboring residues using the representation from LSTMs and edges from the contact map. Combining sequence information with protein structure data enhances GO term classification for input enzymes, while also allowing for the interpretation and identification of residue-level contributions to GO term prediction. In another approach, TransFun employed protein structures predicted by AlphaFold2, which create adjacency matrices indicating neighboring residues of each residue in proteins [109]. Equivariant GNNs were used to predict GO terms, with node and edge features defined by embeddings from ESM-1b and relationships between neighboring residues.

With abundant protein three-dimensional structure data available, pretraining deep learning models on protein structures similar to protein sequences has been employed to explicitly capture spatial information crucial for protein function determination. GearNet, for example, a GNN pretrained on AlphaFoldDB, predicts EC numbers and GO terms [90, 94]. Unlike pretraining on sequence data using masked language modeling, pretraining on structural data is more complex. To address this challenge, GearNet employed multiview contrastive learning, an approach that distinguishes views (i.e. subsequence and substructure) of the same protein from those of different proteins, embedding biologically related substructures closely within the latent space. Although the pretraining dataset contained fewer than one million data points, much smaller than the millions to billions of protein sequences used for pLMs, GearNet showed high prediction performance in downstream tasks of EC number and GO term prediction, highlighting the potential of structure-based protein function analysis.

GNNs can also be utilized to learn information about protein-protein interaction networks, in which relationships between proteins serve as an important factor, as it is difficult to determine the role of a protein independently, such as in the context of GO terms. DeepGOGAT-SE was designed using a graph attention network, a type of GNN, to apply graph structure derived from protein-protein interaction, employing the ESM2 model to extract sequence-derived embeddings as inputs [78]. DeepGOGAT-SE achieved high performance in GO term classification by effectively integrating representations learned from ESM2 with functional contexts derived from protein-protein interaction networks.

5.5 Concluding Remarks

In this chapter, we introduce the enzyme functional classification with the development and progression of various prediction schemes using computational learning algorithms (Table 5.1). The conventional machine learning algorithms were initially used to predict enzyme functions utilizing computational resources. As various classification schemes are devised, such as kNN, SVM, and random forest, the machine learning-based models have become more reliable with protein-derived features as inputs, yet encountered limitations, including data quality, feature extraction, computational resources, and parametric constraints of traditional algorithms. To address these challenges, deep learning approaches have emerged alongside advances in computing devices such as graphics processing units, significantly expanding the field of computational biology. Thus, we discuss various types of deep neural networks initially designed for other fields but now applied to biology due to shared characteristics, such as spatial locality in images and the sequential nature of natural language.

Additionally, we review how deep neural networks have been used to classify enzyme functions in terms of well-defined classification nomenclature schemes – EC numbers and GO terms – illustrating deep learning-based models categorized by representative deep neural architectures. However, despite these numerous efforts, the fundamental limitation remains in predicting EC numbers and GO terms using deep learning, leading to constraints on predictive accuracy caused by data imbalance in underrepresented EC number and GO term classes. These challenges are unavoidable but must be addressed to achieve more robust and reliable predictions of enzyme functions in real-world applications. Moreover, with the growing availability of biological big data, trends in enzyme functional prediction using artificial intelligence have shifted toward integrating diverse biological resources and proteins. This approach has proven efficient for predicting various properties, including functions, of proteins at the omics levels [79]. Furthermore, by leveraging the characteristics of generative models such as the hallucination effect, enzyme engineering strategies are expanding their area into non-natural enzyme space, where engineered enzymes exhibit low sequence similarity to natural ones but retain the same or similar structural and functional properties [112–117]. These innovative changes are propelling biology into a new phase, accelerating the advancement of enzyme engineering through enzyme functional predictions.

6
Design of Biochemical Pathways via AI/ML-Enabled Retrobiosynthesis

Hongxiang Li

1University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, NSF Molecule Maker Lab Institute, Urbana, IL, 61801, USA
