8
Machine Learning Approaches for High-Throughput Microbial Identification/Culturing

Mohamed Mastouri

1Harbin Institute of Technology (Shenzhen), School of Biomedical Engineering, Taoyuan Street, Taoyuan, Guangdong, 518055, China
2Tianjin University, School of Pharmaceutical Science and Technology, No. 92, Weijin Road, Nankai District, Tianjin 300072, China
3Shenzhen Loop Area Institute, 1068 Xueyuan Avenue, Shenzhen University Town, Shenzhen, Guangdong, China

8.1 Introduction

Microbial identification and culturing are essential techniques in microbiology for understanding the diversity, structure, and function of microbial communities. Culturing involves growing microorganisms under controlled laboratory conditions, while identification aims to determine the taxonomic classification of these organisms [1, 2]. The importance of these methods lies in their ability to reveal previously unknown microorganisms and provide insights into their ecological roles. For instance, culturomics has enabled the cultivation of hundreds of new microorganisms associated with humans, offering new perspectives on host-bacteria relationships [1, 2]. Similarly, coupling traditional cultivation with advanced sequencing techniques has revealed that some cultured soil bacteria were rare or absent in culture-independent community analyses, demonstrating unexpected accessibility to the rare biosphere [2]. However, it's crucial to note that traditional culturing methods have limitations. Only a small fraction (0.1–1%) of microorganisms in natural ecosystems can be cultured under standard laboratory conditions [3, 4]. This has led to the development of culture-independent approaches like metagenomics and single-cell genomics, which allow for the analysis of uncultured microorganisms and provide a more comprehensive understanding of microbial diversity and ecology [5].

Traditional methods for microbial identification have long relied on culture-based and biochemical techniques. These approaches involve isolating microorganisms in culture media, followed by enzymatic reactions and morphological analyses [6]. While these methods remain the core basis and standard practice in most laboratories, they are known to be time-consuming, labor-intensive, and may not detect all microorganisms present in a sample. Interestingly, molecular techniques have revolutionized microbial identification, offering faster and more accurate results. Methods such as 16S ribosomal RNA gene sequencing based on polymerase chain reaction (PCR) have become increasingly popular for comprehensive bacterial studies. Other molecular approaches include fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH), denaturing gradient gel electrophoresis (DGGE), and terminal-restriction fragment length polymorphism (T-RFLP) [7]. While traditional culture-based and biochemical methods remain important, especially for antibiotic sensitivity testing [8], molecular techniques have significantly enhanced our ability to identify and study microorganisms. These newer methods offer advantages such as higher sensitivity, specificity, and the ability to detect unculturable microorganisms. However, it's important to note that each method has its own strengths and limitations, and the choice of technique should be based on the specific research objectives and sample types [7].

Traditional approaches in various fields face significant challenges that limit their effectiveness and efficiency. In microbial diagnostics, conventional methods struggle with sample handling, culture difficulties, misidentification, and delays in determining susceptibility [9]. These limitations can lead to inaccurate or delayed diagnoses, potentially impacting patient care.

High-throughput (HTP) techniques have revolutionized microbiology by enabling rapid and comprehensive analysis of microbial genomes, transcriptomes, and communities. These techniques, particularly high-throughput sequencing (HTS), have significantly advanced our understanding of microbial diversity, function, and interactions in various environments, including food systems [10, 11]. HTS technologies allow researchers to generate vast amounts of genetic data at an unprecedented pace, facilitating genome-wide analysis and the elucidation of molecular mechanisms in biological systems [12]. Interestingly, HTP techniques have found applications beyond traditional microbiology. In food microbiology, HTS has been used to predict the prevalence of microorganisms in food samples, study microbial responses to food-associated conditions, and develop genome-assisted approaches for correlating genotype and phenotype. Moreover, the combination of single-cell genomics and metagenomics has improved the efficiency and accuracy of obtaining whole genome information from complex microbial communities, enabling researchers to link function to species and study host-virus interactions. HTP techniques, particularly HTS, have become indispensable tools in microbiology, offering unprecedented insights into microbial communities and their functions. These technologies have applications in food safety, optimization of food fermentations, understanding probiotic mechanisms, and investigating the effects of ingested microbes on the human gut microbiota [13]. As sequencing and computational methods continue to advance, the role of HTP techniques in microbiology is expected to expand further, providing deeper insights into microbial ecosystems and their interactions with the environment and human health.

ML and artificial intelligence (AI) are revolutionizing the field of microbiology, offering powerful tools for data analysis, prediction, and decision-making. These technologies are being applied to various aspects of microbiology, including clinical diagnostics, AMR detection, and laboratory automation [14]. In clinical microbiology, ML algorithms are being used to reduce diagnostic workload through laboratory automation, detect and identify clinically relevant microorganisms, and detect AMR [14]. These applications have the potential to significantly improve the efficiency and accuracy of microbiological analyses. For instance, AI-based systems can analyze digital data from medical imaging and diagnostic techniques in a comprehensive, rapid, and noninvasive manner, offering unprecedented insights into diseases [15]. However, it's important to note that despite the promising potential of ML and AI in microbiology, their integration into routine clinical laboratory practice is still limited.

This chapter explores the synergy of MI with various HTP platforms such as genomic and metagenomic sequencing, mass spectrometry (MS), flow cytometry (FCM), and imaging technologies. The integrated strategies enable precise microbial species identification, AMR prediction, and phenotypic characterization on an unprecedented scale. Moreover, ML models are being applied for automated strain selection, process optimization in bioreactors, and even synthetic biology applications like CRISPR-based genome editing. We also revisit the fundamental ideas of ML, compare different paradigms of learning (supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement), and briefly mention their application to microbial research. Issues like standardization of data, model interpretability, and computational overheads are critically analyzed. Finally, we also hint at directions ahead, such as the potential of multi-omics integration, eXplainable AI (XAI), and newer technologies like quantum computing and federated learning for advancing microbial research and diagnostics. This chapter will attempt to give an in-depth overview of how ML is revolutionizing HTP microbial research, providing both seminal context and current examples to inform future scientific inquiry.

8.2 High-Throughput (HTP) Techniques in Microbial Research

8.2.1 Definition and Scope of HTP Microbial Techniques

HTP microbial technology refers to cutting-edge strategies and platforms for efficient, rapid, and large-scale processing or analysis of microbial samples. HTP technology has applications in many areas, including genomics, biofuel generation, and environmental monitoring. In microbial genomics, HTP sequencing generates huge levels of high-quality sequence data, allowing for rapid accumulation of evidence and robust identification of microbial-related evidence in forensic science [16]. This technology has highly improved the rate and accuracy of microbial analysis and identification, crucial in solving bio-crimes and responding to bio-terrorism attacks. HTP technologies have also found application in microbial fuel cells, where microbial metabolism is utilized in biofuel production, energy, and bioremediation [17]. These systems interest various disciplines and offer scope for sustainable applications in various environments. In the production of recombinant proteins, HTP screening techniques have been developed for increased efficiency at initial process design. For instance, the BioLector micro-bioreactor platform has been used as an HTP cultivation system to screen E. coli expression clones with high transferability of results to large-scale bioreactor systems [18]. This approach largely obviates the need for experiments in fully controlled bioreactors, accelerating process development at lower costs. HTP technology has also been applied to produce membrane proteins, which have been considered in the past a formidable challenge. A parallel HTP approach to cloning and expression screening of membrane proteins has shown unexpectedly high success rates, with 71% of E. coli integral membrane proteins that are expressed at the levels needed for purification [19]. HTP approaches have revolutionized microbial research, delivering novel and powerful systems for rapid analysis of microorganisms and microbial interactions. These approaches have also been applied to all areas of microbiology, from food microbiology to environmental microbiology and clinical diagnostics [10, 20, 21]. HTP sequencing has been utilized for microbial communities and metagenome studies with insights into microbial diversity and functionality [20, 22]. Even as microbial research became overrun with HTP sequencing, there are other HTP approaches which have emerged as powerful tools. For instance, MALDI-TOF MS bio-typing has been promising in the rapid identification of microbes, particularly in medical settings [23]. Droplet microfluidics has also opened new avenues for HTP microbial culture and analysis with the ability to explore single-cell heterogeneity and microbial interactions [18, 24]. HTP methodologies have immensely facilitated us in exploring microbial systems and their applications. From sequencing-based approaches to novel cultivation methods, these approaches are transforming various fields of microbiology. As technology continues to evolve, we can expect new advances in HTP approaches, which may open the door to more comprehensive and efficient microbial research strategies (Figure 8.1) [22].

8.2.2 Metagenomics and Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS)

Metagenomics, the analysis of DNA from microbial communities in environmental samples without prior culturing, has been revolutionized by advances in Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS) technologies [25]. NGS enables rapid analysis of microbial community composition and diversity in various habitats, providing HTP sequencing of millions of DNA fragments simultaneously [26, 27].

Interestingly, NGS has expanded beyond traditional genomics to include metagenomics, allowing for the detection of unexpectedly disease-associated viruses and the discovery of novel human viruses, including cancer-related viruses [28]. Moreover, NGS has facilitated the exploration of the human virome in both healthy and disease conditions through metagenomics-based strategies [28].

NGS has significantly impacted metagenomics research, offering comprehensive insights into microbial diversity, community structure, and functional activities [29]. This technology has been applied across various fields, including clinical microbiology, public health, food and agriculture, energy, and environment [30]. As NGS continues to evolve, it promises to further enhance our understanding of microbial-host interactions and provide valuable insights into the complex world of microorganisms [26, 27].

8.2.3 Mass Spectrometry-Based Proteomics (MALDI-TOF MS)

Matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time of flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS) is a groundbreaking technology used in clinical microbiology that identifies microorganisms immediately and accurately. MALDI-TOF MS is more convenient, quicker, and more precise than conventional biochemical tests [31, 32]. This technology allows for the direct identification of bacterial species from newly grown colonies in minutes, a decrease of approximately one day in microbial identification time in typical workflows [32, 33].

While initially designed for bacterial identification, follow-up studies have witnessed the use of MALDI-TOF MS being expanded to cover the identification of yeasts, molds, and mycobacteria [34]. Besides, the technique is explored for various other leading-edge applications such as strain typing, antibiotic resistance detection, and antifungal susceptibility [34, 35]. Despite its multiple uses, one of the limitations of MALDI-TOF MS is analyzing small molecular compounds. To overcome the limitation, newer nanomaterial-based matrices have been developed that have enhanced the sensitivity and accuracy of the technique to analyze these compounds [36].

With its ever-wider variety of applications, MALDI-TOF MS has emerged as an asset in clinical microbiology, which could be used to improve patient outcomes by facilitating the speed of diagnoses and reducing hospital stays [32, 37]. With its ongoing innovation in application, the technique is poised to continue developing microbial diagnostics even further and further.

8.2.4 Flow Cytometry

FCM is a high-sensitivity technology widely used for HTP sorting and single-cell analysis of cells, based on their physical and biochemical properties. It combines microfluidics, optics, and data collection to provide quantitative data about populations of cells [38]. This technology offers the provision for the simultaneous measurement of various parameters such as cell size, shape, complexity, and fluorescence to obtain accurate characterization and separation of well-defined subsets of cells [38].

High-end systems with enhanced capability have been a product of recent FCM advancements. For example, imaging flow cytometry (IFC) combines digital microscopy and traditional FCM to enable high-content cellular function and morphology analysis [39]. Moreover, breakthroughs in all-silica fiber microflow cytometers have enabled portable HTP devices with the same performance as commercial hardware [40]. Furthermore, label-free techniques, such as Raman FCM, are utilized to study the chemical composition of living cells without fluorescent tagging [39].

In short, FCM continues to advance, with advancements in microfluidic technologies being one of the driving factors behind this [41]. Such advancements have remarkably widened the scope of application of FCM in fields ranging from biomedical research to clinical diagnostics and drug development. With advancing technological progress, we can anticipate increasingly higher resolution, sensitivity, and throughput, hence converting FCM into a valuable resource for sorting and analyzing individual cells.

8.2.5 Microfluidics and Lab-on-a-Chip Systems

Microfluidics and Lab-on-a-Chip (LOC) devices have transformed healthcare diagnostics and analytical laboratory methods by miniaturizing, integrating, and automating complex processes on a single chip, thus enabling precise manipulation of extremely small fluid volumes typically in the order of 10−9 to 10−18 L via microchannels of 10 to 100 μm [42]. This development has immensely expanded the applications of LOC devices in many biomedical fields, such as integrated bioassays, cell analysis, metabolomics, drug discovery, and personalized medicine [43]. Such developments have the potential to revolutionize diagnostic activities through more efficient, portable, and cost-effective means compared to traditional laboratory techniques.

However, while microfluidic systems have developed significantly from an engineering point of view, the development of chromatographic separation systems has stalled in the last few years. Initially, the tremendous promises of microfluidics for chromatographic use created high enthusiasm, but the challenges of miniaturizing the systems effectively, particularly in terms of reproducibility, sensitivity, and interfacing to other analytical techniques, have kept them from becoming generally established [44].

One such potential development to break through these constraints is the integration of electrowetting-on-dielectric (EWOD) actuators with other microfluidic manipulation techniques. The integration has been observed to hold potential in elevating the capability of digital microfluidics (DMF) for sophisticated biomedical assays, enabling more precise regulation of fluid manipulation and the development of more complex and multifunctional LOC devices [45]. Despite such advances, the integration of various operational steps within a microfluidic system, fluidic handling, molecular recognition, and signal amplification remains a key limitation for achieving complete, functional, and robust point-of-care diagnostic devices [46].

While the promise of microfluidics and LOC systems to transform point-of-care diagnostics, environmental monitoring, and drug discovery remains enormous, the translation from prototype to complete and ruggedized systems requires additional advances in engineering, materials science, and biological integration. The mastery of the remaining technical challenges, particularly in system integration and reproducibility, will hold the answer to unlocking the full potential of such systems for biomedical research and healthcare diagnostics [46]. The technologies are highly promising, yet their more extensive adoption will depend on overcoming the complexities of integrating multiple components into streamlined, functional platforms.

8.2.6 High-Content Imaging and Phenotyping

High-content imaging and phenotyping have greatly enhanced plant and cell biology research by enabling large-scale, automated screening of complex biological systems. The techniques combine sophisticated microscopy with sophisticated image analysis algorithms to extract quantitative information on several cellular or organismal features automatically at the same time [47]. In plant biology, HTP phenotyping facilities that utilize various imaging modalities have been set up to nondestructively measure growth-related characters, stress response, and crop performance, which deliver information previously challenging to acquire with traditional methods [48]. Since phenotype screening experiments began earlier on with model Arabidopsis, it has gradually begun shifting toward establishing approaches for high-content imaging technologies for economically important crops such as sorghum to extend the platform for high-content imaging within agrarian research [48].

The integration of multiple imaging techniques like visible light, thermal imaging, chlorophyll fluorescence, and hyperspectral imaging has boosted the potential for completely phenotyping morphological and physiological traits and biochemical responses in horticultural plants [49]. The holistic approach enables researchers to realize plant performance, hence making crop improvement methods more accurate. At the same time, in the field of cell biology, high-content screening has become an extremely powerful tool to profile drug action, investigate gene function, and investigate cellular response to various perturbations at single-cell resolution [50]. One of the key contributors to success with high-content imaging is the development of advanced image analysis pipelines and MI approaches, which have played an essential role in extracting useful biological information from the large datasets generated by these technologies [51].

These computational tools allow researchers to quantify complex phenotypes, detect nuanced treatment effects, and uncover hidden biological mechanisms. With advances in the field, the integration of high-content imaging with other omics technologies, as well as the development of standardized data repositories, holds enormous potential to further propel biological discovery and crop breeding. While these advances are full of promise, innovation in computational technologies and data integration will be needed to fully realize the potential of high-content imaging for plant biology at both the basic and applied levels.

8.3 Fundamentals of Machine Learning

8.3.1 Definition of Machine Learning and AI

ML is a branch of AI that enables computers to make conclusions and improve performance based on learning from experience, without explicit programming for specific tasks [52]. AI, however, describes the overall concept of machines performing tasks typically associated with human intelligence, such as reasoning, solving problems, and decision-making [52, 53].

While ML is widely regarded as a subfield of AI, some researchers differentiate ML as a narrow AI, focusing on its ability to learn through data and prediction, in contrast to AI, which encompasses various types of machine intelligence [53]. This differentiation emphasizes the specificity of ML in its application, where the goal is to design algorithms and statistical models that enable machines to improve task performance through experience, data patterns, and learning.

AI, as a general discipline, aims to create intelligent systems that can mimic the cognitive abilities of humans. On the other hand, ML specifically targets algorithm development to enhance machine performance through learning from data and is hence an integral component of AI success. Both AI and ML hold tremendous potential across a wide array of applications in medicine, optics, photonics, and industry by automating complex decision-making, function optimization, and enhanced prediction accuracy [52–55]. These technologies are transforming industries by enabling more efficient and accurate analysis, with the potential to deliver improvements in diagnostics, manufacturing, and other fields.

8.3.2 Supervised vs. Unsupervised vs. Reinforcement Learning

ML is a branch of AI which allows computers to make inferences and enhance performance through learning from data without direct programming for the purpose [52]. AI is the more extensive idea of machines executing tasks conventionally related to human intelligence like reasoning, problem-solving, and decision-making [52, 53].

While ML is commonly viewed as a subfield of AI, other scholars differentiate ML as a type of narrow AI, highlighting its specialization in data-driven learning and predictive function, in contrast to the general scope of AI, which encompasses other types of machine intelligence [53]. This distinction emphasizes the uniqueness of ML in its application, where the goal is to develop algorithms and statistical models that facilitate machines to improve task fulfilment through experience, data patterns, and inferences.

AI, in the widest sense, focuses on creating smart systems that can mimic human intellectual functions. On the other hand, supervised, unsupervised, and RL are three different ML methodologies based on their strategy and area of application.

Supervised learning (Figure 8.2a) is the training of a model on labeled data, for which input features and corresponding output labels are provided [56]. The algorithm is trained to map input values to target outputs, most typically for classification or regression issues. For example, in classification, the model is trained to make an estimate of a function that maps input vectors to previously given classes based on labeled examples [56]. Supervised learning works best when there is an abundance of high-quality labeled data available, where the algorithm can adequately predict or classify. However, the significant limitation here is the acquisition cost and time of labeled data, which might be prohibitively costly in most actual applications.

Unsupervised learning (Figure 8.2b), conversely, processes unlabeled data with the aim of identifying inherent patterns or organization without target output labels [56]. This approach is particularly handy when having labeled data is difficult or scarce because it allows discovering the patterns that are implicit in the data. Perhaps the greatest difficulty with unsupervised learning is discovering and analyzing these underlying structures within the data [57]. Unsupervised learning tends to utilize methods like clustering and dimensionality reduction. For example, unsupervised feature learning can be used to learn discriminative features from high-dimensional data, for example, in hyperspectral image analysis, where the goal is to reduce data complexity without losing useful information [58].

Though supervised and unsupervised learning are the most developed paradigms, RL is another important one not covered in this book. RL concerns training models by interacting with an environment, where the algorithm gets feedback (reward or penalty) for actions taken, rather than employing labeled data. The paradigm is best applied to decision-making issues in dynamic and uncertain environments.

ML framework-supervised learning, unsupervised learning, and RL have their own strengths and are optimal for a particular kind of problem. Supervised learning shines when labeled data exists, allowing for very accurate models for classification and regression tasks. Unsupervised learning, on the other hand, is used particularly when it is used to reveal hidden patterns or structures in unlabeled data and is thus particularly well-suited for clustering and dimensionality reduction. RL is distinct from the others in that it focuses on decision making in changing circumstances where an agent learns by interacting with its environment and receiving rewards or penalties accordingly. It is particularly useful for sequential decision-making problems [56].

ML contributes directly to the success of AI through the development of algorithms that optimize performance through data-driven learning. Both AI and ML have immense potential in many fields like healthcare, optics, photonics, and industry because they can be employed to automate complex decision-making processes, optimize performance, and increase predictive capability [55]. Both are transforming industries because they enable more analyses that lead to diagnostics, manufacturing, and other category breakthroughs.

RL differs from supervised and unsupervised learning in that it focuses on learning optimal actions based on feedback from the environment [56]. Here, an agent learns to maximize the cumulative sum of rewards by trial and error, and it has had success in, for example, video summarization [59].

There are also hybrid approaches that embed elements of such learning paradigms. Semi-supervised learning, for example, makes use of both unlabeled and labeled samples to improve the performance of a model, and is thus practical when there isn't much labeled data but an abundance of unlabeled data. Techniques such as self-training, co-training, and deep learning (DL)-based methods are generally applied to semi-supervised learning [60].

While each learning paradigm has its merits, they each have demerits too. Supervised learning can be quite demanding when it requires large amounts of labeled data, unsupervised learning does not necessarily translate to tangible task objectives, and RL is challenging to implement in intricate environments. Emerging breakthroughs in hybrid approaches have reported encouraging outcomes. For instance, contrastive learning methods have bridged the gap between unsupervised and supervised learning in computer vision applications [61]. The use of unsupervised feature learning within supervised tasks has also been seen to improve performance, particularly where there is a lack of sufficient labeled data [58].

Lastly, choosing an adequate ML paradigm is contingent on the problem one is facing, the existence of labeled data, and the objectives of the task. As more research continues, new techniques and hybrid approaches are being developed, broadening the field of ML to meet the demands of diverse areas.

8.3.3 ML Algorithms Commonly Used in Microbial Identification

ML algorithms have become increasingly important in microbial identification and classification. Several commonly used ML algorithms have shown promising results in this field. Decision Trees and Random Forests (RFs) are popular choices for microbial identification. Decision Trees create a flowchart-like structure to classify samples based on features, while RFs combine multiple decision trees to improve accuracy and reduce overfitting. These algorithms are particularly useful for handling complex datasets with many features [63]. SVMs have demonstrated high performance in microbial classification tasks. SVMs work by finding the optimal hyperplane to separate different classes in high-dimensional space. They are effective in handling both linear and nonlinear relationships in the data [64]. K-nearest neighbors (KNN) is another widely used algorithm in microbial identification. It classifies samples based on the majority class of their KNN in the feature space. KNN has shown good results in various studies, particularly when dealing with smaller datasets [64]. Neural Networks and DL approaches have gained significant attention in recent years. These methods can automatically learn complex patterns from large datasets, making them suitable for analyzing high-dimensional microbial data. DL models have shown remarkable performance in image-based microbial identification tasks [63, 64]. Feature selection and dimensionality reduction techniques play a crucial role in improving the performance of ML models for microbial identification. These methods help identify the most relevant features and reduce the complexity of the dataset, leading to more efficient and accurate models. Techniques such as Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and recursive feature elimination are commonly employed [65]. The role of big data in microbial ML applications cannot be overstated. With the increasing availability of large-scale genomic and metagenomic datasets, ML algorithms can leverage this wealth of information to improve their predictive capabilities. Big data approaches enable the discovery of novel patterns and relationships in microbial communities that may not be apparent through traditional analysis methods [64]. Model validation and performance metrics are essential for assessing the reliability and effectiveness of ML models in microbial identification. Common metrics include accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. Accuracy measures the overall correctness of predictions, while precision and recall focus on the model's ability to correctly identify positive cases. The F1-score provides a balanced measure of precision and recall. Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curves and Area Under the Curve (AUC) are valuable tools for evaluating the performance of binary classification models. They illustrate the trade-off between true positive rate and false positive rate across different classification thresholds [64]. It's important to note that the performance of ML algorithms can vary depending on the specific microbial identification task and the nature of the dataset. For instance, in a study on cervical cancer prediction, RF, Decision Tree, Adaptive Boosting, and Gradient Boosting algorithms achieved 100% accuracy, while SVM reached 99% accuracy [63]. In another study on brain tumor classification, KNN and Neural Networks outperformed other models with accuracies of 98.5% and 98.4%, respectively [64]. The choice of data scaling methods can also significantly impact model performance. For example, in a heart disease diagnosis study, the CART algorithm combined with Robust Scaler or Quantile Transformer outperformed other combinations, achieving 100% accuracy.

8.4 Machine Learning Approaches for High-Throughput Microbial Identification

ML techniques are increasingly applied to search through intricate datasets of diverse provenances, including genomic information, microbiota information, microscopy images, and spectroscopy information [66]. The objectives of these techniques are to improve the accuracy and speed of microbial identification, which transcends traditional techniques.

Some of the algorithms applied by ML to identify microbes are SVMs, Artificial Neural Networks (ANN), RF, and logistic regression [67, 68]. The algorithms work efficiently to manage large volumes of data and determine complex patterns that are difficult to detect by human experts [69]. For instance, in MALDI-TOF MS analysis, ML methods have been employed to enable improved identification of species and improved determination of AMR [69].

Surprisingly, while more sophisticated models like RF may offer improved performance under certain circumstances, even extremely simple models like L2-regularized logistic regression can offer comparable performance in most cases. The advantage of simpler models is that they can be learned quickly and are easier to explain, which is particularly valuable where such transparency considerations and computational speed are of crucial importance [68]. This then gives rise to the need to select an appropriate ML model depending on the specific research objectives, making compromises on the model's complexity, its accuracy, and interpretability.

In general, ML is revolutionizing microbial identification by offering the possibility to process complex microbial data quickly and precisely. Sufficient attention should be paid to the trade-offs between model complexity, computational power, and interpretability, though, to ensure that the chosen ML approach aligns with the research study or clinical practice goal.

8.4.1 Genomic and Metagenomic Data Processing

Metagenomic and genomic data analysis have become more and more important in microbial ecology and environmental science. Sequence alignment and feature detection are central activities involved in the interpretation of such intricate datasets, and ML tools have emerged as powerful methods for species identification and classification for metagenomic samples.

Sequence alignment is most often the first step when working with metagenomic data. Traditional methods, such as 16S rRNA gene amplicon (AMP) sequencing, are popular but can be subject to amplification bias and only look at a restricted genomic range. To break through such restraints, shotgun metagenomic sequencing has been the preferred choice, with an extended view of microbial communities. This is at a greater expense and is computationally more demanding [70].

Feature extraction from metagenomic data is necessary for downstream analysis. A new approach is the Operational Genomic Unit (OGU) method, which uses sequence alignment hits to individual reference genomes as the minimal unit to quantify microbial community diversity [71]. This method provides high-resolution community composition information and frames features into a phylogenomic tree hierarchy, in which phylogeny-aware tools not ordinarily applied to shotgun metagenomics can be utilized [71].

ML use in species recognition has revolutionized metagenomic data analysis. Various ML approaches, including SVMs, decision trees, RF, neural networks (NN), and deep learning (DL), are used to classify, regress, or cluster complex metabolomic data [72]. The methods have shown great potential in improving disease modeling and diagnosis through metabolomic profiling [72]. DL has been particularly successful in 16S rRNA classification. For example, DL-TODA, a program based on a convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture, has been demonstrated to classify metagenomic reads with high accuracy without the need to construct a reference database [73]. On synthetic data simulated with 2,454 genomes from 639 species, DL-TODA achieved over 0.98 classification accuracy, ranks above the genus level and 0.97 at the species level, outperforming state-of-the-art tools like Kraken2 and Centrifuge.

Another new solution for 16S rRNA classification is RiboDetector, a software package that utilizes a bidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTM) neural network [74]. RiboDetector rapidly and precisely identifies rRNA reads from various types of sequence data, including transcriptomic, metagenomic, and metatranscriptomic datasets. It showed superior performance to existing methods, with fewer misclassifications and great generalizability for identifying novel rRNA sequences [74].

An interesting case study of ML-based metagenomic species profiling is DeepVirFinder, a reference-free and alignment-free method for viral sequence identification from metagenomic data [75]. DeepVirFinder was trained using viral RefSeq sequences and evaluated using recently discovered sequences, and was shown to be better than the existing tools with varying contig lengths. In application to human gut metagenomic samples, it identified over 50,000 viral sequences from colorectal carcinoma patients and suggested possible viral presence vs cancer status correlations [75].

Wang et al. constructed a novel ML framework in a 2015 paper titled MetaBoot, whose goal was to facilitate the discovery of nonredundant taxonomical biomarkers in metagenomic data. MetaBoot integrates the minimum Redundancy Maximum Relevance (mRMR) method with bootstrapping resampling to enhance robustness, accuracy, and biological relevance of biomarker selection. The system works through data normalization, initial feature selection, repeated bootstrapping for redundancy and noise reduction, and final ranking based on the frequency of selection of biomarkers. MetaBoot was compared with synthetic data of varying statistical distributions (normal, gamma, and mixed) and with actual oral and soil microbiome datasets. MetaBoot, compared to traditional methods like LEfSe, Metastats, and Wilcoxon tests, performed superiorly in detection of biologically relevant and nonredundant biomarkers with enhanced classification accuracy. The study is called MetaBoot as a reliable platform for biomarker discovery in taxonomical applications, with significant application in microbial community profiling, environmental monitoring, and clinical diagnosis [76].

During their review, Fiannaca et al. [77] highlight the growing significance of ML, particularly DL architectures, in achieving accurate bacterial taxonomic assignment within metagenomic studies. They note that traditional approaches, alignment-based methods, and the widely used RDP classifier pose challenges in terms of computational costs and reduced accuracy, especially in handling short-read sequences from NGS data. To address these constraints, the authors suggested and tested two DL models, CNNs and deep belief networks (DBNs), in combination with k-mer-based sequence representation. Their models surpassed, particularly in handling AMP sequencing data, with more than 91% accuracy at the genus level, surpassing the 83.8% of the RDP classifier.

ML, more so DL, plays a critical role in tackling sequence noise, hypervariable regions of the 16S rRNA gene, and the vast quantities of metagenomic data. This study points out that DL offers a precise and scalable solution for the detection of bacteria, paving the way for its use in diagnostic devices, environmental sampling, and microbiome research, where precise microbial community profiling is critical [77]. The study introduces ANNA16 (Figure 8.3), a novel DL-based estimator of the 16S rRNA gene copy number (GCN) from DNA sequence, addressing a significant gap in 16S rRNA-based microbial community profiling. Bacteria and archaea possess variable 16S GCN between 1 and 21, and traditional read count-based methods are prone to biasing correct cell abundances in microbial communities. Existing methods, by being taxonomy- or phylogeny-based, are constrained by database heterogeneity, high computational complexity, and reduced accuracy.

ANNA16 outvies all these constraints by utilizing a Stacked Ensemble Model (SEM), combining multilayer perceptron (MLP) and SVM architectures. The algorithm was trained against over 19,000 full-length 16S rRNA gene sequences of the rrnDB database. By 6-mer representation-based prediction, ANNA16 enables direct regression-based prediction of 16S GCN without phylogenetic placement. Performance comparison suggests that ANNA16 performs much better than the traditional tools, such as rrnDB, CopyRighter, PAPRICA, and PICRUSt2 for both full-length sequences and universally amplified hypervariable regions (V1–V9). The model performed best in root mean squared error (RMSE), suggesting that it possesses the best accuracy and generalizability.

Additionally, by applying SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) analysis, the authors demonstrate that ANNA16 can identify very informative sequence positions, such as noncanonical conserved positions that are normally overlooked by traditional methods. The observation suggests that DL algorithms like ANNA16 can detect subtle evolutionary signals beyond the established hypervariable sites. The paper also describes potential future improvements, such as the implementation of transfer learning and addressing data imbalance for species with very high GCN values.

In short, ANNA16 illustrates the power of DL in microbiome research by providing a scalable, accurate, and interpretable program for resolving 16S rRNA GCN biases. The program plays a key role in quantitative microbiome profiling in clinical diagnostics, environmental studies, and microbial ecology [78].

8.4.2 Mass Spectrometry-Based Identification

MALDI-TOF MS has transformed microbial identification in clinical microbiology laboratories by offering ease, speed, accuracy, and affordability compared to traditional biochemical methods [32, 75]. Technology can gain around a day in everyday practice for microbial identification, and it has become an essential clinical microbiology tool [32]. The MALDI-TOF MS method is based on whole-cell fingerprinting, in conjunction with dedicated bioinformatic software programs for spectral analysis and identification [79]. ML algorithms, and particularly those integrated into the MALDI Biotyper software, are what enable processing of spectral data and matching with reference databases for accurate identification [79].

A case study in clinical microbiology demonstrated that MALDI-TOF MS was very accurate in the identification of staphylococcal strains, with 99.3% of isolates correctly identified to the species level [79]. This technology has also shown great promise in the identification of other medically relevant microorganisms, including mycobacterial species, yeasts, and a variety of pathogens [34]. Additionally, MALDI-TOF MS is also promising for application in AMR detection and strain typing, with utility in epidemiological investigations [80]. Despite its rapid development, there are still challenges in optimizing sample preparation, expanding reference databases, and refining identification algorithms for certain microbial taxa [81]. Resolving these challenges will be instrumental to the further evolution of MALDI-TOF MS in clinical diagnostics.

Systematic review by Weis et al. [69] considers the integration of ML techniques with MALDI-TOF MS for microbe identification and antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST). In reviewing 36 studies, the review details the most common ML algorithms employed, i.e. SVM, Genetic Algorithms (GA), ANN, and RFs. These techniques significantly enhance discrimination among species, particularly among closely related microbes such as Staphylococcus, Streptococcus, and Klebsiella, and facilitate proper prediction of AMR, e.g. methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and vancomycin-intermediate strains.

Despite these results, the review reports several important limitations: small sample sizes, limited external validation (a paltry 11% of studies), and poor reproducibility due to dependence on commercial software and lack of open data or shared code. The authors propose collaborative steps to generate publicly available datasets with resistance profiles, adopt transparent ML workflows, and incorporate external validation to improve clinical utility of such methods.

This study underscores the potential of ML-augmented MALDI-TOF MS to further speed up fast microbial diagnosis but points to the need for standardization and reproducibility to gain broader clinical approval [69]. The research by De Bruyne et al. [14] created a benchmark protocol for the identification of bacterial species using the method of MALDI-TOF MS followed by data processing and ML algorithms. The researchers targeted Leuconostoc, Fructobacillus, and Lactococcus species and optimized sample preparation protocols, like cell smears and cell extracts and utilized rigorous preprocessing protocols like normalization and background correction.

PCA, multidimensional scaling (MDS), and kNN analysis were conducted to reveal species-specific spectral patterns. Identification accuracy of 84.6% for Leuconostoc and Fructobacillus, and 94.2% for Lactococcus species was achieved. Upon application of ML models in the form of SVMs and RFs, classification accuracy was significantly enhanced, with SVM achieving a high 98.4% accuracy and 96.8% F-score.

The study found that MALDI-TOF MS and ML-based identification is an efficient, economic, and reliable process of bacterial species identification and hence has a very vast field of application in microbial taxonomy and diagnosis [14].

The study by Feucherolles et al. [82] investigates the combination of MALDI-TOF MS and ML for rapid AMR screening in Campylobacter jejuni and Campylobacter coli, two major foodborne pathogens. A total of 224 C. jejuni and 116 C. coli isolates from humans, animals, and the environment were tested for resistance to seven antibiotics, including ciprofloxacin and tetracycline. Protein spectra were analyzed using RF and Logistic Regression models, achieving high sensitivity (up to 92.3%) and precision (up to 81.2%) in detecting resistant strains, particularly for ciprofloxacin and tetracycline.

The study also assessed species-specific and extraction method impacts, finding no significant differences between extraction types. Furthermore, potential AMR biomarkers were identified, contributing to the understanding of resistance mechanisms in these pathogens.

The authors conclude that the integrated MALDI-TOF MS and ML pipeline represents a promising, fast, and cost-effective tool for early AMR screening, facilitating faster and targeted antibiotic treatments in clinical and food safety contexts. However, they recommend larger datasets and expanded pathogen coverage for clinical validation to further refine and validate the approach [82].

This study established an end-to-end pipeline of MALDI-TOF MS and supervised ML models to enhance three related Enterococcus species' (E. faecalis, E. faecium, and E. lactis) identification at the species level. With 410 strains and 1,640 spectra, the authors compared KNN, SVMs, and RF models. Traditional MALDI-TOF MS and commercial Biotyper software incorrectly identified E. lactis as E. faecium. Conversely, the Random Forest model performed better, with 99.1% accuracy and AUC values greater than 0.98.

The study also detected species-specific mass spectral biomarkers that were validated by whole-genome sequencing, including peaks for proteins like the Type I toxin-antitoxin system and isoleucyl-tRNA synthetase. The authors concluded that ML-enhanced MALDI-TOF MS significantly improves classification accuracy and discrimination of very similar Enterococcus species, providing a rapid and cost-effective tool for clinical diagnostics and food safety monitoring.

8.4.3 Imaging-Based Identification

AI has revolutionized the study of microbial colony morphology into quick and precise identification of microorganisms. The Annotated Germs for Automated Recognition (AGAR) dataset of 18,000 images of five microorganisms was developed to aid in the automation of microbial colony analysis [83]. The dataset includes single and mixed culture images under various light conditions, which are annotated as countable, uncountable, or empty. The application of deep neural network architectures, such as Faster R-CNN and Cascade R-CNN, to the AGAR dataset, has demonstrated the vast potential of applying DL methods in automatically localizing microbe and classifying it from Petri dish images [83]. Label-free single-cell IFC, when combined with digital holography microscopy, has emerged as a powerful imaging technique for life sciences and clinical diagnostics [84]. DL applied to holographic imaging has enabled the effective use of point-of-care devices. A combined approach of Mask R-CNN for cell detection, a convolutional autoencoder for feature extraction, and a feedforward neural network for single-cell classification has been proposed to avoid biases from data derived under varying experimental conditions [84]. The approach has already been used successfully for the challenging problem of drug-resistant endometrial cancer cell recognition. Real-time visualization and automatic detection and classification of untreated cancer cells in blood in stain-free IFC have been achieved by digital holographic microscopy and ML [85].

This approach enables the classification of primary and metastatic colon cancer cells, along with four types of blood cells, with high precision (92.56%) at a throughput of 15 cells per second [85]. Furthermore, an image-guided cell sorting and classification system integrating microfluidics, photonics, computational microscopy, real-time image processing, and ML has been developed, offering the high throughput of FCM and the informational richness of microscopy [86]. Özel Duygan et al. [87] report CellCognize, an ML workflow that quickly identifies and classifies microbial cell type diversity from FCM data. After learning from multiparametric FCM data of 32 reference standards consisting of bacterial strains, yeast, and beads, CellCognize achieved an average prediction accuracy of 80% through training ANN. The system was able to resolve microbial species, identify physiological states such as growth stages, and quantify biomass production. It worked as effectively as conventional methods, such as 16S rRNA gene sequencing and 14C-labeled substrate incorporation. The pipeline was applied to both synthetic microbial communities and natural freshwater microbiota, where it accurately documented community responses to chemical amendments. Furthermore, CellCognize returned similarity scores for unknown microbiota by comparing their FCM profiles to the reference standards. This aspect shows its promise for quick, low-cost microbial diversity analysis in clinical, environmental, and industrial contexts [87]. Martis et al. [88] proposes a DL architecture for computerized bacterial classification that bridges the limitations of time and labor-consuming and error-prone conventional manual methods. Architecture takes advantage of transfer learning by fine-tuning existing pretrained CNN models, VGG16, MobileNet, and Inception v3, on a dataset of 12,000 images of bacteria divided into 12 classes. Preprocessing tasks like rotation and resizing standardize the images before classifying them. Among the models, VGG16 performed the highest accuracy of 99.99%, far exceeding MobileNet (73.33%) and Inception v3 (80.24%). Not only does architecture predict bacterial clusters by structure and shape but it also provides a confidence value for each prediction, providing reliability. The study determines that VGG16 performs best among models for identifying bacteria and suggests potential future system extensions for viruses and other single-celled organisms' identification [88].

8.5 Machine Learning Approaches for High-Throughput Microbial Culturing

8.5.1 ML-Driven Microbial Growth Prediction

ML-driven microbial growth prediction has emerged as a powerful approach for accelerating the development of high-performing microbial strains for the sustainable production of valuable compounds. Both constraint-based modeling (CBM) and ML techniques used independently or in combination have proven effective in analyzing and optimizing fermentation parameters [89]. These methods enable the prediction of cellular phenotypes from genotypes and uncover patterns in complex biological systems, resulting in more accurate and reliable models for fermentation processes.

In industrial contexts, ML has been successfully applied to predict biogas production performance in large-scale garage dry fermentation systems. A novel intelligent system utilizing AutoML algorithms, such as AutoGluon and H2O, achieved high predictive accuracy for both digester and percolate tank biogas outputs. Beyond accurate forecasting, this system offered interpretable insights and early warning capabilities, underscoring the potential of ML in optimizing complex industrial fermentation workflows.

The integration of ML with HTP robotic platforms has significantly enhanced microbial culturing. An open-source robotic strain isolation platform, coupled with ML algorithms, was developed to rapidly generate microbial isolates on demand. By leveraging colony morphology and genomic data, the system maximized microbial diversity and enabled targeted selection of specific genera. When applied to human fecal samples, it successfully generated personalized gut microbiome biobanks representing over 80% of abundant taxa, highlighting its utility in systematic microbiome analysis and biobanking.

ML has also been instrumental in optimizing culture conditions in miniaturized screening platforms. The Berkeley Lights Beacon® system, an HTP, perfusion-based platform, allows real-time monitoring of strain productivity under continuous culture conditions that closely mimic industrial fed-batch fermentation [90]. This approach has facilitated the selection of high-productivity strains following whole-genome random mutagenesis.

In addition to culture optimization, ML is increasingly applied to the analysis and interpretation of experimental data. ML-enhanced spectral analysis and kinetic modeling have enabled efficient characterization of catalysts and the optimization of synthesis conditions, accelerating materials discovery in microbial culturing [91].

Innovations in culture chip technology have expanded the scope of HTP microbial culturing. A micro-engineered ceramic sheet containing up to one million growth compartments has been employed for fast viable cell counting, HTP screening, and target recovery of specific phenotypes [92]. This versatile platform enables rapid and dynamic environmental changes, facilitating the detection of specific enzymatic activities and the screening of metagenomic libraries. Together, these advances demonstrate the transformative potential of ML across the entire microbial culturing pipeline from strain selection and fermentation optimization to data analysis and biobanking.

8.5.2 AI in Microbial Cultivation Process Optimization

Advanced bioreactors and computerized culture monitoring platforms are spearheading this revolution, enabling real-time data collection and analysis for better process control [93]. Raman spectroscopy has been demonstrated to be a very useful tool for in-line monitoring of mammalian cell culture bioreactors. This nondestructive technique allows concurrent prediction of several culture parameters like glutamine, glucose, lactate, and cell density [93]. Similarly, electron-probing devices like Zn2GeO4:Mn@Fe3+ enable real-time monitoring of microbial metabolism, that is, Fe(III) respiration, and provide insight into complex metabolic activities and enhance biosynthesis [94].

RL has been highly promising in adaptive culture systems, particularly for the control of cocultures in continuous bioreactors. RL agents can maintain populations at specified levels and do better than standard controllers when infrequent sampling occurs. Astonishingly, an effective control policy can be acquired within 24 hours by running five bioreactors in parallel, which verifies the efficacy of this approach (Figure 8.4) [95]. The marriage of process analytical technology (PAT) and AI has enabled the development and use of enormous cultural datasets. Data-driven models (DDMs) can now correlate process and biological conditions with cell culture states and forecast dynamic behaviors like viable cell density, product titer, and metabolite concentrations. These models maximize computational load against accuracy and reliability, which makes it possible to make proactive decisions in bioprocess engineering [96].

A clinical illustration of AI-assisted optimization of bioprocessing for pharmaceutical microbiology is seen in the design and construction of a fully automated 24-parallel mini-bioreactors robot facility. The system, managed by a model-based adaptive input design model, supports scale-down characterization of clone libraries under conditions mimicking industrial-scale bioreactors. The cultivation strategies are optimized regularly by a macro-kinetic growth model, demonstrating the power of AI in the optimization of strain selection and process development [97].

The other breakthrough method is the HTP perfusion-based screening platform developed using the Berkeley Lights Beacon® platform. It allows real-time measurement of continuous culture strain productivity and provides phenotypes with high correlation with behavior in industrially relevant bioreactor processes. The platform has been effectively utilized to improve high-productivity strains through whole-genome random mutagenesis, producing mutants with drastically increased peak-specific productivity in bioreactors [90].

The eVOLVER platform is a scalable, HTP growth experiment DIY platform applicable for use in microbiology, molecular evolution, and systems biology. The system achieves controlled microbial cell growth conditions such that it's possible to observe subtle phenotypic differences. The eVOLVER platform has been applied to determine the adaptive niches in yeast as well as to detect temperature-sensitivity-altered strains, indicating applicability of the platform to optimizing processes [98]. Miniature bioreactors (MBRs) are also turning out to be extremely significant in the bioprocessing acceleration through enabling HTP parallel cell cultivations. MBRs find applications in media development, strain optimization, and process optimization. With automated robotic systems and other miniature process modules, MBRs can offer highly integrated, HTP cell cultivation process development solutions [99].

8.5.3 Synthetic Biology and AI-Driven Strain Engineering

Synthetic biology and AI-guided strain engineering have revolutionized the field of metabolic engineering, enabling precise genetic modifications and optimized strain design. ML plays a key role in predicting gene knockouts for enhanced growth and productivity, and AI-based programs have significantly improved CRISPR/Cas9 target prediction.

ML algorithms have been instrumental in predicting gene knockouts that can enhance microbial growth and metabolite production. ML algorithms take complex genomic and metabolic data to search for potential targets for genetic engineering. With the utilization of large datasets and complex computational models, ML can predict the effect of gene deletions or alterations on cellular metabolism and growth rates. This approach has been particularly valuable for the optimization of microbial strains for industrial applications, e.g. biofuel production or high-value chemicals. AI-powered CRISPR/Cas9 target prediction has greatly improved the efficiency and accuracy of genome editing.

Computational methods like AcRanker, an ML-based method, have been developed to predict putative anti-CRISPR proteins from just protein sequence information [100]. This has led to the discovery of new anti-CRISPRs, AcrIIA20 and AcrIIA21, which can inhibit various Cas9 proteins. These discoveries have important implications for the control of gene editing technologies and our understanding of CRISPR-Cas systems.

The CASPER (CRISPR Associated Software for Pathway Engineering and Research) tool demonstrates the ability of AI to do CRISPR target prediction. CASPER reports higher accuracy for prediction of on- and off-target activity compared to conventional methods, a 2.4% boost for on-target, and a stunning boost by 30.2% for off-target prediction [101]. This tool also enables novel applications such as multitargeting analysis and multispecies population analysis, which are critical for advanced genome editing projects and consortium-based engineering. ML has been applied in numerous aspects of strain engineering in microbial synthetic biology. For instance, in the well-known microbial cell factory Pichia pastoris, CRISPR-based instruments for gene editing and transcriptional regulation have been set up [102]. These tools include mechanisms for efficient gene knockout, repression, and activation. The CRISPR-ARE (Activation, Repression, and Editing) system demonstrated in P. pastoris allows for the simultaneous activation, repression, and editing of a gene, mirroring the versatility of CRISPR-based approaches in synthetic biology. Similarly, CRISPR/Cas9 systems have been extensively employed in Saccharomyces cerevisiae for various forms of genetic manipulation, including single-nucleotide resolution editing, multigene editing, transcriptional regulation, and genome-scale remodeling.

These advances have opened the door to accelerating microbial engineering, reducing labor and time requirements while maximizing our understanding of cellular genetics and physiology. The synergy between AI and synthetic biology has also led to the development of genome-scale engineering technology. Tools such as CRISPR-based control, synthetic small regulatory RNA (sRNA)-based knockdown, promoter design, and multiplex automated genome engineering (MAGE) are now very effective microbial genome-scale engineering tools. The technologies allow fine-level control of gene expression and genome editing, which makes it feasible for scientists to optimize microbial metabolism for application. Overall, the synergy of synthetic biology and AI-strain engineering opened new avenues in metabolic engineering.

8.6 Challenges and Limitations of Machine Learning in HTP Microbial Research

Several challenges and limitations still exist in its application to this area. Data quality and data standardization are among the significant challenges of HTP microbial research. The accuracy and reliability of ML models depend significantly on the quality of data input. Data collection procedures, storage, and processing strategies in microbiology can be extremely heterogeneous, adding inconsistencies and potential biases to datasets [103]. This lack of standardization can result in models that fail to generalize across laboratories or experimental systems. Furthermore, the diversity and complexity of microbial systems also make it challenging to determine shared data collection protocols, again contributing to the issue of data quality.

Bias and interpretability of ML models are another challenge. ML algorithms, particularly DL models, are “black boxes” in which it is difficult for researchers to understand the reasons behind the predictions [104]. Interpretability is an issue in microbiology because knowing the biological pathways involved in predictions is important. In addition, training dataset biases can lead to biased results, potentially reinforcing existing prejudices or overlooking important but underrepresented microbial species or phenomena [105]. To mitigate these issues, researchers are exploring XAI techniques to enhance model interpretability and transparency, as evidenced in the meibomian gland dysfunction classification study.

Computational complexity and high processing cost are significant challenges to the widespread application of ML in HTP microbiological studies. Massive genomic and metagenomic data analysis requires large computational power, which may not be accessible to every research facility [104]. The need for specialized hardware, such as high-performance computing clusters or GPU arrays, may limit accessibility and increase the cost of research. Moreover, the complexity of some ML algorithms, particularly in DL, demands significant expertise in both computer science and microbiology, leading to a shortage of skills that is not straightforward to rectify. The lack of comprehensive training datasets for some microbial species is a significant limitation to the implementation of ML on HTP microbial studies. While well-studied model organisms have abundant data, many microbial species are poorly represented in existing datasets. This lack of data can lead to poor or biased models when extrapolated to less-studied microorganisms. To overcome this shortcoming, scientists need to prioritize the generation and dissemination of data on a wider range of microbial species, as well as the development of transfer learning and domain adaptation methods that can lend knowledge from data-abundant species to make better predictions for data-scarce ones.

Ethical and regulatory concerns of AI-based microbiology are arising as ML applications in this area grow. Issues such as data confidentiality, consent to use data, and the potential for misuse of AI-derived insights within microbial research need to be carefully addressed [106]. There also has to be a set of precise rules and regulations for applying ML in microbiology, particularly where there is a direct concern with human health, e.g. the prediction of antibiotic resistance or the detection of pathogens. Having ethical standards and regulatory procedures in place that balance innovation with proper use of AI in microbiology is crucial to the long-term health and public trust of the profession. To address these problems, there are several conceivable solutions and topics for future study that can be entertained. Data quality and standardization must be addressed, prioritizing the development and implementation of standardized protocols of data acquisition, processing, and storage in microbial research [107].

8.7 Future Perspectives and Emerging Trends

The integration of ML with multi-omics technologies is revolutionizing microbial studies and their applications in numerous fields. The use of multiple technologies is resulting in a more advanced and detailed understanding of complex biological processes. In multi-omics integration, ML software is evolving essential tools to interpret and analyze the vast amount of data generated by genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics studies. These approaches are particularly powerful in uncovering intricate interactions among different biological layers and identifying novel biomarkers and therapeutic targets. For instance, in the field of oncology, multi-omics technologies combined with ML enable a deeper understanding of the tumor microbiome and its role in carcinogenesis, metastasis, and treatment response. Similarly, in osteoarthritis research, multi-omics techniques are facilitating the identification of molecular signatures and cellular subpopulations, allowing for more precise diagnosis and personalized therapeutic strategies [108]. Application of ML to combine multi-omics data is not without challenges. The complexity and volume of data from heterogeneous omics platforms require sophisticated computational tools and algorithms. However, developments in ML and DL algorithms are increasingly improving our ability to process and interpret such complex datasets. With the advancement of technologies, we can expect even more accurate predictions and insights into microbial behavior and interactions. For personalized medicine applications, the integration of multi-omics data with ML is opening new avenues for targeted therapeutic interventions. This approach allows for a more precise characterization of personalized health profiles and may lead to more effective treatments with fewer side effects [109]. Pharmacometrics is also being revolutionized by these technologies, with ML techniques being integrated into model-informed drug development and discovery strategies [110]. Stepping ahead toward the future, future applications of microbial ML include possible implementation using quantum computing. Not being specifically mentioned in the provided papers, quantum computing can possibly better handle complex computations that go into the analysis of multi-omics data at a large scale using normal computers. This could lead to faster speed and accuracy in the predictions that are made in microbial research. Federated learning and decentralized AI approaches, though not directly referred to in the context presented, could be of utmost significance in microbiome studies. These approaches could facilitate collaborative research with data privacy, a critical factor in personalized medicine and clinical research. Practical applications of ML and multi-omics integration are already observed in numerous fields. In microbiology and environmental microbiology, these approaches are expanding our understanding of microbial community function and function in biogeochemical cycles [111]. In agriculture and horticulture, the integration of multi-omics information and AI is transforming plant phenotyping toward precision horticulture, predictive breeding, and improved crop management [112]. The role of XAI in microbial science, while not directly discussed in the papers presented, will become even more prominent. As ML models become more sophisticated, it will be crucial to provide transparency and interpretability of results to build confidence in AI-driven microbial science and its applications. The future of AI in microbial sciences, in general, looks bright and revolutionary. Leveraging ML with multi-omics approaches is going to speed up progress in personalized medicine, drug discovery, and environmental microbiology. As progress is made with technologies and computational power, we are likely to see better predictions, deeper insight into microbial systems, and new uses across multiple disciplines.

8.8 Conclusion

The intersection of ML with HTP microbial techniques is a paradigm shift in microbiological diagnostics and research. As traditional culture-based and molecular methods are being depleted, ML offers quick, scalable, and extremely accurate solutions for microbial identification, AMR prediction, and cultivation optimization. Given access to different data sources from metagenomic sequences and MS spectra to imaging and FCM profiles, ML models can recognize hidden patterns and make predictions with unparalleled accuracy.

This chapter illustrates how supervised, unsupervised, and RL techniques are being successfully applied across various fields of microbial science, including strain classification, growth prediction, and synthetic biology. The combination of ML with cutting-edge platforms such as MALDI-TOF MS, microfluidics, LOC devices, and CRISPR-based genome editing accelerates innovation in diagnostics, drug discovery, and personalized medicine. There are still challenges in data standardization, model interpretability, computational requirements, and regulatory approval. Resolving these issues will be crucial to making ML-based microbiology reproducible and trustworthy. Future breakthroughs, such as XAI, federated learning, and quantum computing, have the potential to continue revolutionizing the field, enabling the performance of robust, ethical, and globally collaborative microbial science. As ML expands, its role in shaping the next generation of microbiological tools will be critical to propelling progress in science and medicine.
