11.1 Introduction

The biotech industry is being transformed by the Big Data advent, made possible by the unprecedented capacity to massively profile and process data, resulting in an explosion of usable information on individual biosystems. Representative sources of biotech Big Data include (bio)process data and various types of omics data (e.g. genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics) that are systematically stored and managed at several publicly available repositories for a wide range of healthcare, agriculture, industrial, and environmental endpoints [1–4]. Although the production of data in the most diverse biotechnology areas is increasing at a high rate, nevertheless, computational techniques are necessary to process such data and subsequently tap into their full potential. The power of machines to transform and learn from biodata is reshaping the current outlook [5]. However, the structural complexity, heterogeneity, high-dimensionality, and increasingly massive volumes of bioprocess and omics data, coupled with the context-sensitive and stochastic nature of living systems, challenge the capacity to reach the desired phenotypes.

Complementarily, recent advancements in molecular engineering have revolutionized strain engineering and flux design, enabling the redirection of metabolic flux toward desired products [5, 6] (for further details about metabolic flux analysis, see Chapter 12). The metabolic engineering field relies on genetic modifications (activation, underexpression, knockout, and/or modulation of regulatory elements) to reprogram native metabolic pathways for producing a wide variety of valuable compounds. This process has been further streamlined by the Design-Build-Test-Learn (DBTL) cycle framework for strain engineering, leveraging on high-throughput profiling to accelerate and optimize the development of strains [7]. In this pipeline, the Design component outlines the strategic approach, while the Build step involves the techniques used to introduce sequence diversity. The Test phase includes the workflows for phenotyping, and the Learn component involves the application of computational tools to analyze the data collected during the testing. While computational tools are integrated throughout the cycle (from statistical analyses to complex simulations) to guide the process (analyze experimental results and identify new modification targets), the Learn stage remains an area with significant room for improvement [8].

A combination of multi-experiment data and data-driven analytical approaches (machine learning (ML) techniques) offers a compelling solution to address the introduced challenges while complying with the DBTL cycle. Currently, many biomanufacturing companies are investing in the digitalization of biotechnological systems and processes, recurring on various computational modeling formalisms, including mechanistic constraint-based modeling (CBM), ML, and hybrid modeling approaches. CBM approaches are based on fundamental principles such as mass and energy conservation, knowledge of the stoichiometry of metabolic networks that describe the range of steady-state flux distributions, using, for instance, the popular flux balance analysis (FBA) approach [9], and require relatively less experimental data. On the other hand, ML explores the capability of computers to perform tasks without explicit programming and no necessity to integrate background knowledge on metabolic processes. To carry out these tasks, ML algorithms can identify patterns, derive predictions, and continuously improve their performance through adaptive mechanisms [10, 11]. Moreover, the adaptive mechanisms present in ML allow computers to learn from datasets. These learning mechanisms, including ongoing deep learning (DL) breakthroughs, enable computers to progressively improve performance in diverse biotechnological applications, such as enzyme optimization, discover relevant genes in biosynthetic pathways, and propose new designs for the next DBTL cycle [12–14]. In this regard, sharing large-scale, high-quality data from bioreactor experiments and monitored organisms is crucial for learning purposes. ML techniques able to represent, integrate, and process high-dimensional data are an invaluable asset in any future biotechnology area to achieve a deep understanding of biosystems [15]. In parallel to the emergence of pure ML models, integrative approaches that combine mechanistic CBM with ML (e.g. hybrid ML/FBA models) are gaining traction in computational strain design [16, 17].

This chapter is structured as follows. The first part reviews critical ML-based approaches for the descriptive and predictive modeling of Big Data in the biotech domain. An overview of hybrid ML/CBM approaches is also provided. The second part of the chapter presents several successful case studies and associated methodologies in the context of metabolic engineering research for the principled illustration of the introduced methods. Lastly, open challenges and future perspectives are outlined.

11.2 Big Data in Biotechnology: Prerequisites for ML-Based Approaches

The design of experimental studies in the biotechnological domain should abide by fundamental principles for the optimal application of subsequent learning tasks, including devising standardized protocols across experiments to ensure comparability between samples and reproducibility, recording all relevant endogenous and exogenous features that can impact the study (e.g. bioreactor cultivation conditions, strain backgrounds), guaranteeing a good coverage of diverse experimental parameterizations (e.g. unbiased sampling techniques for gene knockouts, media composition, environmental conditions) to promote the learning capacity, selecting control groups whenever applicable, isolating causes of noise and artifacts, calibrating instruments regularly and validating measurements to ensure data quality and accuracy, collecting replicates to assess/reduce variability and improve reliability, ensuring sufficient sample size to enable robust statistical analysis and generalization capacity, collecting data across various scales (e.g. multiple omics layers) for holistic learning, and monitoring longitudinal experiments at fine and consistent sampling rates. Complementarily to design considerations, the following sections devise subsequent data preprocessing principles to handle the multimodal, high-dimensional, longitudinal, and noisy nature of bioprocess and omics data.

11.2.1 Data Multimodality and Heterogeneity

In metabolic engineering experiments, data can be collected from a wide variety of biological and physicochemical modalities. First, multiple modalities can be identified at each omic layer, including genomics (genotyping, methylation), transcriptomics (RNAseq, chromatin accessibility), proteomics (abundance, post-translational modifications), and metabolomics (see Chapter 10). Complementarily, molecular interactions (interactomics) between metabolites and other molecules, such as proteins, whether binding or regulatory, can be profiled. Second, metabolic flux analysis (fluxomics) allows the estimation of intracellular fluxes. Third, accompanying biophysical and biochemical measurements are generally relevant to assessing enzyme activity, kinetics, binding affinities, and reaction energetics. Fourth, imaging data, including fluorescence, electron, or confocal microscopy for structural and functional analysis, as well as cellular imaging, may also be available for specific ends. Fifth, phenotype profiling (phenomics) can encompass growth rate measurements (e.g. biomass accumulation), metabolite yield and productivity (production rates of desired compounds), stress response, and morphological analyses (e.g. characterization of cell size, shape, and structure). Finally, and most central, physiological measurements of environmental parameters, nutrient availability (e.g. concentrations of substrates, cofactors) and byproduct accumulation (e.g. toxic or inhibitory compounds) are generally critical.

Complementarity, data heterogeneity can arise due to variations in the monitoring protocols, instrumentation, environmental setups (e.g. temperature, pH, media composition, oxygen availability, and other conditions), (epi)genotypic and phenotypic diversity of strains and organisms, data annotation process sampling rates on longitudinal studies, and feature coverage (e.g. specific omics and fluxes only profiled on a subset of all samples leading to blockwise missing data). Such sources of heterogeneity – whether caused by collection methods, populations, or environments – can introduce several types of biases that hinder the subsequent learning goals, including sampling biases toward specific conditions that lead to generalization difficulties, measurement biases associated with systematic differences that can be assigned to the protocol and not the measured phenomenon, confounding biases due to spurious associations between variables or temporal patterns, and batch effects capturing systematic nonbiological forms of variation [18]. Differences in the extent of recorded features or denormalized protocol variations can lead to feature spaces where large segments of missing entries will occur in blocks, generally claiming for dedicated handling principles, ranging from manifold alignment and domain-aware imputation to multi-source ensemble learning (models learned from subsamples and subspaces without block-wise missings) [19].

To guarantee the capacity to learn from multimodal and heterogeneous sources of data, several principles should be considered (e.g. [20]), including data integration principles to consolidate datasets from different modalities using mapping tables and ontologies for cross-referencing or more advanced principles (e.g. kernel-based fusion, hierarchical integration); standardization principles to handle heterogeneity such as scaling methods, batch effect correction (e.g. ComBat, RUV), and quantile normalization; adding protocol variations as covariates for ensuring sensitivity to protocol-specific biases; integrative learning principles such as graph-based approaches (e.g. heterogeneous networks) matrix factorization techniques (e.g. NMF) to find common patterns; quality assessment principles to quantify signal-to-noise ratios and subsequently apply filtering criteria to retain high-quality data; sampling principles to guarantee an uniform penetration of heterogeneity sources across training, validation, and testing observations; and harmonization principles such as cross-dataset alignment using canonical correlation analysis (CCA), Procrustes analysis, and embedding techniques; representation learning and multi-view learning principles can be used to learn from experimental data combining two or more distinct data structures (e.g. time series data, imaging data).

11.2.2 Stratification and Data Transformations

Complementarily, data sampling challenges pertaining to strata representativity, as well as the presence of categorical targets exhibiting class imbalance and numerical targets displaying skewed distributions, are common and stem from distinct underlying causes, including biases of experimental setups toward certain outcomes (e.g. neglection of certain conditions or emphasis on specific outputs of interest), experimental design choices, annotation inconsistencies, as well as natural biological constraints that make specific outcomes typically rare (e.g. successful strain designs, high-yield production), a common case with targeted modifications where successful interventions are relatively few compared to the vast number of possible perturbations.

Strategies to mitigate these challenges include resampling to reduce imbalances and skewness, incorporating domain-specific knowledge to transform and engineer input and/or output features with more adequate statistical distributions, optimizing the subsequent learning approaches (e.g. adjust decision thresholds, penalize misprediction of minority classes and numeric ranges via dedicated losses) and opt for their pretraining on related data, and acquiring new experimental data from underrepresented strata. Complementarily, data augmentation strategies recurring to variational autoencoders, metabolic models, perturbations to the existing data samples, or generative adversarial networks can be applied to generate synthetic data to handle limits pertaining to data availability, sampling biases, and imbalance of targets. Finally, pairwise learning principles under contrastive loss functions [21] can be used to counteract generalization difficulties.

Given the nature of (bio)process and omics data, alternative data transformations are further recommended to aid descriptive and predictive learning tasks, including normalization of molecular variables to avoid biases from varying scales (e.g. moving from absolute countings toward transactions per million to account for sampling differences, scaling features to a shared distribution for distance-dependent ML approaches), log transformation to address distribution skewness (e.g. gene expression or concentration measurements), dimensionality reduction (DR) approaches to reduce complexity and noise (e.g. PCA, tSNE, UMAP, feature selection methods), encoding of categorical variables (e.g. embedding of experimental conditions, numerical encodings of ordinal variables, one-hot-encoding of nominal variables), discretization of features, particularly targets, for simplifying complex relationships and enhancing interpretability, correcting batch effects [18], and time series or signal transformations for frequency domain representations (e.g. spectral analysis of electrical measurements) and noise reduction (e.g. piecewise aggregation, moving averages, wavelet transforms, filtering).

11.2.3 Handling of Missing Values and Outliers

In the context of metabolic engineering, missing values can arise from a variety of causes, including misaligned longitudinal sampling, measurement errors, abnormal conditions, instrumentation sensitivity limits (e.g. mass spectrometry or chromatography may not cover all metabolites in the sample, technical variability of single-cell RNA sequencing). Missing data can be preserved to be handled at the subsequent learning step or imputed using domain-specific knowledge, mechanistic models, centrality statistics, interpolation or regression in time series, predictive methods (e.g. nearest neighbors), and ensemble views (e.g. multiple imputation) [22, 23]. Less commonly, missing values can be removed by dropping the corresponding records or variables, depending on criteria such as data size and missing rates.

Similarly, the presence of outliers – observations that significantly deviate from the expected data patterns (beyond natural biological variability) – can arise from a variety of factors, including experimental errors related with instrumentation (fluctuations in sensitivity or signal), operation (fluctuations in expected experimental conditions), sampling biases (e.g. parts of a culture experiencing localized abnormal growth or metabolic activity), and contamination (e.g. by substances or microbes); variations in strain or genotypes; and unexpected metabolic instability due to unaccounted conditions, and experimental design choices (e.g. stress tests such as oxidative stress, nutrient limitations, extreme pH changes or other perturbations). The detection of outliers should, whenever possible, be guided by domain knowledge and follow contextual stances since the experimental context can create meaningful deviations. The detection can be aided by statistical methods to measure deviations from model expectations (ranging from univariate z-score/IQR views toward multivariate views) and nonparametric methods such as clustering approaches [24]. Outlier observations, when meaningful or informative, can be preserved to reshape the learning of descriptors and predictors. To reduce their impact on the learning stage, outliers can be further treated using capping (Winsorization) and multivariate corrections.

11.2.4 Longitudinal Studies

Metabolic engineering experiments involve the profiling and/or optimization of dynamic systems. The temporal dimension is generally present, whether monitoring strain adaptation, fed-batch fermentation (e.g. cell growth, metabolite production, substrate consumption), regulatory responses, bioprocesses, cellular adaptation and recovery from stressors, changes in pathway activation and metabolite accumulation after genetic or environmental perturbations, among others. These experiments generate time-varying data in the form of multivariate time series data when the systems are measured at approximately regular periods or timestamped multivariate event data when measurements occur at an irregular pace or after specific phenomena or perturbations. In this context, multiple principles should be considered to aid descriptive and predictive tasks (e.g. [18, 25]), including the alignment of data points to a common timeline; the application of interpolation or resampling techniques (e.g. spline, Gaussian processes) to standardize time intervals; the normalization of measurements per time point or over the entire time course to prevent cumulative views on metabolic products from creating biases; the extraction of statistical features such as trends, peaks, spectral/frequency features, rates of change, and oscillations over the entire time course or along sliding windows; the creation of lagged variables to capture dependencies along time; the application of dynamic mode decomposition or recurrent autoencoders for temporal compression; the application of smoothing filters to reduce experimental noise and power transformations to stabilize variance; the selection of dedicated ML methods to learn from multivariate time series and event data; the partitioning of data into training, validation, and test sets ensuring temporal coherence (e.g. walk-forward or rolling-window schema).

11.3 Types of ML-Based Approaches for the Design of Microbial Cell Factories

With Big Data being generated at an unprecedented rate, ML-based approaches are becoming a prevalent option for their integrative analysis and interpretation. This section introduces essential background on the application and mechanisms of data-driven predictive and descriptive modeling approaches, with a focus on ML-based techniques, including pure ML and hybrid ML able to incorporate constraint-based methods. Figure 11.1 illustrates the major ML-based approaches described in this section.

11.3.1 Machine Learning (ML) Models

ML provides a powerful framework for developing computational algorithms that learn from experimental data. By leveraging a diverse range of algorithms, ML enables the automatic construction of data-driven models for descriptive, predictive and prescriptive ends. Descriptors can be used to understand bioprocess dynamics for knowledge acquisition, predictors can estimate latent features of interest or iteratively recommend the next steps in lab experiments, and prescriptors can leverage longitudinal bioreactor studies to explore the suitability of unseen conditions for ultimately enhancing various process outcomes [26, 27]. Numerous ML algorithms have been developed and are readily available via open-source Python packages (e.g. [28]). Generally, ML models can be categorized into two main classes: supervised and unsupervised learning methods (reinforcement learning (RL) will not be addressed due to the limited examples in the context of engineering microbial cell factories). The selection of the most suitable ML method depends on the desired outputs. Here we provide an overview of ML methods commonly employed in the field of industrial biotechnology, highlighting their applications.

11.3.2 Supervised ML

Supervised learning methods [29], including regression (for continuous outcomes) and classification (for categorical outcomes), single-output and multiple-output predictors, aim to establish a relationship between input features (denoted as x) and corresponding outcomes (y) using training data, {(x1, y1), … , (xn, yn)}. This relation is mathematically expressed as:

(11.1)

where θ represents the model parameters. In parametric ML approaches, the objective is to optimize θ by minimizing a loss function that measures the error between the model's predictions and the true values, . The loss function can be assessed in training data or, more rigorously, a set-aside validation (out-of-sample) dataset to ensure that the predictor is able to generalize toward unseen observations, thereby mitigating overfitting risks.

After the pretreatment steps described in Section 11.2, the essential stages involved in a typical supervised learning workflow consists of problem scoping, feature engineering (select and create key variables), and the model selection, hyperparameterization, training, and evaluation (elaborating on this topic is not the scope of the chapter; we redirect interested readers to [30] for more details on these stages).

Selected supervised ML methods applied to various biotechnological tasks are briefly introduced. Some of the targeted tasks include optimizing pathways, classifying cellular phenotypes, predicting metabolic production, optimizing metabolic fluxes, and designing genetic modifications, all of which involve extracting insights from complex biological data.

11.3.2.1 Neural Networks

Inspired by biological neural systems, neural networks (NNs) consist of interconnected processing units, known as perceptrons or nodes, generally organized into layers [31]. Each node receives input from connected nodes, typically from previous layers, processes this input, and generates an output that influences nodes in subsequent layers. The network, f, receives an external signal, x, at the input layer and iteratively transforms it at each intermediate hidden layer, x[p+1] = ϕ[p](x[p]), until it returns the system's outputs, , at the final output layer. Different NN architectures with particular topologies and node activation functions have been proposed for different applications [32].

Recent advances in DL, the learning of NNs with a high number of parameters (θ), have renewed interest in their application across various domains, including, in the context of metabolic engineering, enzyme and pathway design [33], and pathway optimizing [34, 35]. DL have also proven useful for productivity optimization in bioprocesses using historical data [36]. From an ML stance, advances in DL have been mostly driven by expressive layering (e.g. recurrent, convolutional, contrastive, residual, attention-based), alternative learning schema (e.g. self-supervision, transfer learning), novel architectures (e.g. transformers, generative adversarial networks), and data augmentation strategies [37].

11.3.2.2 Decision Trees and Ensembles

Decision trees (DTs), as originally described by Quinlan [38], are simplistic nonparametric supervised functions of input features. The function, f(x), is a composition of rules according to a tree structure that is learnt from training data, where each node's rule defines a feature test according to its predictive information. Each data observation falls within a decision path from root to a leaf based on the tested features (x) along the path, and is annotated with the decision outcomes – e.g. continuous and/or categorical values – observed at the corresponding leaf (). The depth of DTs is controlled during the training process to mitigate both underfitting and overfitting risks associated with shallow and deep trees, respectively. DTs are widely used due to their simplicity, ease of implementation, and high interpretability.

In strain engineering and bioprocesses, they have been applied to predict which protein expression levels result in high production yield or to identify input process conditions of various fermentation runs that maximize the production efficiency [39].

The Random Forest (RF) algorithm is an ensemble of DTs based on two major procedures: bootstrapped data sampling, along with feature subspace selection, to learn multiple independent trees (i.e. bagging) with reduced correlation. The ensemble of k ∈ ℕ+ trees, {f1(x), … , fk(x)}, is then used to produce corresponding output estimates, , which are subsequently used to produce the final estimate through uniform weighting schema, preventing both underfitting and overfitting risks [40].

Alternative successful tree ensembles, such as extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) [41], are able to learn trees sequentially, where each tree corrects errors made by the previous ones, and optimally assigns efficacy scores for nonuniform weighting schema.

Tree ensembles are versatile, being capable of handling arbitrarily high dimensionality, missing data, numerical and/or categorical outcomes, and feature importance analysis. This flexibility makes them suitable for a wide range of biotechnological applications. For instance, they have been used for pathway optimization [42], differential metabolic flux analysis from varying physical traits [43], and predicting recombinant protein concentrations based on online process parameters [44].

11.3.2.3 Alternative Predictive Approaches

Bayesian approaches for ML use data to update beliefs, where beliefs are given by parameters that describe the distribution of inputs and their associative dependency with targets. Parameters are generally estimated from frequentist views or prior knowledge if available, making Bayesian predictors eligible candidates for hybrid ML in the biotech domain. Predictions for new inputs are inferred from maximum likelihood estimates using the existing beliefs, p(y|x, θ) ∝ p(x|y, θ)p(y|θ). Joint distributions can be factorized by identifying a network of conditional variable dependencies for greater capacity to learn from high-dimensional inputs. Ultimately, naïve Bayesian approaches place an independence assumption between all input variables, offering a simple baseline reference of performance for more sophisticated ML predictors.

In contrast with Bayesian approaches, similarity, a central concept for pattern-centric learning, is at the center of analogizer approaches. In its simplest form, the nearest-neighbor algorithm predicts the targets for a new observation by weighting the targets recovered by the most similar observations in the training data, , where N is the neighborhood of x, wi is the similarity degree between x and xi, and τ is a metric of centrality (weighted mode, mean, or median).

Support vector machines (SVMs), a different class of analogizer approaches, rely on kernels to map the original space into a new space where critical observations (support vectors) can be identified to learn (one or more) hyperplanes that define the classification boundaries or regression surface (herein SVMs are commonly referred to as support vector regressors). Despite the linearity of SVMs, the kernel trick generally promotes their capacity to handle high-dimensional data [45].

SVMs have been shown to be useful in addressing cell factory design challenges. Examples include multigene pathway optimization problems to maximize production titers [35] and automated enzyme search to predict protein–chemical interactions (i.e. whether the enzyme catalyzes a reaction) using both protein sequence and chemical information [46].

11.3.2.4 Selected Case Studies

Two application examples are now introduced to show how supervised ML can be used, highlighting important advances in biotechnological projects: (1) prediction of metabolic fluxes [47] and (2) maximization of 1-dodecanol production [48]. These examples were chosen as they closely align with the routine tasks of a systems metabolic engineer.

The first example explores the use of ML models to predict metabolic fluxes [47]. While constraint-based models (CBMs) are valuable for modeling metabolic networks, they require extensive prior knowledge, tuning objective functions, and rely heavily on predefined assumptions, which limit their applicability under diverse conditions (e.g. less-studied perturbations, infrequent exogenous conditions). Gonçalves et al. [47] highlight the growing potential of ML approaches, particularly in leveraging large-scale omics data, such as proteomics and transcriptomics, for metabolic flux prediction. The authors benchmarked state-of-the-art ML models, including RFs, SVMs, DTs, and NNs, against the parsimonious version of FBA (pFBA) [49], using omics data as inputs. The ML models were subjected to nested cross-validation for decoupling hyperparameterization from evaluation. The analysis revealed that ML models, particularly RFs, are competitive in predicting both intracellular and extracellular fluxes compared to pFBA, achieving statistical significance superiority for specific conditions. These findings were consistent when using transcriptomic and proteomic layers individually and jointly. The results suggest that ML approaches can effectively overcome traditional methods in scenarios where these methods struggle. To evaluate generalization, the ML models were also tested on an independent dataset. While RFs demonstrated superior performance in certain cases, their generalization was nevertheless limited, given the limited number of training examples and distinct experimental conditions.

The second example, conducted by Opgenorth and colleagues [48], explored the optimization of 1-dodecanol production in Escherichia coli using a combination of ML and two iterative DBTL cycles. This systematic framework represents a significant shift from traditional trial-and-error approaches in metabolic engineering. The study focused on leveraging proteomics data to guide strain development, ultimately improving production efficiency. In the first DBTL cycle, the authors examined 36 engineered E. coli strains, systematically modulating ribosome-binding sites (RBSs) and acyl-ACP/acyl-CoA reductases within a single operon. Measured variables included dodecanol titers and pathway protein levels. The results revealed that Maqu_2507 reductase consistently outperformed other reductases for dodecanol production, whereas Maqu_2220 yielded the highest total fatty alcohol production. This initial cycle generated a valuable dataset for training ML models, including RFs and NNs, to predict optimal protein profiles for further strain improvement. The second DBTL cycle implemented the predictions generated by the ML models from the first cycle. Fourteen new strains were designed, with the ML models guiding the adjustments of protein expression levels. The results revealed a 21% increase in dodecanol titer, reaching 0.83 g/L, which is significantly higher than previously reported values for batch cultures. However, certain challenges, such as inaccuracies in the predicted strength of binding sites and unexpected operon-wide effects, limited the extent of improvements. The significance of this work lies in showcasing how ML can effectively complement systematic frameworks like DBTL to advance metabolic engineering, while underscoring the potential of iterative cycles to achieve improvements in production over time. The study further emphasizes the importance of balancing exploration and exploitation within the DBTL framework. While initial cycles should focus on exploring diverse design spaces, subsequent iterations should leverage the accumulated knowledge for a more targeted optimization. This balanced approach is crucial for maximizing the efficacy of ML algorithms and refining strain engineering processes. In conclusion, this study provides a compelling example of how integrating ML with high-throughput DBTL cycles can advance metabolic engineering. While challenges remain, such as refining predictive tools and addressing data limitations, the results highlight the presence of a promising way toward more efficient production of bio-based products.

11.3.3 Unsupervised ML

Unsupervised learning constitutes a crucial aspect of ML for acquiring knowledge on the behavior of biosystems, particularly considering the significant effort often required for their annotation [50]. The main goal is to identify patterns in complex, multivariate input data by either grouping similar instances, learning representations, retrieving local patterns, or modeling dynamics. Common examples of unsupervised ML techniques in biotechnology include clustering [51], representation learning [52], biclustering [53], parametric modeling [54], and DR [55].

11.3.3.1 Clustering

Clustering aims at grouping data observations in clusters to uncover relevant structures. Common approaches including hierarchical clustering, which builds a nested hierarchy of clusters using agglomerative (bottom-up) or divisive (top-down) methods; density-based clustering, which groups points based on dense regions; and model-based clustering, which assumes data is generated from a mixture of probabilistic distributions, like Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs), to learn soft structures, i.e. structures where observations are assigned a membership probability to each cluster. Partition-based clustering, where K-means is the paradigmatic example, assigns data into a parameterizable number of K clusters by minimizing intra-cluster variance,

(11.2)

i.e. cluster assignment based on the distance (d) between an observation (xi) and the nearest cluster centroid (). Distances can be customized depending on the variable types (e.g. Gower distance for mixed variables) and data structure (e.g. DTW for time series data). The algorithm iteratively updates the cluster centroids,

(11.3)

and reassigns observations until it meets a stopping criterion – no further changes occur in data point assignments or when the total sum of distances within clusters is minimized.

Clustering has been used for different ends [56, 57]: categorize microbial strains based on their metabolic profiles, aiding in the selection of best candidates for bio-production; differentiate enzymatic reactions, aiding in the identification of novel biosynthetic pathways; and grouping metabolites from mass spectrometry data, distinguishing between core metabolic pathways and potential byproducts. Clustering methods, however, have some limitations. For instance, they generally group molecular entities based on all available features, which may hide relationships that exist only within specific subsets of features. Furthermore, each entity is restricted to a single group in hard clustering structures, even though they can participate in multiple groups depending on their biological functions. These shortcomings can be addressed by biclustering, making it valuable for identifying patterns of co-regulation [58].

11.3.3.2 Biclustering

Biclustering, originated in the context of gene expression data analysis [59], is a unique category of clustering techniques that can group observations and variables simultaneously, hence often positioned as a pattern discovery method. The problem, also referred to as subspace clustering, aims at identifying a set of biclusters, such that each bicluster Bk satisfies specific criteria of interest. To guide the formation of these biclusters, homogeneity criteria are commonly employed, typically implemented through the use of a merit function [60]. A given bicluster B = (I, J), where I and J are, respectively, the subset of observations and variables, is generally characterized by its pattern, ϕJ, i.e. the set of expected values on the given variables. Different types of homogeneity can be pursued, including:

  • constant overall if for all xi ∈ I and yj ∈ J, aij = μ + ηij, where μ is the typical value and ηij is the observed noise;
  • constant on variables, i.e. pattern on observations, if aij = μj + ηij, where μj represents the expected value in variable yj;
  • additive (multiplicative) if for all i ∈ I and j ∈ J, aij = μj + γi + ηij (aij = μj × γi + ηij) where μj is the expected value in variable yj, and γi the adjustment for observation xi;
  • order-preserving on variables if there is a permutation of J variables, πJ, under which the sequence of values in every observation in I is strictly increasing.

In addition to homogeneity, biclustering searches can incorporate statistical significance criteria [61] to ensure that a bicluster's occurrence deviates from what is expected under a null model, and dissimilarity criteria [62] to prevent redundancies among biclusters.

In biotechnology, biclustering has numerous applications, including the identification of co-regulated metabolic pathways and the discovery of drugs with similar activity patterns [63]. Biclustering can provide valuable insights on putative regulatory modules (e.g. coordinated sets of genes and metabolites) or correlated metabolic fluxes and enzymatic activities under specific conditions [64, 65], as well as understand how microbes or engineered strains adapt to different environments by clustering metabolic responses under stress conditions [66].

11.3.3.3 Representation Learning and Dimensionality Reduction

DR focuses on decreasing the number of features in a dataset while retaining most of its relevant information or structural patterns [67]. DR techniques are generally categorized into two main approaches: feature selection and feature extraction/transformation. Feature selection involves identifying a subset of features based on specific criteria, such as minimizing information loss or maximizing predictive power, via filter techniques, embedded methods, and wrapper models [68]. In contrast, feature extraction generates new features by transforming or combining existing ones, often through nonlinear transformations. One of the most widely used DR techniques in biotechnology is Principal Component Analysis (PCA) due to its inherent simplicity. PCA reduces the dimensionality of a dataset by capturing the maximum variance with the fewest possible dimensions, effectively summarizing the data while preserving its essential patterns [69]. The resulting k dimensions (components) are a linear projection of original dimensions given by the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix from centered data, with the explained variance computed according to the corresponding eigenvalues, , where k ≤ m.

DR techniques like t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE) and Uniform Manifold Approx. Projection (UMAP) are also particularly suitable to visualize correlations and select variables in highly complex multidimensional data [70–72].

They have been consistently applied to characterize cellular types and states, including discrimination of stressed cells [73] and healthy cells from diseased ones [74]. Recently, they have also been applied for classifying cells as high producers or low producers [75].

Representation learning offers an alternative to classic DR methods by leveraging DL techniques such as autoencoders and variational inference for feature extraction [76]. It is increasingly applied in metabolic engineering to acquire numeric representations (embeddings) of complex data, such as high-dimensional, multilayered, temporal, and/or imaging data. Representation learning has been applied to learn embeddings from metabolic reactions to predict novel biosynthetic pathways, protein sequences to predict enzyme activities (novel biocatalysts), multi-omics to optimize microbial strains, or context-aware genotypic data to predict strain phenotypes [77].

11.3.4 Hybrid ML and Constraint-Based Models

A promising avenue for analyzing high-dimensional biological data involves the integration of mechanistic modeling methods [78, 79], such as the widely utilized FBA approach (for a comprehensive review of CBM, see [80] and [81]) with ML stances. Hybrid ML/CBM approaches combine state-of-the-art ML techniques (either supervised or unsupervised learning paradigms) with mechanistic CBM methods (here referred to as FBA approach) for exploring synergies and opportunities of both formalisms [27]. This integration allows ML to leverage mechanistic knowledge, ultimately translating into an improved predictive capacity and interpretability, as reviewed recently [16, 82].

Various data- and knowledge-driven pipelines can be established depending on the available data types and specific research goals. Currently, the different workflows/approaches for integrating constraint-based models and ML using omics data can be classified into two main groups: i) CBM-FBA as input for ML, in which condition-specific CBMs are generated using multiple datasets from high-throughput technologies to obtain metabolic fluxes prediction and from which ML techniques can infer important patterns, and ii) ML as input for CBM-FBA, in which ML methods are directly applied to single/multi-omics datasets for feature selection that are then used as input constraints to build/improve CBM-FBA models. In this section, we highlight some of these integrative studies, providing an overview of the steps involved in each workflow.

11.3.4.1 CBM-FBA as Input for ML

When available, experimental data can be combined with FBA-derived fluxes to create multi-omic features, enabling the prediction of targets of interest [83, 84]. The fluxes generated by metabolic models can then feed the ML algorithms for further analysis. Plaimas et al. [85] supplied ML with descriptors derived from FBA, biochemical knowledge and transcriptomic data to predict essential enzymes/reactions within a metabolic network. By employing an SVM algorithm, this system demonstrated a significant improvement in the prediction accuracy compared to FBA approaches alone. A different hybrid pipeline integrating FBA and ML was described by Vijayakumar et al. [86, 87]. This novel approach involves constructing condition-specific metabolic models by incorporating transcriptomic data as constraints that are then simulated using a multi-objective FBA model. The ML model is then trained on transcriptomic data and the predicted fluxomics profile, enabling the identification of key genes/reactions under different conditions. Similarly, another approach is to incorporate input fluxes predicted from pFBA combined with omics data to improve the predictive power of microbial growth rates [88].

A recent innovation is the development of a hybrid approach that embeds FBA directly into ML (artificial NNs) [89]. Unlike traditional FBA, which requires extensive experimental data to define medium uptake fluxes, the proposed artificial metabolic network (AMN) incorporates a neural preprocessing layer to capture relationships between medium composition and uptake fluxes, facilitating accurate phenotype predictions without additional experimental measurements. By constraining ML with CBM, this hybrid approach achieved higher predictive accuracy for metabolic fluxes and growth rates while reducing data requirements. The AMN framework also shows potential for broader applications, including designing gene knockout strategies, thus representing a significant advancement in strain engineering. Alternatively, unsupervised modeling strategies, including PCA, have also been applied with FBA-derived results [90, 91].

Numerous computational methodologies exist for data integration to develop context- and condition-specific metabolic models [92]. An interesting direction is to combine condition-specific metabolic modeling with Bayesian ML to infer the metabolic pathway's responsiveness to various environmental conditions [93]. Furthermore, alternative ML approaches (bridging supervised and unsupervised algorithms) can also be integrated with FBA results to estimate the main metabolic features of CBM [94].

While FBA-based approaches have successfully been used in analyzing multi-omics data to address specific limitations inherent to each data type, they require prior knowledge of the appropriate objective function (which is often unknown) of an organism [95]. Additionally, these approaches necessitate several preprocessing steps to effectively integrate CBM with multi-modal data, which can be a complex and challenging process [96].

11.3.4.2 ML as Input for CBM-FBA

An alternative approach involves incorporating input features from ML into FBA-based models for improving their predictive power or aiding model creation. Instead of solely relying on direct flux estimates generated by FBA, ML can be employed to analyze multi-omics data and generate data-driven flux boundaries. These can then be passed as additional constraints within the FBA model, effectively narrowing the solution space and improving the accuracy of the predictions.

A representative example integrates ML with constraint programming to predict metabolic fluxes [97]. This approach has demonstrated the power of ML to generate data-derived fluxes, which can then be incorporated as input constraints within the FBA framework, thereby guiding predictions. By integrating quadratic programming, the approach ensures that the predicted flux profiles satisfy stoichiometric constraints, enhancing the biological relevance of the results. Additionally, ML methods can also be used to estimate enzyme catalytic turnover numbers (kcat in vitro or kapp,max) at the genome-scale to parameterize FBA models, leading to more accurate predictions [98].

Also, efforts on unsupervised approaches to obtain additional constraints for the FBA formulation have shown promising results [99]. An interesting strategy is the learning of representations to characterize strain variations and identify metabolic states, which can be further utilized by CBM [100]. Similarly, an unsteady-state FBA framework has been successfully applied by incorporating PCA of the time-dependent metabolomic data, which helps identify the linear metabolic states to predict metabolic fluxes under dynamic conditions [101]. Beyond dimensional reduction techniques, clustering methods can also be applied in combination with FBA to group flux distributions (e.g. [102]).

Figure 11.1 synthesizes the major pipelines for integrating ML and CBM. The pipeline selection depends essentially on the desired output and the type of data available. Despite their successful application, these pipelines remain challenged by the high dimensionality, quality, and heterogeneity of multi-omics data, often showing significant forms of imbalance and skewness [103, 104]. To overcome this, more research is needed to further assess new ways to integrate complex data with these computational approaches.

11.4 ML-Based Approaches in Microbial Cell Factory Design: Case Studies

The rapid progress of ML, coupled with the increasingly wide data collection efforts, jointly offers a flexible and efficient toolkit for overcoming challenges in biotechnology and microbial biomanufacturing. This section illustrates how various computational approaches described in Section 11.3 can leverage Big Data to address various challenges in cell factory development using reference case studies. Particularly, some examples are highlighted to show how integrating ML with multiple recorded experiments can promote a variety of applications ranging from strain engineering and flux design to metabolic production.

11.4.1 ML-Based Approaches in Strain Engineering and Flux Design

Strain engineering aims to identify genetic strategies to optimize microbial performance. Traditionally, this was achieved through random alterations of genes, such as knockouts, changes promoting overexpression, or the introduction of heterologous pathways. A key focus of modern strain engineering is the iterative DBTL cycle [105], where large datasets are acquired to evaluate strain performance and orient improvements. In this regard, ML can play a critical role in extracting meaningful insights from Big Data, thereby guiding successive rounds of strain engineering and pathway design [106]. To accelerate the adoption of ML-driven strain development, significant efforts have been made to integrate these technologies into the DBTL framework, leading to increased efficiency and precision in bioproduction. As a first example, an integrated DBTL pipeline for strain optimization of fine chemicals was proposed by Carbonell et al. [107]. The workflow integrates computational pathway design, robotic-assisted DNA assembly, high-throughput screening, and ML-based learning cycles to efficiently prototype metabolic pathways. The Design stage employs bioinformatics tools for enzyme selection and pathway construction, followed by Build automation through robotic DNA assembly. The Test phase uses high-throughput metabolite screening, feeding results into the Learn phase, where ML models refine pathway performance predictions. By leveraging intelligent sampling and statistical learning, this approach significantly reduced experimental workload while accelerating strain development, achieving a 500-fold improvement in the production of (2S)-pinocembrin. Later, HamediRad and coworkers [108] demonstrated the power of ML-driven optimization within the DBTL cycle by developing an automated algorithm-driven platform called BioAutomata. BioAutomata employs Bayesian optimization to efficiently explore the vast design space of possible gene expression levels. This Bayesian approach effectively balances exploration of the design space with exploitation of promising regions, enabling efficient identification of optimal gene expression levels while minimizing the number of experiments required. By optimizing the lycopene biosynthetic pathway, their system evaluated less than 1% of possible pathway variants yet outperformed random screening by 77%. The combination of predictive modeling and high-throughput automation enabled rapid discovery of optimal pathway configurations, reducing both experimental cost and design complexity. Another interesting example is the Automated Recommendation Tool (ART) [109], an ML-based platform that integrates probabilistic modeling and a Bayesian ensemble ML approach to systematically recommend strain designs in the DBTL cycle. Using protein expression levels or promoter combinations as input, ART has been showed to be capable of predicting production levels of target molecules. A significant strength of ART is its capacity to quantify uncertainty in its predictions, allowing researchers to identify and explore under-characterized regions of the design space. A different ML-assisted workflow (called MiYA) designed for the combinatorial optimization of heterologous metabolic pathways was demonstrated successfully by Zhou and collaborators [110]. This innovative system combines artificial NNs with the YeastFab Assembly strategy to enhance the DBTL cycle. To demonstrate its effectiveness, MiYA was applied to optimize two biosynthetic pathways in Saccharomyces cerevisiae to improve violacein production. These studies highlight the significant potential of integrating ML algorithms into the DBTL cycle to accelerate strain development efforts.

More recently, deep NNs have demonstrated significant promise in rational strain engineering, including the discovery of pathways via retrosynthesis (i.e. identifying a series of biochemical reactions from substrates to desired molecules). Biswas et al. [111], introduced a data-efficient DL model for low-N protein engineering, utilizing the UniRep framework [33] trained on labeled mutants for extrapolating functional predictions of 10 million sequences via in silico directed evolution. Their approach was tested on two distinct proteins (avGFP and TEM-1 β-lactamase), where top AI-designed candidates exhibited up to 500% improvement in function from a single assay cycle. By leveraging global protein sequence knowledge and fine-tuning representations on local mutational landscapes, their method demonstrated superior generalization compared to classical protein engineering strategies. In another study, Segler and coworkers [112] employed a Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)-based retrosynthesis system that integrates deep NNs and symbolic AI to predict synthetic routes for small organic molecules. Their system incorporates three NNs: an expansion policy network to guide the search, a filter network to assess reaction feasibility, and a rollout network to estimate the best retrosynthetic moves. Trained on 12.4 million reactions from the Reaxys database (www.reaxys.com), the model significantly outperformed traditional rule-based retrosynthesis planning, solving almost twice as many synthesis problems 30 times faster than prior methods.

Various other strategies that allow precise control of gene expression and pathway optimization can also be enhanced using ML. A typical approach involves fine-tuning gene expression by modifying promoter and RBS elements. In this regard, ML has been used to guide the design of promoters and RBS sequences in a data-driven manner, a common strategy for regulating gene expression in rational pathway engineering. For instance, Meng et al. [113] demonstrated the power of NNs in quantitatively designing regulatory elements critical for controlling gene expression, such as promoters and RBSs. In this study, an NN was trained from a library of 100 mutated Trc promoters and RBS sequences, capturing a wide range of expression strengths. The model achieved a high correlation coefficient for both training and test datasets, indicating its strong predictive accuracy. Recently, ML has also been utilized to optimize multigene pathways for chemical production. For example, Jervis and coworkers [35] implemented an ML-guided approach (using SVM and feedforward NNs) to optimize the translational control of biochemical pathways in E. coli. This methodology was demonstrated on the mevalonate pathway, a nine-step metabolic route leading to the production of monoterpenoids. By analyzing a 5184-member RBS library, their model accurately predicted high-producing pathway variants while screening only 3% of the library. Applied to a recombinant monoterpenoid biosynthetic pathway, this strategy increased production titers by over 60%. These two last examples demonstrate the potential of systemically integrating high-throughput strain construction, testing, and ML to optimize multistep pathways for improving titers and yield. However, these strategies depend on the creation of extensive mutant strain libraries, restricting the applicability of ML to microorganisms with well-developed genetic engineering tools and protocols. One possible alternative approach is to feed an NN trained on available mRNA expression data to a multi-objective optimizer, such as the non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm-II (NSGA-II). This method was utilized by Kang and colleagues [114] to identify the optimal strain design that was showed to be capable of improving the lycopene titer, reducing the necessity for a large library. While less explored in the context of strain engineering, RL holds significant promise for optimizing strain performance. As a proof of concept, Sabzevari et al. [115] introduced a multi-agent RL approach, validated on a combinatorial strain library of Saccharomyces cerevisiae, focused on enhancing L-tryptophan biosynthesis. Their results highlight the potential of RL-based strain optimization, reducing reliance on trial-and-error methods.

Combining ML and CBM approaches using large-scale data has also emerged in strain engineering and flux design (i.e. selection of gene targets and their subsequent optimization). For instance, a comprehensive framework for multi-omics integration and predictive modeling in E. coli was introduced by Kim and coworkers [84]. They developed a multi-omics compendium integrating 4389 genome-wide profiles across 649 conditions, including transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, and fluxomic data. Using this resource, they constructed a multi-scale predictive model – integrating recurrent NNs, LASSO regression, and constraint-enriched FBA – trained on omics data and interaction networks to predict cellular states under unexplored conditions, outperforming previous models. Another interesting example of integrating FBA with data-driven approaches involves a hybrid framework that combines FBA with Bayesian factor modeling to predict metabolic pathway activation under various environmental conditions [93]. This approach uses multi-omic data, such as gene expression profiles, to augment an FBA model, enabling the integration of fluxomic and transcriptomic layers. By linking gene expression levels to metabolic flux constraints, the method captures cellular responses to dynamic environmental stimuli. The study focused on E. coli as a model organism and demonstrated the framework's capability to infer pathway activation profiles across time and under varying conditions, such as stress responses. This work highlights the ability of hybrid frameworks to elucidate genotype and phenotype relationships, providing valuable insights into bacterial metabolic responses for industrial strain optimization.

ML-based approaches have also been used to acquire fluxomic information from enzyme or gene expression data [116]. For example, Oulia and coauthors [117] applied DL techniques to predict metabolic fluxes based on enzyme levels in the glycolysis pathway of Entamoeba histolytica. In their study, they demonstrated how a deep NN model, trained on a large dataset of 68950 instances generated through synthetic data augmentation, outperforms classical ML. Similarly, Costello et al. [118] introduced an ML approach to predict metabolic pathway dynamics from time-series multi-omics data. Using metabolomics and proteomics, they demonstrated that supervised ML models (including RF and SVM) outperform traditional kinetic models in capturing metabolic flux dynamics. The model was validated on two biofuel-producing pathways, limonene and isopentenol, showing that predictions improved significantly with increased training data.

Biclustering has also been applied in strain engineering and flux design with relevant results. Alzahrani et al. [119] applied a graph-based biclustering algorithm to analyze growth phenotype datasets and identify co-fit genes that exhibit similar essentiality or dispensability under different stress conditions. By representing growth phenotype data as a two-dimensional matrix, they mapped the problem into the search for subspace patterns with constant values on columns (i.e. genes with similar growth patterns). More recently, Karim et al. [120] applied biclustering to analyze species-volatile organic compound (VOC) relationships by constructing bipartite networks linking species to their emitted VOCs. Biclustering was used to categorize species based on shared VOC emissions, uncovering evolutionary adaptations and enabling the engineering of VOC biosynthesis pathways.

11.4.2 Application of ML-Based Approaches for Metabolic Production

Metabolic production involves the use of microbes to synthesize valuable compounds, such as pharmaceuticals, biofuels, and industrial biochemicals from renewable bioresources. Following the design and construction of biosynthetic pathways within a microbial host, the efforts focus on enhancing the metabolic production of the target compound. In addition, scaling up the bioprocesses in microbial cell factories is essential for successful commercialization. While conventional approaches depend on trial and error, generally inefficient and time-consuming, ML-based approaches accelerate this process by analyzing large datasets to predict metabolic production and subsequently optimize fermentation conditions. Several studies in literature report advances from the application of ML-based approaches to enhance metabolic production [39, 44]. For instance, Colletti et al. [121] and Varman et al. [122] developed pure ML models to a priori estimate the chemical productivity of engineered E. coli and S. cerevisiae strains, given a set of inputs such as the number of biosynthesis steps, cultivation conditions, and genetic modifications. These regression models accurately predicted the product yields, providing important guidelines in fermentation processes. Another study examined the enhanced xylitol production by Debaryomyces nepalensis in a bioreactor through NN regressors coupled with a GA [123]. Using a dataset containing fermentation variables such as temperature, pH, oxygen transfer rate, biomass, and glycerol concentrations from previous time points, NN models were trained to predict the biomass growth and xylitol yield. By coupling these predictors with GA, they optimized fermentation conditions, demonstrating that ANN-GA outperformed regression-GA, improving xylitol production from 59.4 g/L to 65.73 g/L.

Other approaches have also shown reliable results in improving metabolic production of valuable compounds using large-scale data by combining metabolic modeling with ML. For example, Zhang et al. [124] integrated CBM (FBA) and ML models to optimize tryptophan metabolism in yeast. By employing CBM, they identified key metabolic engineering targets and constructed a combinatorial metabolic pathway library of potential strain designs controlled by various promoter combinations. To facilitate high-throughput characterization, they developed a biosensor screening system, generating a fluorescence-based dataset of over 124000 experimental time-series data points from more than 500 different strain designs. The dataset, consolidating genotype data, growth profiles, and the biosensor output, was then used to train ML algorithms (EVOLVE [125] and ART [109]), which successfully predicted optimized metabolic pathways. The acquired results showed that this hybrid approach achieved up to 74% higher titer of tryptophan compared to the best initial design. In another study [126], a hybrid ML framework was integrated with genome-scale metabolic models to assess microbial factory performance. Using E. coli as an example, the authors manually curated a dataset of approximately 1,200 engineered strains from around 100 research articles, including key genetic modifications, bioprocess conditions and production metrics for over 20 different compounds, including succinate, L-lactate, and isobutanol. Then, by augmenting this dataset with FBA simulations, they generated additional metabolic features. Employing ensemble ML techniques, they demonstrated a high cross-validation accuracy in predicting strain performance based on titer and yield. Similarly, Czajka and colleagues [127] introduced an integrated framework combining knowledge mining, CBM, and an ML ensemble model using gene expression data and environmental conditions to predict bioproduction yields in Yarrowia lipolytica, spanning various products like organic acids, terpenoids, and lipids. While the framework showed promising results, its success depends on the availability of broad-scope data sources.

Recently, in 2020, a novel hybrid ML/CBM approach for controlling nutrient availability in a fed-batch culture has been developed [128]. Schinn and collaborators developed a hybrid computational approach integrating CBM with ML to predict the amino acid profile from bioprocess measurements in CHO cell cultures. By utilizing bioprocess data from 10 CHO clones with varying growth and productivity profiles, they trained a metabolic model to estimate amino acid uptake rates based on observed cell proliferation and recombinant protein production. Then, by applying statistical regression models, they corrected systematic biases in metabolic model predictions and implemented an exponential decay function to extend forecasts beyond steady-state assumptions. Their approach correctly forecasted the amino acid consumption dynamics over an 8-day culture period with an accuracy of up to 86%, enabling anticipatory control of nutrient feeding in bioreactors.

In the context of multi-omics integration, Zampieri et al. [129] employed a poly-omics ML approach to predict lactate production in CHO cells, integrating gene expression data with metabolic flux simulations. By reconstructing condition-specific genome-scale metabolic models based on gene expression from 127 CHO cultures, they estimated metabolic reaction rates using FBA. Then, by applying ML methods such as PCA and elastic net regression, they refined metabolic predictions and trained generalized linear models to predict lactate yields under different bioprocess conditions. In a second study, a CBM of Pseudomonas putida was developed, incorporating gene expression data and FBA to predict rhamnolipid biosynthesis [90]. Statistical and ML techniques were then applied to FBA-generated flux distributions to identify biomarkers and metabolic pathways for increasing rhamnolipids production.

Unsupervised approaches have also been used to improve the production of desired chemicals in microbial systems. For example, Morris et al. [130] proposed an unsupervised big data analytics pipeline focused on multivariate associations for identifying metabolic inhibitors and promoters to optimize the production process of monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) in CHO cell cultures. By applying the analytical pipeline to metabolomics data under varying fed-batch bioreactor conditions, the authors identified key metabolites influencing production titers. This analysis enabled the prioritization of the top metabolites, then used for metabolic pathway enrichment studies to better understand their roles in productivity. To validate these findings, the authors integrated transcriptomics data with metabolomics results, correlating gene expression changes with the production of specific metabolites. They identified amino acids that either inhibited or enhanced metabolite production and proposed modifications to feed media based on these insights. The optimized feed media resulted in an 8.2% improvement in mAb production, underscoring the practical value of this integrated analytical approach. A PCA-based framework was also applied to proteomics data to identify specific enzymes that limit the production of target molecules [131]. The analysis guided the manipulation of gene expression levels of the mevalonate pathway enzymes in E. coli and improved the production of limonene up to 40%.

11.5 Conclusions and Perspectives

This chapter covered notable advances in the application of ML-based approaches to address ongoing challenges in metabolic engineering to show how Big Data is revolutionizing industrial biotechnology. To this end, we first established essential grounds on descriptive and predictive modeling techniques in this domain, along with critical principles for experimental study design and data preprocessing. Particular attention is placed on examining the synergy between ML and existing approaches, including CBM and DBTL cycle framework, to fully tap into the transformative potential of hybrid approaches in metabolic engineering.

Real-world case studies in strain engineering, flux design, and metabolic production were explored to form a comprehensive picture of how ML-based approaches are driving innovations, paying particular attention to the quantification of their impact when possible.

Despite the opportunities of both supervised and unsupervised ML stances, challenges pertaining to the full exploration of multimodal data sources, the longitudinal nature of most experiments, emerging profiling technologies (e.g. single-cell multi-omics, fine-grained molecular binding activity), and ongoing DL advances, remain open. In addition, the design of the “best” ML-based approach is not trivial and is critically dependent on the specificities of the target problem and available data. In this context, broader efforts toward systematic comparisons and the automation of ML-based pipelines are expected [132]. In addition, as ML algorithms may show limits of extrapolating beyond the given data training ranges, particular care to the generalization capacity of the models (e.g. uncertainty-bounded estimates) is key to guarantee their suitability for unseen combinations of endogenous-exogenous factors, a critical need when optimizing metabolic systems.

Perspectives

A greater penetration of Deep Learning approaches in the metabolic engineering domain is expected in the upcoming years [133]. Deep generative models (e.g. GANs, VAEs) can be used to guide novel strain designs with improved metabolite production. Attention-based models yield the potential to capture complex relationships between metabolic inputs and fluxes. Sequence-to-function models can leverage transformer architectures for designing synthetic regulatory elements. Transformers like AlphaFold and ProtGPT2 are already assisting enzyme design for enhanced metabolic pathways. Finally, the capacity of DL architectures to capture the inherent dynamic nature of bioprocesses using, for instance, recurrent layering, as well as complex multilevel relationships using graph NNs, makes them appropriate candidates to directly learn from raw multivariate time series data produced by longitudinal studies without laborious feature engineering needs.

Transfer Learning can leverage knowledge from related tasks or organisms for improved predictive and descriptive capacity (e.g. [134]). Paradigmatic examples include transferring learned representations from well-characterized organisms (e.g. E. coli and S. cerevisiae) to predict metabolic functions in less-studied organisms, pretraining models on simulated or experimental pathway data to predict pathway performance across different conditions or strains, or fine-tuning models trained on fluxomics data from one condition (e.g. aerobic growth) to predict fluxes under different culture conditions or bioprocess setups.

Complementarily, Multitask Learning (MTL) can be applied to simultaneously solve multiple related prediction tasks by sharing knowledge across tasks (e.g. [135]), thereby leveraging synergies to improve model generalization and performance. MTL can be applied to predict multiple metabolic traits (e.g. yield, productivity, robustness) during strain design, predict molecular properties (e.g. binding affinity, toxicity, stability, solubility, activity) from shared molecular representations, design genetic circuits with optimal performance across diverse conditions or hosts, predict diverse phenotypes from omics data, or leverage different microbial strains or conditions to generalize metabolic engineering strategies.

We further expect the community to translate the ongoing potentials of Self-Supervision into the metabolic engineering domain by devising artificial tasks that do not require manual labeling for pretraining models (e.g. [136]), which can then be fine-tuned for specific downstream tasks. In this context, fluxomics can be reconstructed from incomplete or noisy data by predicting masked flux values to learn the underlying network structures. Similarly, shared embeddings of unlabeled multi-omics data can be learnt by masking whole layers, phenotypes, and molecular markers, as well as latent representations of bioprocess data by predicting masked growth rates, metabolite abundance or yields under varying conditions.

Finally, the emergence of ML approaches with guarantees of trust (e.g. uncertainty quantification), explainability, and traceability [137] can be further leveraged by metabolic engineering tasks for a diversity of ends, including avoiding unintended consequences like toxic by-product formation or biosafety hazards, acquiring new insights into metabolism and pathway interactions, enhancing transparency for regulatory compliance, and strengthening agency in collaborative innovation and industrial applications.

Next-Generation Metabolic Flux Analysis Using Machine Learning

Ahmed Almunaifi

1University of California, Department of Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering, 420 Westwood Plaza, Boelter Hall 5531, Los Angeles, CA, USA
2Stevens Institute of Technology, Department of Chemical Engineering and Materials Science, 1 Castle Point Terrace, Hoboken, NJ, USA

12.1 Introduction

For much of the 19th and 20th centuries, biochemistry and computing have taken independent paths. Following the crowning achievements of solving the double helix structure of DNA and building the first modern computer in the mid-20th century, the two fields grew exponentially and started influencing each other (Figure 12.1). Neurons and their network formation in the human brain inspired mathematicians and computer scientists to develop artificial neural networks (ANNs). Automation and information handling in computers inspired biologists and biochemists to develop next-generation sequencing (NGS) and bioinformatics. As the two fields become more intertwined, innovative solutions to global challenges in health and energy are arising. One of the outcomes is the development of advanced metabolic profiling frameworks that propel biotechnology and medicine. These approaches build on the efforts of metabolic models (described in Chapters 1 and 2), metabolomics (described in Chapter 10), and flux models (described in Chapters 9 and 11). Here we focus our attention on the dynamics of metabolism and explore the role of machine learning (ML) in elucidating them.

12.2 Dynamic Nature of Metabolism

Organisms consist of several complex networks of biochemical reactions (see Chapters 1 and 2). Metabolism is one of them that is fast-acting and responsible for generating cellular energy currency and biochemical building blocks in changing environments. In other words, while the structures of metabolic networks are invariable, they are dynamic and constantly regulated to maintain homeostasis.

Metabolic networks consist mostly of enzyme-catalyzed reactions and some spontaneous reactions. In both reaction types, increasing substrate concentrations leads to higher reaction rates. In the former, however, a finite number of enzyme active sites leads to saturation behavior of reaction kinetics, which is known as Michaelis-Menten kinetics. Enzyme activity, or the rate of enzyme-catalyzed reaction, is also influenced by the concentrations of products and effectors, which can exert positive or negative regulation. Thus, each metabolite wears many hats, acting as a substrate and a product as well as an activator and an inhibitor to various enzymes. Putting together enzymes and metabolites engenders a metabolic network and an emergent property, autoregulation, which guides transient metabolic states to stable steady states.

Let us look at an example of a reaction in glycolysis that is catalyzed by phosphofructokinase (PFK).

PFK catalyzes the phosphorylation of fructose-6-phosphate (F6P) to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate (FBP) by coupling the conversion of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) to adenosine diphosphate (ADP). The reaction rate, vPFK, may be expressed as a reversible Michaelis-Menten-like equation.

(12.1)
