Determination of reaction rates requires the concentrations of substrates, products, effectors, and enzymes as well as kinetic, thermodynamic, and regulatory information. In practice, determination of fluxes across metabolic networks is challenging due to the number of concentration measurements and kinetic parameters that are necessary to compute fluxes.

Mathematical models of metabolism that detail reaction kinetics and thermodynamics confer a quantitative knowledge of time-dependent metabolic activities. However, the kinetic and thermodynamic parameters constituting mathematical models (Michaelis constants km, catalytic constants kcat, equilibrium constants Keq, etc.) are seldom known for exact physiological conditions of interest (e.g. pH, temperature, and ionic strength). The use of mathematical optimization, ensemble modeling, and deep learning obviates the need for measuring the full set of model parameters. The concentrations of enzymes and metabolites, with the help of the measured and predicted parameters, determine reaction rates, which in turn constitute ordinary differential equations (ODEs) describing the time evolution of metabolite levels through mass balance.

An example of a global optimization technique used to infer kinetic parameters is a genetic algorithm (GA) [1]. The method generates multiple starting points for local optimization, crosses, mutates, and selects improved solutions iteratively. GA has been used to determine the parameters of large kinetic models starting from a set of “guessed” values as well as time course experimental data of metabolite concentrations. The input values are used to parameterize kinetic models and simulate the concentrations of metabolites, which are then compared to experimental measurements. The results are a set of model parameters that best represent observation (1, 2). GA approaches have been used to study allosteric regulation of enzymes in modeling a metabolic futile cycle, glycolysis, and the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) in E. coli, and fed-batch fermentation processes, to name a few (3–5).

Ensemble modeling is another approach that circumvents the need for complete information on enzyme kinetics of reactions in a metabolic network [6]. In this method, an “ensemble” of kinetic models is created to reach the same steady state in terms of metabolite concentrations and flux distribution. The kinetic models are primed to a steady state. The steady-state flux can either be measured from experiments (often nutrient uptake and product secretion rates) or obtained from a flux balance of each metabolite. Thermodynamic constraints can be incorporated to parameterize the ensemble as well as the inclusion of enzyme regulation information if available. Ensemble kinetic modeling has been used in several studies, including its application in central carbon metabolism of E. coli and cyanobacteria, and the trehalose pathway in Saccharomyces cerevisiae (6–8).

Neural networks are emerging alternatives in kinetic modeling. RENAISSANCE (reconstruction of dynamic models through stratified sampling using ANNs and concepts of evolution strategies) is an ML framework that can parameterize kinetic models with physiological relevance without the need for training data. RENAISSANCE captures the nonlinear behavior of parameterized kinetic models through feedforward neural networks (FFNNs) and optimizes them with natural evolution strategies (NES). The ML framework has been used to model Escherichia coli metabolism in agreement with experimentally observed steady states and dynamic responses [9]. Another example of an ML framework that has been used for dynamic modeling is REKINDLE (reconstruction of kinetic models using deep learning). REKINDLE is an unsupervised deep learning-based method that utilizes generative adversarial networks (GANs) [10]. REKINDLE trains the GANs with data generated from existing kinetic modeling frameworks, such as Monte Carlo sampling. These computational techniques have facilitated kinetic modeling despite the limited availability of kinetic parameters (Table 12.1).

12.3 Flux Balance Analysis and Metabolic Flux Analysis

The combination of biochemical measurements and computational tools has enabled kinetic modeling of metabolism. Let us consider a scenario in which we have incomplete knowledge of enzyme regulation. The knowledge gap would lead to incorrect kinetic equations for reaction steps with missing regulation. Would a kinetic model built upon the incorrect equations accurately depict biochemical reality and physiology? Likely not, but perhaps under limited circumstances. How can we quantify metabolic activities and elucidate the dynamics of metabolism under any circumstances without knowing the full details of reaction kinetics and regulation?

Flux balance analysis (FBA) and metabolic flux analysis (MFA) come to our rescue by providing a systems-level overview of metabolic pathway utilization. Both analyses are computational approaches that yield flux distributions throughout a metabolic network without reference to underlying catalytic and regulatory mechanisms. In mammalian systems, including human cells and organoids as well as research animals, flux analysis reveals anomalies and dysregulation in metabolism that lead to or accompany diseases. In model systems such as E. coli or S. cerevisiae, flux analysis reveals bottlenecks in metabolic pathways for bioproduct synthesis and suggests metabolic engineering strategies. In non-model organisms, whose metabolism is even less understood, FBA and MFA enable the mapping of metabolic activities and provide the basis for deeper mechanistic studies.

How do FBA and MFA compute fluxes and how are they different? Unlike the parameterized kinetic modeling approach, FBA and MFA rely solely on steady-state mass balances on individual metabolites in the metabolic network. In FBA, steady-state mass balances are expressed as a system of linear equations with reaction fluxes as variables. The linear system can be expressed in the matrix form Sv=0, where S is the stoichiometric matrix and v is the vector of steady-state fluxes that satisfy mass balances for all metabolites (Figure 12.2). The solutions to this linear system lie in the null space of S, and a specific vector of fluxes for all reactions in the metabolic network are chosen by linear optimization of a physiologically relevant objective function (e.g. maximizing ATP production, maximizing growth rate, maximizing product synthesis, etc.) within linear constraints defined based on thermodynamics and experimental measurements. Due to its computational efficiency, FBA is widely employed with genome-scale models containing hundreds to thousands of metabolic reactions.

While flux solutions from MFA must also lie in the null space of S, MFA requires an experimental input to discern the “best” fluxes that correspond to experimentally measured isotopic labeling patterns imprinted on metabolites when cells metabolize nutrients that contain heavy isotopes [16]. The isotopes can be traced across reaction networks using mass spectrometry (MS) and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy. MFA solves the nonlinear least squares problem of fitting measured isotope labeling patterns, which adds computational costs with increasing numbers of reactions in the metabolic network. Thus, MFA most often employs pathway-scale metabolic models containing a dozen to a few dozen reactions. The cumomer [17] and the elementary metabolite unit (EMU) [18] frameworks simplify the mass balance equations by reducing the number of equations that need to be solved. A cumomer represents cumulated isotopologues that share the same isotopic state in a subset of atoms in a compound (Figure 12.3). An EMU is a subset of atoms in a compound. These frameworks facilitate the simulation of isotopic labeling patterns on metabolites without using the complete set of isotopologues. Software applications, such as INCA, Metran, 13CFLUX2, mfapy, and freeflux, integrate isotopomer measurements from MS and NMR for MFA (Table 12.1) (14, 15, 19–21).

Carbon-13 (13C) is the most frequently used isotope for flux determination. Carbon makes up the backbones of metabolites and biomass; thus, studying 13C labeling patterns unravels the different metabolic pathways utilized to create them [22]. MFA uses mathematical optimization to obtain fluxes that simulate labeling patterns that are most consistent with experimentally measured isotope labeling patterns [23]. Simulated isotope patterns are compared to measured isotope patterns by the variance-weighted (σ2) sum of squared residuals (VarSSR) of mass isotopomer distributions (MIDs) of individual metabolites (Figure 12.4).

(12.2)

Since atom mapping differs between pathways, pathways of interest dictate which tracer(s) should be used for flux determination. Thus, the accuracy of fluxes determined by 13C MFA depends on the composition and the positional labeling of tracers [24].

12.4 Incorporating Machine Learning into Metabolic Flux Analysis

FBA identifies the limits of a metabolic network and predicts overall phenotypes such as growth rate, gene essentiality, and feasibility of bioproduct synthesis. Compared to FBA, MFA predicts fluxes more accurately by incorporating isotope tracing information; however, MFA comes with a steeper learning curve. Expertise in atom mapping, isotope tracing, metabolic model construction, and mathematical optimization is required for implementing MFA.

The complexity of MFA has motivated the exploration of ML techniques to streamline MFA (Figure 12.5). A variety of ML algorithms exist today with their unique strengths and weaknesses. These algorithms can be broadly categorized into supervised and unsupervised learning methods. Supervised learning involves training models on labeled data, where the input features and desired outputs are known, while unsupervised learning aims to discover patterns and relationships in unlabeled data. The performance and applicability of ML models derived depend on the quality and quantity of the datasets used during the training stage.

12.4.1 Challenges in Applying ML to MFA

Before describing the different ML tools available for use in MFA, we discuss some challenges in applying ML to MFA. These challenges are rooted in data availability and the computational power needed to train ML models.

12.4.1.1 A Lack of Isotope Labeling Patterns and Flux Data for Training Machine Learning Models

Training datasets for flux analysis may be sourced from prior MFA results (25–27), including isotope labeling patterns [28] from MS or NMR [29]. While these methods provide detailed insights into metabolic fluxes, the availability of comprehensive and high-quality flux data is limited. The increasing scale and complexity of metabolic models present further challenges. For instance, the E. coli iAF1260 model [30], a widely studied genome-scale metabolic network, consists of 2,077 internal reactions, 304 exchange reactions, and a biomass objective function. Generating sufficient experimental and MFA data to train ML models for such large systems is laborious and costly.

Experimental results from different sources and different measurement techniques also pose undesirable variability, which may lead to discrepancies that can propagate through the training data [31]. Missing data, corruption, and errors impact the ML models' training and prediction accuracy. Addressing these problems through data cleaning is essential to ensure effective learning [32]. Consistent annotation of data, whether human- or machine-generated, is also critical.

12.4.1.2 Variable-Size Input of Isotope Labeling Patterns for Flux Prediction

Fluxes may be obtained through the use of different isotope tracers and the measurement of different metabolites. For example, for glucose, which has six carbons, there are 62 positionally 13C-labeled glucose tracers (26=64 less two trivial glucose isotopologues that are uniformly 13C-labeled and uniformly unlabeled). Depending on the organism of interest and available instrumentation, measurable metabolites would also vary. Therefore, the size and type of input isotope labeling patterns to ML models have large variability.

12.4.1.3 Incorporation of Disparate Data Types

Multi-omics data (e.g. transcriptomics and proteomics) and thermodynamic constraints constitute additional information about metabolic fluxes. However, since these data and constraints are in different formats, integration of heterogeneous datasets for training ML models and predicting fluxes poses challenges. Furthermore, the relationship between other omics data and fluxes is not fully established except in the simplest cases (e.g. gene knockout or silencing resulting in zero or negligible flux through the reaction that the corresponding enzyme catalyzes), adding to the challenge of incorporating datasets beyond isotope labeling patterns for flux prediction.

12.4.1.4 Initial Computational Cost

Substantial computing power is needed for gathering, generating, and cleaning up training data as well as for training, validating, and testing ML models. Furthermore, if the structure of metabolic networks or atom mapping across metabolic networks is unknown, constructing a metabolic model suitable for flux analysis would be computationally and experimentally costly. On the upside, once ML models are trained, using them should be less computationally intensive than running mathematical optimization to obtain fluxes.

12.4.2 Available Computational Tools

ML models are based on algorithms that learn patterns from training data to make predictions or decisions. We demonstrate computational tools and examples of ML algorithms that have been used and may be adapted for various tasks in flux determination.

12.4.2.1 Sampling Metabolic Fluxes for Training ML Models

Since an ML model is only as good as its training data, sampling fluxes that are feasible and physiologically relevant is an important task. One of the most common ways to sample fluxes is Monte Carlo (MC) sampling, a randomized algorithm that explores constrained flux spaces. When the flux space is large (genome-scale models), MC sampling, such as the hit-and-run (HR) algorithm, is efficient. Improved HR algorithms, such as the artificial centering hit and run (ACHR) and the coordinate hit and run with rounding (CHRR), have been developed to satisfy narrow solution spaces [33]. COnstraints-Based Reconstruction and Analysis (COBRA) is a constraint-based FBA toolbox available in MATLAB and Python that facilitates imposing physicochemical constraints on a metabolic network to obtain steady-state fluxes [12]. COBRA utilizes the MC-HR techniques mentioned above to estimate flux distributions in metabolic networks. ANNs and GANs are ML frameworks in which MC sampling algorithms can be integrated to generate flux training datasets.

12.4.2.2 Atom Mapping Throughout Metabolic Networks

Determining the fate of atoms through a metabolic network forms the basis of isotope tracing. Atom mapping across individual reactions from the substrate sides to the respective product sides provides information about the relationship between flux distributions and isotope labeling patterns. Atom mapping models may be developed by integrating the knowledge of reaction mechanisms of metabolic enzymes in literature, but it becomes tedious as the scope of the metabolic model increases and with unknown reaction mechanisms. Therefore, computational methods have played a complementary role in mapping atom transitions [34]. Potential ML tools for atom mapping include graph convolutional network (GCN) and transformer architectures. GCNs are a specialized type of neural network designed to operate on graph-structured data. GCNs have been employed for studying cell-wise metabolic flux using single-cell RNA sequencing data [35] and predicting gene essentiality in E. coli [36]. Transformer encoder models are an unsupervised ML approach commonly used for text analysis. They have been used for mapping chemical reactions exclusively from reaction SMILES as training data [37]. The transformer architecture has also been used to develop an ML language model called BERT (bidirectional encoder representations from transformer) that has been widely used in synthetic chemistry for predicting chemical reactions and retrosynthetic pathways (22–24).

12.4.2.3 Selection of Information-Rich Isotope Tracers

Information-rich isotope tracers should provide a quantitative knowledge of fluxes through metabolic pathways of interest. Software packages such as INCA have been developed to aid in the selection of information-rich isotope tracers. INCA allows users to simulate isotope labeling patterns from metabolic fluxes [38]. Supervised learning ML models called support vector machines (SVMs) are used for classification and regression tasks and have been used to analyze gene expression, protein abundance data, and metabolomics data [39]. The ability of SVMs to separate and categorize data makes them a promising computational tool in the selection of isotope tracers. Another example of a supervised ML model is random forests (RFs). RFs are ensemble learning methods that combine multiple decision trees and aggregate them to enhance prediction accuracy and robustness. RF models have been employed in drug discovery for the identification of bioactive molecules, in studying cancer metabolic pathways, and risk prediction of heart failure patients (40–42). RFs may also be used to identify the utility of isotope tracers for flux prediction.

12.4.2.4 Other Helpful ML Tools

Reinforcement learning is a paradigm in which an agent learns to interact with an environment and maximize cumulative rewards through trial and error [43]. Reinforcement learning can be used to optimize dynamic pathways, which involve the temporal regulation of enzyme expression, and control gene expression in response to environmental cues or cellular states, allowing for precise regulation of metabolic processes. Transfer learning is a technique that leverages knowledge acquired from one domain to enhance performance in another related domain [44]. Transfer learning has shown promise in reconstructing gene regulatory networks by transferring knowledge from well-studied organisms to less-characterized ones [45], thereby accelerating network modeling in data-scarce contexts. Unsupervised ML tools that can be used for different tasks in MFA are clustering and association algorithms. Clustering algorithms analyze unlabeled raw data, find patterns and then group the data into clusters based on similarities [46]. K-means clustering algorithms are capable of handling large datasets and have been used to aid in the mapping of metabolite distributions in human tonsil tissue using unlabeled data [47]. Association algorithms are another way of finding patterns in datasets and correlations between variables [48]. These algorithms can be harnessed to discover new patterns in complex systems such as metabolic networks and isotope tracing therein.

12.4.3 A General Workflow for Machine Learning-Based Metabolic Flux Analysis

ML-based flux determination consists of four steps, which can find approximate counterparts in MFA. It begins with metabolic model construction, followed by training data generation, ML model training, and testing (Figure 12.6). To train and test ML models for flux quantitation, paired data consisting of isotope patterns and fluxes are needed. The differences in ML-based and optimization-based strategies have implications for the execution of flux computation and the analysis of the resulting fluxes. Nonetheless, both flux determination approaches rely on the same fundamental relationship between fluxes and isotope labeling patterns, and the ingredients needed for flux determination remain the same.

Ingredients for flux quantitation are:

  1. Metabolic network
  2. Isotope labeling patterns
  3. (optional) Rates of nutrient uptake and product secretion

12.4.3.1 Metabolic Model Construction

As a first of flux determination, a metabolic model that describes the relationship between metabolic fluxes and isotope labeling patterns must be constructed. A metabolic model consists of (1) a stoichiometric matrix and (2) atom mapping. A stoichiometric matrix (S) numerically represents a metabolic model based on the stoichiometric coefficients of substrates and products for individual reactions (Figure 12.2). Each row of S corresponds to a metabolite, and each column corresponds to a reaction in the model. Metabolic models are available from various databases such as BiGG [49]. Atom mapping describes how the atoms are reshuffled from substrates to products through biochemical reactions (Figure 12.4). Atom mapping information is available from databases such as MetaCyc [50].

12.4.3.2 Acquiring Training Data

ML models require a set of true input-output pairs for training. In the context of flux determination, input consists of measured isotope labeling patterns (Figure 12.3) and, if available, transport fluxes, and output is the complete set of intracellular and transport fluxes. However, there is often no measurement-based “ground truth” for intracellular fluxes. Instead, training data may be generated by simulating isotope labeling patterns (e.g. isotopologues and MIDs) using physiologically relevant fluxes. An important consideration for data generation by simulation is the sampling of fluxes. Constraining the flux space based on physiology, thermodynamics, and/or heuristics makes sampling more effective. To minimize bias in flux prediction, sampling should evenly cover the constrained flux space (15, 51). Once the flux space and sampling algorithms are chosen, the size of training dataset should be determined to balance between computational efficiency (which may mean insufficient coverage of the flux space) and accuracy (which may require exhaustive flux sampling). Once a set of fluxes has been chosen for labeling simulation, data generation for ML-based MFA is analogous to the step in MFA where isotope labeling patterns are simulated in the search process of optimization. The key difference is that while optimization-based MFA requires iterative simulations for each flux prediction, ML-based MFA frontloads all simulations and learns the relationship between isotope labeling patterns and fluxes for all future flux predictions.

12.4.3.3 Training Machine Learning Models

The paired data, consisting of isotope labeling patterns and metabolic fluxes, are split into three bins for training, validating, and testing ML models. Training involves ML model (algorithm) selection and parameter tuning. The performances of ML models are evaluated on the accuracy and precision of their flux predictions. A loss function that quantifies the discrepancy between the true and predicted fluxes is used to guide the training and evaluation of ML models.

(12.3)

The loss function in ML model training and evaluation contrasts with the objective function in optimization-based MFA, which quantifies the discrepancy between the measured and simulated labeling patterns.

(12.4)

The different loss functions mean that optimization-based MFA aims for the accurate simulation of isotope labeling patterns, whereas ML prediction aims for accurate flux prediction. While it is expected that the two approaches would yield similar fluxes from the same isotope labeling pattern input, the results may not necessarily be similar because the same or similar isotope patterns may arise from disparate flux sets.

12.4.3.4 Evaluation of Machine Learning Models

The trained ML models may be evaluated for their accuracy and precision of flux prediction using the testing data that ML models have not seen during the training stage. Comparison between the predicted and true fluxes from the reserved testing data quantifies the bias and width of the error distribution, which sets the basis of accuracy and precision of ML flux predictions. The evaluation process in ML-based MFA contrasts with that of optimization-based MFA, which involves multiple rounds of optimization starting from different initial flux sets to map local and global minima and confidence interval determination by how sensitive VarSSR is to the fluctuation of fluxes at the identified minimum VarSSR. In evaluating ML models, goodness-of-fit analyses (e.g. coefficient of determination, reduced X2 test, etc.) should be performed.

12.4.3.5 Execution: Computing Metabolic Fluxes Directly from Isotope Labeling Patterns

Major advantages of ML-based MFA are ease of use, minimal computational cost, and accessibility. Unlike optimization-based MFA, which requires iterative simulations of isotope labeling patterns, ML models require a single round of computation. Furthermore, while the present optimization-based MFA software is a powerful tool for interpreting isotope labeling patterns and computing metabolic fluxes, expertise in metabolic model construction and programming is required to obtain reliable flux output. The execution of ML-based MFA requires one simple step of inputting experimental measurements of isotope labeling patterns. Given these considerations, prebuilt metabolic models and pretrained ML models streamline flux determination and open up the utility of MFA to the broader research community.

12.4.4 Improved Speed and Accuracy of ML-Based MFA

Various ML architectures and overall software designs may be implemented to improve MFA. Recent work has demonstrated that ML models predict fluxes accurately and rapidly from isotope labeling patterns [11]. ML-Flux, a two-stage ML framework, employs deep-learning-based imputation to handle variable measurements of isotope labeling patterns and successive neural networks to convert the full isotope patterns into metabolic fluxes (Figure 12.7 and Table 12.1).

To understand the ML-Flux framework, it is helpful to begin by describing the second-stage ML model, which is a fully connected feedforward ANN that takes in isotope labeling patterns of all metabolites within a metabolic model and outputs linearly independent free fluxes. Free fluxes are expanded using linear algebra and knowledge of the network solution space to produce the full flux distribution through the metabolic model. This approach ensures that no redundant flux predictions are made and that all metabolites are mass balanced.

One issue with using the ANN model trained with complete isotope labeling datasets is that the requirement for flux prediction is a comprehensive measurement of isotope labeling patterns of all metabolites, which is technically challenging due to low metabolite concentrations and stability. To bridge this gap between experimental measurement and rigid ANN input, ML-Flux employs another deep learning model that uses a partial convolutional neural network (PCNN). PCNNs have been used for image inpainting, in which damaged parts of an image are restored. Since isotope labeling fractions take values between 0 and 1, analogous to grayscale pixels in black and white images, ML-Flux uses PCNN-based inpainting to fill in the isotope labeling pattern matrix that may have missing elements to metabolite measurement challenges.

The two-stage ML platform for flux prediction demonstrates how deep learning can streamline flux quantitation from experimentally measured isotope labeling patterns. The results of ML-Flux show promise as flux predictions were as accurate, if not more accurate, compared with optimization-based MFA software. Some other unmistakable advantages of ML-Flux are its speed and accessibility as flux prediction is done in a single step within a few seconds. Development of advanced ML architectures and their application to MFA would further increase the accuracy and speed of flux predictions.

12.4.5 Toward Dynamic Flux and Isotope Labeling Analysis

Dynamic metabolic flux analysis (DMFA) tracks metabolic states that change over time, whereas classical MFA maps metabolic steady states. In batch and fed-batch cultures, cellular metabolism does not stay constant throughout the whole culture process. Thus, DMFA is needed to extend flux analysis to more real-world applications.

DMFA assumes that metabolism is at pseudo-steady state; the process dynamics occurs at a time scale that is slower than the time scales of intracellular metabolic changes. For example, consider a fed-batch reactor in which E. coli is cultured to produce acetate. The extracellular environment changes as glucose is consumed and acetate is produced. Intracellular metabolism responds and adjusts to these changes.

Two common techniques used in studying the dynamics of metabolic systems are the average flux method and the piecewise flux dynamics method. The average flux method provides a way to acquire snapshots of metabolism broken into distinct phases of metabolic state. The average transport fluxes are calculated and implemented into standard MFA for each phase. The downside of this method is that fluxes are not time-resolved. To determine time-resolved fluxes, data smoothing techniques such as spline fitting, moving average, and polynomial fitting followed by applying MFA consecutively over narrow time intervals are used. Alternatively, using piecewise linear flux function over time segments, the piecewise flux dynamics method enables the direct fitting of the time series data to determine fluxes [52].

Another approach to conducting DMFA is a hybrid of dynamic modeling and MFA. The hybrid method is a quasi-dynamic analysis that integrates a series of steady-state MFA models with a system of differential equations representing the dynamics of biochemical networks. The MFA equations cover the reactions with unknown kinetic properties, whilst the ODEs include the reactions with known parameters [53]. DMFA becomes computationally demanding with increasing time resolution and kinetic details. The use of neural network layers can augment kinetic and regulatory insights, which impart mechanistic insights useful for drug discovery and treating diseases. ML frameworks have been developed to predict metabolic pathway dynamics better than traditional kinetic models through abundant proteomic and metabolomic datasets [54]. This shows the potential of data-driven models for predicting pathway dynamics, though the abundance of data remains a challenge.

A class of deep learning architecture, Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), are neural networks that are constrained by physical laws. PINNs constrained with known kinetics can solve ODEs faster than traditional solvers and thus can be used in solving DMFA problems. PINNs enabled studying the dynamics of wound healing assays, considering both biological and reaction-diffusion laws [41]. Another ML approach that can potentially be applied to DMFA is long short-term memory (LSTM). LSTM models are a type of recurrent neural network (RNN) designed to learn long-term dependencies over sequential data. LSTM models have been shown to predict real-time data about process variables using multivariate input for process monitoring and control [55]. Therefore, LSTM may be used for predicting dynamic fluxes from the time evolution of isotope labeling patterns.

12.5 Future Outlook

MFA has provided quantitative and actionable insights into biotechnology and medicine [56]. Researchers are tackling increasingly complex biological systems such as microbial communities [57] and genome-scale metabolic networks (58, 59). The increased complexity of metabolic networks demands a new paradigm of MFA. Furthermore, experimental limitations on metabolite measurement by MS or NMR pose challenges for resolving metabolic fluxes in large models.

To further improve flux quantitation in complex systems, the development of ML algorithms designed specifically for solving biological problems, including metabolic fluxes, rather than borrowing algorithms designed for different purposes, is essential. Since black box algorithms hamper the interpretability of the relationship between isotope labeling patterns and fluxes, explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) approaches are desirable so that we do not blindly rely on ML predictions [60]. By uncovering patterns and relationships within complex datasets, the application of ML to MFA imparts intuition for the inner workings of metabolism. In conjunction with the new knowledge, the development of sophisticated ML models would fully realize the next generation of MFA and its full potential in determining fluxes in metabolically heterogeneous populations of cells, such as microbial communities and multicellular organisms.

On the experimental front, use of novel isotope tracers and comprehensive measurement of metabolites would spur flux analysis beyond central carbon metabolism. Nitrogen tracing (e.g. using 15N-labeled glutamine) has already been used for mapping amino acid and nucleotide metabolism in cancer research, neuroscience and immunology, and gut microbiota (61, 62). Once 13C and 15N tracing is conquered, with advances in metabolite detection and quantification, other isotope tracers such as 2H, 18O, and 34S will broaden the horizon of MFA. We are cautiously optimistic that artificial intelligence will complement advances in biochemistry and analytical chemistry to become a transformative tool for improving quantitative metabolic analysis, imparting new knowledge, and advancing biotechnology and medicine (Figure 12.8).

Streamlining the Design-Build-Test-Learn Process in Automated Biofoundries

Enrico Orsi

1Technical University of Denmark, The Novo Nordisk Foundation Center for Biosustainability, Søltofts Plads 1, Kongens Lyngby, Denmark
2Microbial Cultivation Process Development Department, Novo Nordisk A/S, Novo Alle 1, Bagsværd, Denmark

13.1 Introduction

In the era of synthetic biology, the design-build-test-learn cycle (DBTLc) has become a formalized pipeline for standardized, iterative optimization of biological parts [1–4]. Each module in the cycle serves a specific function and fulfills distinct objectives, each presenting its own set of challenges. Notably, the standardization inherent in the DBTLc framework can significantly enhance the throughput of iterations, enabling faster and more efficient advancements in synthetic biology [3].

As we are witnessing the pervasion of big data, artificial intelligence (AI), and machine learning (ML) technologies in all areas of biology [5–8], the DBTLc demands high-throughput approaches to generate and analyze vast amounts of data efficiently. In principle, the entire workflow in industrial biotechnology – from DNA synthesis to bioprocess optimization with engineered strains – can now be studied while generating (and analyzing) high-throughput data at every step [9]. Each phase of this pipeline is supported by iterative rounds of DBTLc, allowing researchers to refine designs systematically based on experimental results.

Successfully executing these high-throughput iterative cycles within biofoundries represents one of the grand challenges of this decade. To address this aspect, a global alliance of biofoundries has been established as a collaborative network [10]. This alliance aims to support the sustainable implementation of biofoundry infrastructures, advancing practices that contribute to a sustainable bioeconomy [11, 12].

This chapter provides an overview of how automated biofoundries accommodate high-throughput DBTLc and their applications in industrial biotechnology. It begins with an overview of the classic DBTLc framework, accompanied by examples of successful applications that highlight its transformative potential. The discussion then transitions to adaptations required for implementing DBTLc pipelines in automated biofoundry setups, emphasizing how automation enhances efficiency, scalability, and standardization in high-throughput data generation and collection.

Subsequently, we explore the global development of biofoundries, offering insights into their characteristics and contributions to synthetic biology. Then, we address current challenges that hinder biofoundries from reaching their full potential. These include technological bottlenecks, integration issues, and the need for further standardization and collaboration. Finally, we conclude the chapter with further perspectives and trends that are likely to streamline the workflow of automated biofoundries. By examining these aspects comprehensively, this chapter aims to shed light on how biofoundries can be optimized to drive innovation in synthetic biology while supporting sustainable practices in the global bioeconomy.

13.2 The Design-Build-Test-Learn Cycle (DBTLc)

The DBTLc paradigm for standardization and iteration in synthetic biology (Figure 13.1) is a concept that has its roots in (electronic) engineering principles [13]. By default, the DBTLc can be applied to the optimization of any biological part of interest, e.g. DNA assembly [14–18], protein engineering [19], metabolic rewiring [20–22], or even a whole bioprocess [23]. However, as detailed in subsequent sections of Chapter 13, a significant body of literature describes the use of the DBTLc for microbial strain engineering [13]. In this setup, microorganisms are studied and improved as cell factories for performing bioconversions of industrial relevance. For the sake of simplicity, we will adhere to this scope for describing the DBTLc modules in the next section.

13.2.1 The DBTLc Components

Within the context of engineering microorganisms, the DBTLc phases are structured in four segments:

Design. This phase has the scope of determining the strategy for the whole iteration. It includes choices of target modification to implement as well as the design of the biological parts to synthesize and introduce into the host for implementing such modifications. It could include, e.g. choice of heterologous genes to express, or the in silico design of plasmids for gene deletions. In some cases, use of genome-scale metabolic models, such as those described in Chapters 1, 2, and 9, can guide the design phase by identifying target genes to delete or overexpress [24]. Some public databases are also available for guiding the design phase. The Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) is one of the pioneering databases designed for the systematic analysis of gene functions, cellular processes, chemical compounds, and enzymes [25]. Similarly, the BRaunschweig ENzyme DAtabase (BRENDA) serves as a comprehensive resource for enzyme-ligand interactions, enabling the exploration of functional and molecular parameters of enzymatic reactions [26]. MetaCyc provides a curated catalog of metabolic reactions and enzymes across various microorganisms [27]. Software tools developed for extracting data from these databases and identifying viable design strategies have facilitated the rational engineering of metabolic networks. Notable advancements in this domain include Optknock [28], Fastknock [29], Retropath2.0 [30], SelenzymeRF [31], and EnzymeMiner [32]. Once the components for a given metabolic pathway have been selected, the corresponding DNA sequences must be designed and synthesized. This process leverages established frameworks such as BioBricks [33, 34], the SEVA plasmid system [35–37], and computational tools (e.g. RBS Calculator v2.1 [38, 39]), which enable automated, physics-based modeling of gene expression, an aspect covered in Chapter 3.

Build. The aim of this step is to create and assemble the biological parts required for the iteration. In strain engineering, this involves assembling the biological components to be tested, such as plasmids for heterologous gene expression or DNA cassettes for gene inactivation. Routine techniques include, for example, Gibson assembly [40], a one-step isothermal reaction that joins overlapping DNA fragments using exonuclease, polymerase, and ligase; Golden Gate assembly [41], a restriction enzyme-based method that utilizes type IIS restriction enzymes for seamless cloning; USER cloning [42], which uses uracil-containing primers to amplify PCR products, removes uracil residues, and assembles fragments through complementary overhangs; and traditional restriction-ligation cloning. This step also includes transforming these constructs into the final host. Recent advances in genome editing techniques, particularly the CRISPR/Cas toolkit [43–45], have significantly enhanced this process to enable the introduction of diverse types of mutations, including in non-model microorganisms [46–48]. When the goal of the DBTLc is strain characterization, this step can, in principle, be omitted.

Test. Here the scope is to measure the effect of the modifications implemented in the previous phases. It often involves cultivation assays followed by the quantification of a phenotype (e.g. a product molecule), typically through the calculation of titers (g/L), rates (g/L/h), and yields (g/g) [49]. This phase heavily relies on analytical techniques and is consequently considered the technical bottleneck of the DBTLc cycle. When performing multilevel strain characterization, such as through omics analyses [50], the throughput of these techniques is high, generating large amounts of data that require complex interpretation [51]. Genomics provides the foundational blueprint of an organism by analyzing DNA sequences to identify genetic variations and modifications in engineered constructs. Transcriptomics examines gene expression patterns, e.g. through RNA sequencing (RNA-seq), to understand regulatory responses and optimize modifications [52]. Proteomics investigates protein expression, modifications, and interactions, offering insights into the functional outcomes of genetic and transcriptional changes. Metabolomics provides detailed insights into metabolic states by profiling intracellular and extracellular metabolites, enabling a comprehensive understanding of biochemical pathway activities and cellular physiology [53–55].

Learn. Finally, the learning phase evaluates the iteration's success and determines whether a new design phase is needed. This step is often less structured, relying on ad hoc observations and literature data [56]. However, with the increasing amount of data generated per experiment, there is a growing need for a more structured, data-driven approach to this phase. In recent years, the application of ML in biotechnological processes has expanded significantly, driven by the emergence of next-generation algorithms such as deep learning – a subset of neural network methodologies that employs hierarchical architectures – and the availability of user-friendly development frameworks [57, 58]. As discussed in detail in the next section, these approaches enable data interpretation in the context of high-throughput data generation of a biofoundry.

13.2.2 Application of the DBTLc for Strain Engineering

Some examples of DBTLc use have become widely recognized and are now considered the gold standard in the field. One of the earliest DBTLc iterations in metabolic engineering was the decade-long effort to engineer Escherichia coli and Saccharomyces cerevisiae for the production of the antimalarial drug artemisinin. Beginning in 2003 with the heterologous expression of the eukaryotic mevalonate pathway in E. coli, approximately 25 μg/L of amorphadiene – the first committed precursor to artemisinin [59] – were produced. The authors reported improved titers from 25 to 25 g/L, a remarkable million-fold increase, ultimately leading to the one-step chemical conversion of artemisinic acid to artemisinin by 2013 [60]. The rationale behind switching from E. coli to S. cerevisiae as the production host, along with the full roadmap of this achievement, is extensively reviewed in a study summarizing the entire scientific journey [61].

Another notable DBTLc success story from the early 2010s is the engineering of E. coli for the production of 1,4-butanediol, a non-natural chemical building block used in plastics, polyesters, and spandex fibers. This effort, guided by genome-scale modeling in its design phase to inform rational engineering modifications in the build phase, achieved titers of up to 18 g/L [62]. Other DBTLc-driven advancements in biomanufacturing include strain engineering efforts that have achieved titers exceeding 100 g/L for various commodity chemicals, e.g. succinic acid [63], lactic acid [64], L-lysine [65], and glutaric acid [66]. Additionally, DBTLc approaches have been instrumental in optimizing both prokaryotic and eukaryotic strains as cell factories, expanding the number of domesticated strains available for biomanufacturing [67–75].

The growing success of DBTLc campaigns has driven the development of dedicated infrastructure to support these workflows. As we will explore in the next section, biofoundries represent a significant leap forward in standardizing and automating strain engineering. By integrating computation-driven design with robot-assisted workflows, biofoundries enhance throughput and accelerate strain optimization.

13.2.3 Description of Biofoundries and Their Operating Parts

A biofoundry is an advanced laboratory that leverages automation, robotics, AI, and high-throughput technologies to execute and optimize the DBTL cycle (Figure 13.1). These infrastructures are designed to standardize workflows, addressing challenges such as time-intensive manual procedures, variability in results and the increasing complexity of biological systems. The core components of a biofoundry include the following modules:

Design. These systems are blueprinted using computational tools to design DNA sequences, metabolic pathways and synthetic circuits [76, 77]. Advanced software, powered by ML algorithms, predicts the performance of engineered systems, facilitating a more targeted approach to bioengineering. As discussed above, several updated and refined databases provide extensive repositories containing gene functions, cellular processes, chemical compounds, and enzymes from several microorganisms, serving as an initial step for pathway design. These databases undergo continuous updates and refinements, establishing them as primary resources for selecting enzymatic activities and pathways in metabolic engineering and pathway design. The individual components are carefully selected and integrated into an in silico framework, collectively orchestrating complex functions that culminate in a blueprint prototype to be assembled in subsequent steps.

Build. In this step, the focus is on the physical assembly and synthesis of biological constructs through advance laboratory automation steps, including robotic liquid handlers for DNA assembly, high-throughput cloning platforms, automated colony pickers, and microfluidic devices for precise manipulation of biological samples [78]. In recent years, specialized toolboxes have been developed to incorporate novel functions into the microbial host of choice. Genome-wide modifications integrate rapid multipart DNA assembly methods with advanced genome engineering techniques [79–84]. As discussed above, a significant advancement in molecular biology has been the discovery of CRISPR and their associated Cas proteins, which have been adapted for gene and genome editing applications [85–87]. To enhance the scope of these technologies, multiplex-editing strategies have been developed, enabling the simultaneous modification of multiple loci within the eukaryotic and prokaryotic genomes [88]. When automated, these technologies enhance both the speed and extent of achievable mutations. Additionally, when optimizing DNA sequences at the single base-pair level, employing diverse libraries expands the range of potential solutions, particularly in the context of directed evolution efforts [89–91]. In certain cases, in vivo hypermutators can be leveraged to facilitate and refine these evolutionary processes [92, 93].

Test. Automated high-throughput screening (HTS) technologies are essential for evaluating the performance of engineered biological constructs, enabling rapid and efficient assessment of various biological and biochemical properties [94–96]. Automated bioreactors are essential for HTS of engineered biological constructs, providing precisely controlled environments for cell culture while continuously monitoring and adjusting critical parameters such as pH, oxygen levels, nutrient supply, and biomass production [97]. These systems enable real-time data collection, improving reproducibility and scalability in bioprocess development [98, 99]. In parallel, omics technologies play a crucial role in testing and characterizing engineered constructs [100]. The integration of automated cultivations with omics-based testing generates comprehensive, high-resolution datasets, facilitating advanced computational analysis, predictive modeling and iterative design improvements in synthetic biology and biotechnology.

Learn. SynBio relies on both mechanistic and ML models to extract insights from omics data, ultimately refining strain engineering strategies in the DBTLc [101–104]. Integration of advanced ML algorithms with automation enables the efficient utilization of large datasets, facilitating the prediction of novel interventions for process optimization [105]. In practice, mechanistic models represent molecular components and their interactions within a system, which provide enhanced interpretability, transparency, and explainability. These models help researchers understand the underlying mechanisms governing cellular behavior and guide hypothesis-driven engineering. In contrast, ML techniques, which leverage statistical and computational approaches, are particularly effective at identifying complex, nonobvious patterns in high-dimensional omics datasets [106–108]. By distinguishing key features that differentiate strains and experimental conditions, ML models can refine mechanistic models by highlighting missing or inaccurate components and interactions. This integration improves predictive accuracy and aids in designing more informative experiments based on data-driven model topology and simulation outputs. While ML models may lack full interpretability and transparency, they play a crucial role in extracting meaningful insights from large-scale biological datasets, ultimately expanding our understanding of cellular systems and driving the next iteration of strain optimization [109–111].

Finally, biofoundries include data integration platforms that rely on centralized databases and data management tools to ensure seamless integration and retrieval of information across the DBTLc. These platforms serve as the backbone of biofoundry operations by standardizing data formats, enabling interoperability between various software and laboratory automation systems and facilitating real-time data sharing [110].

13.2.4 Laboratory Workflows with Potential of Automation in Biofoundries

As described above, the DBTLc can be applied to several biological scopes. Biofoundries enable the automation of a wide range of workflows in biology, significantly reducing costs and accelerating timelines. A brief overview of the different workflows with potential for automation is presented in Table 13.1. Some examples of DBTLc that can be performed in biofoundries include but are not limited to:

DNA Synthesis and Assembly. The ability to synthesize large quantities of DNA and generate combinatorial libraries is fundamental in synthetic biology [112, 113]. Automated platforms in biofoundries can perform error-free synthesis and assembly of DNA constructs, creating libraries with thousands of variants for the subsequent steps [114]. Once synthesized, DNA fragments can be assembled into larger constructs. Several assembly methods have been developed, including both Gibson Assembly and Golden Gate Assembly. Both techniques have several advantages, being widely used in synthetic biology due to their efficiency and scarless integration of DNA fragments. For example, these techniques can be automated on liquid-handling robotic platforms. Researchers have automated a DNA assembly protocol using the Type-IIS restriction-based Modular Cloning (MoClo) technique on liquid-handling robots by optimizing pipetting parameters for different liquid viscosities (e.g. enzymes, DNA, water, and buffers) [115]. In addition, they developed a web-based tool (mocloassembly.com) that automates script generation and library construction from GenBank files. The tool includes optimized liquid classes, labware settings, and deck layouts, with DNA parts available via Addgene and Boston University's BDC ICE Registry. This workflow enables high-throughput, error-reduced DNA assembly, with sequencing data showing ∼95% accuracy and requiring only 4% of the manual effort [115]. Lastly, the improved version of MoClo, known as the RoboMoClo framework, employs a hybrid approach that integrates both hierarchical and iterative gene assembly strategies while utilizing fewer destination vectors compared to conventional MoClo systems [116].

Library Construction and Cloning. Combinatorial DNA libraries are crucial for exploring genetic diversity and optimizing biological functions. Libraries can be generated through site-directed mutagenesis, recombination-based methods or random mutagenesis. Key approaches include: (1) oligonucleotide-based mutagenesis, which introduces specific mutations at defined locations within a gene [117]; (2) error-prone PCR, which incorporates random mutations during PCR amplification to create genetic diversity [118]; (3) in vivo hypermutators to increase the mutational accumulation rate in the biological system [119]; (4) DNA shuffling, which involves recombination of different DNA fragments to generate novel sequences [120]; and (5) CRISPR-based library construction, relying on utilizing CRISPR-Cas9 to generate genome-wide knockout or activation libraries [121]. These libraries can contain thousands to millions of variants, enabling directed evolution and functional screening for optimized enzymes, regulatory elements, or metabolic pathways [122].

Protein Engineering. Biofoundries also facilitate the development of novel proteins with tailored properties by integrating automated technologies that streamline protein engineering workflows [92]. Automated directed evolution workflows, encompassing mutagenesis and HTS, enable researchers to identify optimized proteins for industrial, pharmaceutical, and agricultural applications. Directed evolution serves as a powerful technique in protein engineering, emulating natural selection to evolve proteins toward predefined functional objectives. This iterative process involves generating a diverse library of protein variants through random mutagenesis, followed by selection or screening to identify variants with enhanced or novel functionalities [123]. The automation of this workflow within biofoundries expedites the evolution process, allowing for the rapid identification of optimized proteins for various applications. HTS plays a crucial role in evaluating large libraries of protein variants to identify those with desirable characteristics [96]. Automated HTS platforms facilitate the rapid assessment of activity, stability, and specificity in thousands to millions of variants, significantly reducing the time and labor required compared to traditional manual methods. Furthermore, the integration of HTS with automated directed evolution, coupled with ML algorithms, enhances the efficiency of protein engineering by enabling predictive modeling of beneficial mutations. These computational approaches refine mutant library design and facilitate the identification of enzyme variants with improved catalytic properties, thereby advancing the capabilities of biofoundries in protein optimization [124].

Strain Engineering for Manufacturing. Engineering microbial or mammalian cells to function as “factories” for the production of valuable compounds, such as biofuels, pharmaceuticals, and specialty chemicals, is a major focus of biofoundries. Automation enables rapid prototyping and iterative optimization of these cellular systems. High-throughput prototyping entails evaluating multiple design iterations to identify the most effective solutions. Automated workflows in biofoundries enable the simultaneous processing of dozens or even hundreds of prototypes, significantly enhancing the efficiency of the DBTLc. This approach is particularly valuable for optimizing genetic circuits, metabolic pathways, and enzyme functionality [125–127]. For example, an automatic platform has been implemented for the biosynthesis of the flavonoid (2S)-pinocembrin in E. coli to demonstrate effectiveness of automated, iterative DBTL cycles. Through two DBTL iterations, the production pathway was enhanced by 500-fold, achieving competitive titers of up to 88 mg/L. Furthermore, the application of this pipeline to optimize an alkaloid biosynthetic pathway highlights its potential for accelerating microbial strain engineering and optimizing the production of diverse chemical compounds.

Process Optimization and Scale-up. Once a design has been validated, biofoundries play a crucial role in optimizing production processes for industrial scalability. Automated systems can fine-tune parameters such as fermentation conditions, media compositions, and downstream processing steps, ensuring maximum yield and cost-efficiency while maintaining product quality [128–131].

13.3 Geographical Distribution of Biofoundries Around the Globe

The implementation of successful workflows in biofoundries comes with its own challenges. As this new type of infrastructure is rapidly being adopted worldwide, the Global Biofoundry Alliance (GBA) was established in 2018 to accelerate the successful implementation of biofoundries through collaboration and knowledge sharing [10]. Initially comprising 15 noncommercial biofoundries from four continents, the GBA consortium has grown to 35 members as of 2025 (https://www.biofoundries.org/members), demonstrating the success of this initiative. Yet, the four continents represented remain North America, Europe, Asia, and Oceania. Despite being intrinsically similar in their equipment and organization, some of these biofoundries have specialized in specific objectives, leading to a certain degree of scope differentiation (Table 13.2).

The high capital costs of building a biofoundry make it challenging for emerging economies to develop such infrastructure. Establishing a biofoundry is complex and expensive, requiring specialized equipment and expert personnel, with operating costs far exceeding those of standard laboratories [11]. However, automation can significantly enhance speed, reproducibility, and reliability, positioning biofoundries as key hubs for synthetic biology programs and drivers of economic development. Moreover, as computational and robotic technologies continue to advance, their costs are expected to decrease, making biofoundries more accessible over time. Therefore, we hope that emerging economies will strategically invest in national biofoundries as part of their development agenda, anticipating future reductions in technological barriers. Finally, the current focus is on enhancing collaboration, optimizing workflows, and ensuring the reproducibility and reuse of efforts within the field. Biofoundries are already playing a crucial role in supporting the growth of startups and small-to-medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), while facilitating cooperation among private companies, academic institutions, and policymakers. This collaborative environment is driving the establishment of reliable, cost-effective standards for synthetic biology that are gaining broad acceptance among users. Additionally, local governments and regional funding bodies are actively supporting platform technologies within biofoundry hubs, helping reduce the risks associated with private investment in new ventures, while also fostering a thriving ecosystem of companies advancing synthetic biology technologies [134].

13.4 Challenges for Implementing Fully Automated Biofoundries

The long-term vision for biofoundries is to develop fully automated bioengineering pipelines that can execute the DBTL cycles seamlessly. However, several practical limitations currently hinder the realization of this goal. These challenges can be grouped into distinct categories based on their underlying causes (Figure 13.2).

One of the most significant hurdles in biofoundry automation is the lack of standardization across different platforms, equipment, and protocols. Unlike traditional engineering disciplines, biology inherently exhibits high variability due to differences in host organisms, genetic constructs, and environmental conditions. Most laboratory instruments still operate using proprietary software and non-standardized data formats, complicating integration efforts. Ensuring compatibility between robotic liquid handlers, analytical instruments, and computational design tools remains a substantial challenge. Without universally accepted standards, reproducibility is hindered, and cross-institutional collaboration becomes more difficult. Addressing these limitations is essential to unlocking the full potential of biofoundries.

Another major challenge lies in the ability of biofoundries to support scaling-up efforts. While small-scale automated workflows have demonstrated success in high-throughput strain engineering, scaling up strain performance to industrial levels remains complex. Many automated workflows require customization for specific applications, making it difficult to establish universally applicable automation pipelines. Additionally, large-scale fermentations present different gradients in nutrient availability as well as gas-liquid transfer dynamics, exposing strains to environments that differ significantly from benchtop reactors. The transition from benchtop automation to large-scale biofoundries necessitates significant investment in infrastructure and process refinement. Furthermore, biofoundries should be flexible enough to accommodate a wide range of biological systems, from microbial strains to mammalian cells. Recent efforts in this direction have been directed to implement “versatile” biofoundries, which can be adapted depending on specific requirements (e.g. anoxic conditions). However, this adaptability is hindered by the limitations of current robotic systems, which are often designed for specific workflows and cannot easily transition between different experimental setups. Overcoming these scalability and flexibility constraints requires innovations in modular automation systems that can be readily reconfigured based on experimental demands.

Biological systems are inherently complex, exhibiting dynamic behaviors, stochasticity as well as intricate regulatory networks. This complexity challenges the predictability and control required for biofoundry automation. Unlike mechanical or electronic systems, biological parts interact in nonlinear ways, making it difficult to design predictable, scalable workflows. Engineering biology at scale necessitates robust modeling and simulation tools capable of accurately capturing cellular behaviors under diverse conditions. Current computational models often oversimplify biological interactions, limiting their predictive power. Furthermore, emergent properties such as genetic instability, metabolic burden, and unintended interactions can introduce unexpected variability, complicating system optimization. Advancements in computational biology and HTS methods will be essential to overcoming these challenges.

AI and ML are poised to revolutionize biofoundries by optimizing experimental design, predicting biological behaviors and accelerating data analysis. However, the effective integration of AI-driven decision-making into fully automated workflows remains a formidable challenge. One key limitation is the availability of high-quality, structured datasets required for training AI models. Biological data often exhibits significant noise, variability, and inconsistencies, making it difficult to derive reliable predictive models. Furthermore, implementing AI in biofoundries requires real-time data acquisition, processing, and feedback loops. Developing robust AI frameworks that can dynamically adjust experimental parameters based on real-time results is an ongoing challenge. Additionally, ensuring that AI-driven decisions align with biological constraints and experimental feasibility is critical for successful implementation.

Another major bottleneck is the throughput variability across the DBTL cycle steps. Differences in the efficiency and duration of each phase can create imbalances, leading to bottlenecks and delays in workflow completion. For instance, while design and build phases may proceed rapidly with automated DNA synthesis and assembly, testing and learning steps often require complex biological assays that take days or weeks to yield meaningful data. Variability in cell growth rates, gene expression levels, and assay reproducibility can further complicate standardization across different DBTL iterations. Addressing these disparities requires improved automation of phenotypic characterization and data integration to ensure smooth progression through all phases.

The massive datasets generated by automated biofoundries present significant challenges in data management, storage, and analysis. High-throughput experiments produce vast amounts of sequencing data, metabolomic profiles, and imaging datasets that require efficient processing and interpretation. Data heterogeneity further complicates integration efforts, as different experiments generate diverse data types that must be harmonized for meaningful insights. Standardized ontologies, metadata frameworks, and cloud-based storage solutions are essential for managing large-scale biological datasets. Additionally, developing AI-driven data analytics pipelines will be key to extracting actionable insights, optimizing workflows, and improving system predictability. Also, high capital costs make it challenging for emerging economies to develop biofoundry infrastructures. Developing and maintaining automated biofoundries require substantial financial investment. High costs associated with robotic instrumentation, protocol implementation, AI-driven software development, and continuous system upgrades pose significant barriers to widespread adoption. While large-scale research institutions and companies can afford these investments, smaller laboratories and startups struggle to access automated biofoundry resources. Infrastructure constraints, including space requirements, power consumption, and maintenance demands, further complicate implementation. Traditional laboratories cannot support large-scale automation, necessitating extensive retrofitting or construction of dedicated facilities. Reducing automation costs and developing compact, modular biofoundries is key to enabling broader accessibility.

The automation of synthetic biology workflows raises concerns regarding biosecurity and ethical implications. Fully automated biofoundries possess the capability to rapidly design and construct genetically modified organisms (GMOs), which could potentially be misused. Establishing biosecurity measures, e.g. access control, screening mechanisms, and regulatory compliance, is essential to mitigate potential risks. Ethical considerations also arise in the context of intellectual property and equitable access to biofoundry technologies. The increasing privatization of synthetic biology tools and automation technologies may create barriers for smaller research institutions and developing nations. Addressing these concerns requires international regulatory frameworks that promote responsible innovation and ensure equitable distribution of biofoundry capabilities.

13.5 Perspectives and Outlook

We have seen how biofoundries can increase the throughput of the DBTLc and assist in iterating through the four phases using automated setups. The challenges mentioned in the previous section can serve as a foundation for developing trajectories that the field may adopt to maximize the impact of these infrastructures, which is the focus of this section.

Regarding the issue of standardization, it is desirable to establish standardized procedures and data management strategies as early as possible within the biofoundry framework – ideally through a pilot campaign before the first official one begins. Standardization should involve all team members across the DBTLc to ensure that generated data is correctly stored and promptly processed by the team responsible for the next phase. Implementing this strategy will help maintain high standards and ensure compliance throughout the entire cycle. Additionally, if the biofoundry's purpose is to serve customers, it should ensure that generated and transferred data is discussed and clearly understood by the customer. The further development of universally accepted standards will enhance reproducibility, streamline automation, and facilitate seamless collaboration between different biofoundries. We believe that associations such as the GBA might favor while developing technical roadmaps for implementing these universally accepted standards.

Optimizing and streamlining procedures within a biofoundry will inevitably emphasize certain types of processes or applications. This trend is already partially evident in Table 13.2, where some biofoundries specialize in specific DBTL cycles. We believe that a well-functioning biofoundry should have a clear mission and focus on refining procedures that align with its objectives – rather than serving as a generalized high-throughput platform for a wide range of scopes and applications. That said, biofoundries are also highly flexible in adapting to new workflows. This adaptability was demonstrated by the temporary repurposing of London's biofoundry for SARS-CoV-2 test screening, showcasing how these facilities can rapidly pivot to address urgent scientific and societal needs [135].

One example of such applications could be biofoundries that specialize in improving the scalability of microbial cultures for large-scale cultivation. There is an inherent limitation in simulating such cultivations in small-scale setups as a biofoundry would offer. However, adopting batteries of miniaturized stirred bioreactors for scale-down experimentation can offer a solution for simulating large-scale fermentation [136], including the investigation of multiple parameters that can hinder the transition from bench-top to cubic-meter fermenters.

When dealing with the unpredictability of biological systems, we believe that by focusing on a specific purpose for the biofoundry (e.g. mammalian cells), it will be possible to learn how the biological samples running through the DBTLc behave. This approach will allow us to understand which variables most affect standardization, thereby reducing variability. In the case of using different species of microorganisms, one potential solution to reduce cross-contamination is to introduce kill-switch mechanisms, e.g. temperature-sensitive mechanisms and CRISPR-based strategies [44], in the strains. This would help prevent their persistence in machinery when those systems are used for other species.

ML can aid in managing the unpredictability of biological systems by employing neural networks to predict biological features. For instance, in protein engineering evolution, models are now capable of creating artificial proteins with desired functions by training the network against millions of sequences available in databases [137]. Moreover, AI is expected to contribute to coordinating dry lab and wet lab activities across the different phases of the DBTLc. Although we are not there yet, we are getting closer and closer [3].

When dealing with different throughput sizes across the DBTL modules, one option could be to simplify (as much as possible) the amount of data to process during the data-heavy test phase. For example, using growth-coupled designs and associated screening campaigns for modules linked to growth fitness can be a useful ally for testing metabolic activities [77138–142] or evolving enzymatic functions of interest [92, 143–146]. Additionally, biosensors that provide fluorescence signals in the presence of a molecule could become useful tools to reduce the burden of the test phase [83, 147–149].

Establishing biofoundries requires high investments in capital and operational costs. To promote the emergence of biofoundries beyond Europe, North America, Asia, and Oceania, early-stage biofoundries could benefit from adopting cheaper and simpler apparatuses for their operational units. For example, small-scale (<20 mL volume) mini-bioreactors that are open source allow customers to interact and program them as needed [150]. We believe that this type of solution offers a good trade-off between throughput, controlled conditions, and lower capital expenses.

We foresee that the implementation of one or more of these perspectives will likely be adopted when developing new biofoundries or improving pipelines in existing ones. These approaches will enable biofoundries to optimize their workflows, reduce costs, and enhance scalability, ultimately fostering the growth and success of synthetic biology across various industries.
