Machine Learning-Enhanced Hybrid Modeling for Phenotype Prediction and Bioreactor Optimization

Oliver Pennington

1The University of Manchester, Department of Chemical Engineering, Oxford Road, Manchester, UK
2Fuzhou University, College of Biological Science and Engineering, North Wulongjiang Avenue, Fuzhou, China

14.1 Bioprocess Modeling and Optimization

14.1.1 Challenges in Bioprocess Modeling

The fourth industrial revolution, often referred to as “Industry 4.0,” requires the integration of smart technologies into manufacturing and industrial processes, playing a key role in the improvement of bioprocess efficiency, sustainability, and profitability [1, 2]. Due to the desire to further explore the potential of bioprocess automation, digitalization is currently at the forefront of bioprocess development [3]. Digitalization itself relies on the development of digital twins, a concept first proposed in 2002, in which bidirectional information transfer between the physical and digital domains occurs automatically. An effective digital twin facilitates real-time decision-making to maximize productivity, efficiency, and sustainability [4]. Modeling plays a key role in the development of a digital twin by simulating the physical domain in real-time, as well as potentially being used to predict unobservable states using soft sensors [5–7]. The main challenge associated with the development of a bioprocess digital twin is having a sufficiently accurate and validated mathematical model of the desired bioprocess to make rapid predictions and process adjustments [6], which is why official records show the first implementation of a digital twin within an industrial-scale bioprocess to be as recent as 2019 [8].

Developing models for fermentation bioprocesses is immensely appealing due to their various potential applications in frameworks such as process control and optimization, design of experiments (DoEs), and robust Quality by Design (QbD) for the ever-expanding production of biofuels, biochemicals, and biopharmaceuticals. In an ideal world, a fully descriptive mechanistic model could be constructed and applied to a bioprocess. However, designing such models and identifying their parameters to an adequate degree is highly challenging in bioprocessing; a fully descriptive bioprocess model would need to include various considerations such as self-inhibitory and self-catalytic feedback interactions, nonhomogeneous cell populations and phases, pH and temperature dependence, and even mass transfer limitations. As a result, simple models, such as first-order kinetics (which are commonly seen in chemical reaction systems [9]), are generally only applicable in narrow operating spaces. Therefore, when constructing a predictive bioprocess dynamic model, a balance must be found between the incorporation of sufficient complexity and the identifiability of the model parameters.

Bioprocess models found in literature can generally be categorized somewhere on the spectrum between machine learning (“data-driven” or “black box”) and mechanistic (“kinetic” or “white box”) [10]. Due to the aforementioned challenges associated with constructing a detailed mechanistic model, similar to those described in Chapters 1–2, 9, and 11–12, a sensible approach can be to build a simplified mechanistic model based on fundamental assumptions, often referred to as “first principles” [11]. Such models contain physically interpretable parameters for the system at hand, providing a degree of process insight. However, when assumptions are made for model derivation, the model itself will only be valid within the operating space where the assumptions hold true, meaning that its generalizability is lost. An example of a relatively simple kinetic model is the Monod model, which can fit some batch processes well; however, it ignores the potential inhibitory effects of high cell density (HCD) and high substrate concentrations [12]. Improving generalizability can be achieved by constructing a more detailed mechanistic model by introducing further process understanding; however, this will require more data, especially if additional state and control variables are introduced [10]. Moreover, adding further detail to a kinetic model without adequate hypothesis testing introduces inductive bias, which can actually reduce predictive capabilities of the model if the additional “knowledge” is not reflective of the system. In addition, increasing the intricacy of a kinetic model can increase the number of model parameters, thus reducing parameter identifiability and increasing model uncertainty [13].

On the other end of the spectrum, machine learning models have no prerequisite assumptions and can have strong generalization capabilities. For example, artificial neural networks (ANNs) are known to be able to approximate any function [14]. Employing pure machine learning models may sound appealing; however, large quantities of data are required to sufficiently capture the potentially nonlinear relationships, such as the relationships between substrates and cell growth, that are known to exist in biosystems. In addition, experiments are expensive to run, with some states being challenging to measure, leading to bioprocess data typically being multisource, multi-scale, noisy, and heterogeneous (a mixture of online and offline, and binary and continuous) [15]. Therefore, it is uncommon to have access to an adequate availability of data to train particularly nonlinear machine learning models for biosystems while avoiding overfitting. Moreover, machine learning models provide limited insight since the model structure itself is not physically interpretable, which is reflected by the poor extrapolative capabilities of machine learning models [10].

Irrespective of the model built, challenges such as batch-to-batch variation can also lead to issues with model training and validation. In addition, models can fall short during upscaling due to various phenomena, including differing flow regimes and more prevalent localized nutrient and cell population heterogeneity. As a result, upscaling often observes different process dynamics that result in lower yields and productivity or even total failure of the culture. Therefore, it is important to develop bioprocess models with the strongest possible extrapolative capabilities and generalizability to maximize both the accuracy of predictions and the ability to incorporate new information. As such, navigating the hurdles of developing a state-of-the-art bioprocess model is no simple task.

In this chapter, we will explore the use of machine learning to enhance our understanding of bioprocesses for modeling and optimization of fermentation processes, while making the most of the limited available experimental data and fundamental process knowledge.

14.1.2 Machine Learning for Bioprocess Modeling

Machine learning is a powerful tool for tackling a lack of process knowledge and high system complexity, which is often the case when assessing biosystems. The ability to handle intricate and poorly understood systems has encouraged the application of machine learning to a multitude of bioprocesses using a variety of techniques. In this section, we will explore a brief overview of different machine learning applications, both recent and not, in biosystems.

14.1.2.1 Principal Component Analysis and Partial Least Squares

Principal component analysis (PCA) is a linear dimensionality reduction technique that generates latent variables, called principal components, to explain the most variance in the original variables as possible [16]. PCA has been applied to several biochemical applications, including the identification of patterns between operating factors for biogas and biofuel production [17, 18], cell phenotype discrimination [19], process abnormality detection [20], and determining statistical similarities and differences between product distributions [21]. Due to the innate complexity of biosystems, dimensionality reduction can be particularly useful for problem simplification; a study combining PCA with an ANN for the productive capacity of Eucalyptus forest sites in Brazil showed that using the latent variables improved the ANN predictive capabilities [22]. Naturally, the biggest limitation of applying PCA to model bioprocesses is the inability to capture nonlinear relationships that can be observed within some biosystems due to the linear nature of PCA.

Partial Least Squares (PLS) is similar in many ways to PCA; however, instead of only using latent variables, it directly relates inputs to outputs in a linear fashion. For Multiple Input Multiple Output (MIMO) models, PLS can be directly used; however, in some cases, multiple models are used in parallel for each individual output in a Multiple Input Single Output (MISO) format [23]. In terms of biosystem applications, PLS has seen multiple applications, including classification and authentication of operating conditions in a yeast fermentation bioreactor [24], bioprocess monitoring [25], bioreactor state estimation and control [26, 27], mapping amino acid sequences with protein functions [28], and identifying flux relationships [29]. Similar to PCA, PLS is limited to applications where nonlinear relationships do not need to be fully captured.

14.1.2.2 Artificial Neural Networks

ANNs can capture complex nonlinear relationships and generally come in the form of an MIMO or MISO model. The inspiration for ANNs came from mimicking the human brain, where a network of neurons can be “activated” to pass on information [14]. Due to the ability of an ANN to capture nonlinear relationships, ANNs have seen a variety of applications in biosystems. For example, previous studies have utilized the potential of ANNs for predicting methane content and biogas production [30], predicting fermentation dynamics online [31], recognizing appropriate kinetic model structures for batch processing [32], optimizing the production of algal biofuel [33], predicting protein structures [34], and classifying the three-dimensional (3D) structures of enzymes [35]. ANNs are a powerful tool; however, the most prominent limitation in the application of ANNs to biosystems is the large amount of data that is required to capture complex nonlinear relationships. Such quantities of data are, at best, time-consuming or expensive to obtain and can be, at worst, infeasible to practically obtain.

However, in certain cases, the fundamental ANN structure can be expanded to enhance its ability to capture different relationships. For example, deep neural networks (DNNs) are a subcategory of ANNs that possess multiple hidden layers of nodes, allowing the approximation of more complex relationships. Successful incorporation of DNNs to biosystems in literature includes the construction of a hybrid model using a DNN for industry-scale fermentation [36], as well as the detection of “optimum tea fermentation,” where the tea has fermented enough to reach a desired quality but is yet to degrade due to over-fermentation [37]. However, since DNNs have multiple layers, they tend to have a higher number of parameters, which means they need even more training data than a shallow ANN to avoid overfitting. Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are another type of ANN that have been applied to biochemical processes. What makes them “recurrent” compared to a feed-forward neural network is the addition of an internal cycle; possessing this internal memory facilitates the learning of sequential data, such as time-series [38]. The capability of RNNs to identify sequential relationships has been harnessed in various biosystem applications, such as statistically summarizing amino acid sequences [39], and recognizing promoter sequences in genetic engineering [40]. In addition, an RNN demonstrated improved fitting and predictive capabilities when compared to a feed-forward neural network in monitoring simultaneous saccharification and fermentation of ethanol [41]. As with most ANNs, RNNs are not always applicable due to a lack of data availability for biosystems.

14.1.2.3 Gaussian Processes

Gaussian processes (GPs) return a probabilistic function, instead of a scalar, for each output variable from a given multivariate input. If no noise is assumed, a GP will fit exactly to the dataset [42]. GPs are particularly useful for uncertainty analysis as they can directly estimate the mean and variance of the output, unlike other machine learning methods. Several applications of GPs to biosystems have been presented in literature, including dynamic modeling and optimization of microalgal lutein production under uncertainty [43], ensuring the meeting of probabilistic constraints in bioreactor control [44], and estimating the cell density distribution in δ-endotoxins batch production from Bacillus thuringiensis [45]. A notable limitation of GPs is the high computational expense of calculating the inverse of the posterior, which scales poorly with higher-dimensional problems [46]. However, studies are being conducted on approximating symmetric positive definite matrix inversions under reduced computational cost, which extends the applicability of GPs [47].

14.1.2.4 Ensemble Learning

Ensemble learning (EL) combines several inducers (machine learning models that relate an input to an output) to generate a single output based on the outputs of each individual inducer. EL structures usually involve either a series structure, such as gradient boosting (GB), where the first inducer provides an initial prediction that is corrected by subsequent inducers, or a parallel structure, such as Random Forest (RF), where inducers in parallel have their predictions averaged or weighted to give a single output [48]. With RFs being the more widely applied EL approach to biosystem modeling [23], application examples include the optimization of fermentation for Rifamycin B production [49], building soft-sensors for industrial-scale fed-batch fermentation [50], and estimating the cetane number of fatty acid methyl esters (FAMEs) for biodiesel synthesis [51]. Although less utilized, GB has still been applied to cases such as liquid–liquid bioseparations [52] and predicting biohydrogen production [53]. Despite being a powerful modeling tool, EL can suffer from overfitting due to the large number of parameters involved and can be computationally expensive to run if the system has an excessive number of inducers.

14.1.2.5 Reinforcement Learning

Reinforcement Learning (RL) is a trial-and-error approach to learning optimal input sequences through the provision of rewards and penalties [54]. RL has proven to be highly effective in the gaming world, with chess engines such as the free-to-access “Stockfish Engine” outperforming the best human players in the world in a fraction of the thinking time [55]. With the ability to identify optimal input sequences, there exists a broad range of potential applications to biosystems, with previous studies exploring topics such as identifying an optimal control strategy for fed-batch biopharmaceutical processes [56], bioprocess kinetics identification [57, 58], and policy optimization subject to chance constraints for a stochastic dynamic bioreactor system [59]. Despite having the potential to be utilized in model-free applications [23], RL can also be limited by large data requirements; a trial-and-error approach can require a large number of experiments that, in certain cases, are too expensive and time-consuming to conduct.

14.1.2.6 Future Prospects for Machine Learning

As the push toward digitalization continues, new applications of machine learning are continually being explored. For example, studies have been conducted on automatic model generation through symbolic regression, which allows the automated generation of interpretable mathematical models for chemical and biochemical systems [60–62]. Automatic model generation has the potential to save large amounts of time by accelerating iterative model design, particularly when coupled with DoE for optimal gain of knowledge [62].

Alternatively, the concept of hybrid modeling, which will be explored in more detail in Section 14.1.3, has seen a recent surge in applications to bioprocesses [63, 64], despite hybrid modeling being first proposed as early as 1992 [8]. Section 14.1.3 will explore the flexibility and applicability of hybrid modeling to infer why this methodology is increasing in popularity over 30 years after its conception.

14.1.3 Introduction to Hybrid Modeling

14.1.3.1 Literature Review

The term “hybrid modeling” falls under the umbrella term “grey box” modeling as it lies on the spectrum between pure mechanistic “white box” and empirical “black box” modeling, as depicted in Figure 14.1. But why build a hybrid model? Combining the two approaches to make a hybrid model allows improvement upon the accuracy of a mechanistic model by integrating a machine learning component that avoids the introduction of extra inductive bias from additional mechanistic terms developed using further assumptions. In addition, less data is required to train a hybrid model than a pure machine learning model because the mechanistic backbone of the model can capture some nonlinear relationships within the system, therefore leaving fewer nonlinear relationships that need to be approximated by the machine learning model.

There are two common structures for hybrid models: parallel and series. In a series hybrid model structure, either the mechanistic or machine learning component feeds into the other, which subsequently yields the output, as shown in Figure 14.2a, meaning the mechanistic and machine learning models do not act independently, though the first model may be independent from the second. Alternatively, in a parallel hybrid model structure, the mechanistic and machine learning components lie independently of one another; their respective outputs combine to give a single output, as shown in Figure 14.2b. The decision on whether a series or parallel structure should be used depends on the problem at hand. Table 14.1 highlights various examples of the applications of hybrid models in biosystems seen in literature, as well as the respective structures of the hybrid models built. The most common motivation for constructing a hybrid model appears to be improving model predictive capabilities for subsequent monitoring, optimization, and control applications. As can be seen in Table 14.1, a common hybrid model structure is that where a data-driven model feeds reaction rates (or time-varying kinetic parameters), in series, to a form of mechanistic model. However, it should be noted that such a hybrid model configuration is not a generic series or parallel structure since, for dynamic systems, the hybrid model updates the state variables, which will in turn update the data-driven model and subsequently the mechanistic component; it is more of a cyclical series structure as illustrated in Figure 14.2c.

14.1.3.2 Hybrid Modeling for Biosystem Optimization

As mentioned in Section 14.1.3, improving model predictive capabilities using hybrid modeling is particularly beneficial for optimization applications. For example, the machine learning component can be easily retrained upon running a new experiment. A potential approach for training and validating a hybrid model is to run an experiment from DoE, whether it be a predicted optimum or an area of poor knowledge, and use the new data to update the machine learning component; repeating this process iteratively can be an efficient way to identify a suitable “optimal” solution while simultaneously generating a well-trained model.

Some examples of biosystem optimization studies using hybrid modeling are presented in Table 14.2. As one may expect, Table 14.2 highlights that objectives are often based on maximizing growth, yield, product titer, productivity, or profitability of the biosystem. Table 14.2 also shows that optimization from hybrid modeling is applicable over a variety of domains, whether it be mammalian cell lines, microalgal cultures, or fungi.

Overall, ANNs and hybrid modeling were first proposed in 1943 and 1992, respectively [8]. However, despite being a modeling technique that is now over 30 years old, hybrid modeling is still proving to be a capable approach for advancing biosystem development at an increasing rate. The relevance of hybrid modeling is thanks to a multitude of factors, including improved computational power, as well as access to new tools and techniques for data collection, such as free-floating wireless sensors, soft-sensors, and chemometrics [81]. Since hybrid modeling possesses a machine learning component, new data does not need to be incorporated directly into the mechanistic model if process knowledge is limited, thus keeping hybrid modeling relevant even as techniques for data collection advance.

14.2 Methodology for Hybrid Modeling

In this section, we explore the construction of a hybrid model for making predictions of a fermentation process. We start with the development of a preliminary mechanistic model before employing a machine learning component to improve model accuracy. Hereafter, uncertainty analysis is incorporated, and process optimization for a fed-batch fermentation system is illustrated. As a running example to show how the described methods are implemented, we imagine a batch process with homogeneous cell culture with a single substrate and a single product.

14.2.1 Mechanistic Model Construction

Preliminary mechanistic modeling aims to incorporate mechanistic information into the mathematical model. Implementing any mechanistic model structures introduces some inductive bias as all mechanistic models rely upon at least one assumption. As a result, it is important to stick to first principles and not venture into overly elaborate mechanistic structures, as they will introduce inductive bias and hinder the accuracy of a hybrid model. An example of an appropriate mechanistic relationship would be the assumption that each cell has the same specific uptake rate of substrate qS, the same specific production rate of product qP, and the same specific growth rate μ, irrespective of cell density, resulting in the system of ODEs shown in Eqs. 14.1a–14.1c:

where CX, CS, and CP represent cell density, substrate concentration, and product concentration, respectively.

In this instance, we know that a model is needed to describe specific rates because, otherwise, the model structure implies that the cell culture will infinitely grow and excrete product while continuing to consume substrate even after substrate depletion, phenomena which we know to be incorrect. Although this may be sufficient mechanistic information for cases with more data, it can be beneficial to include further assumptions to prevent phenomena we know to be unrealistic. Since introducing further assumptions introduces inductive bias, the assumptions should be simple in nature. For example, introducing Monod kinetics for growth and substrate ensures that non-negative substrate concentrations will be maintained while allowing kinetic relationships between zero-order and first-order with respect to the substrate concentration [82]. In order to prevent infinite growth of cells, we can also assume a first-order decay rate with respect to cell density. The resulting mechanistic model is described in Eqs. 14.2a–14.2c:

(14.2a)
(14.2b)
(14.2c)

where μmax is the maximum specific growth rate, μd is the specific death rate, is the maximum specific substrate consumption rate, and KS is the saturation constant (the substrate concentration at which half the maximum specific consumption rate is achieved [82]). It should be noted that although the specific death rate and specific product production rate are likely to be some function of state variables (since products can be self-inhibitory or lead to cell death), we may not have enough knowledge of the system to make valid assumptions. Therefore, it is better to leave unknown relationships to the machine learning component that commences construction in Section 14.2.2.

The next step for the mechanistic component construction is parameter estimation of the mechanistic model, which involves solving the optimization framework described in Framework 14.3:

(14.3a)
(14.3b)

where the objective function in Eq. 14.3a minimizes the difference between the simulated state variables Ci(t, β) and their corresponding experimental measurements and measurement standard deviation for state i at time point t up until the final measurement time tf.

Optimization Framework 14.3 can be carried out using a variety of tools. Gradient descent algorithms such as interior point optimization (IPOPT) are appropriate and can be freely accessed using the fmincon function in MATLAB or the Pyomo and SciPy packages in Python [83–85]. Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) can also be used to generate good initial guesses in cases where gradient descent algorithms converge to poor solutions as a result of sensitivity to the initial guess. However, its gradient-free nature prevents it from guaranteeing convergence to any local optima if used on its own.

Uncertainty analysis of the mechanistic model should also be conducted to assess the model's fitting performance. This can be addressed by calculating the uncertainty of each parameter from the Hessian of the objective function in Eq. 14.3a (referred to here as Z for simplicity) with respect to the estimated parameters β*. The Hessian matrix of the parameter estimation objective function with respect to the estimated parameters H(Z, β*) is inverted to generate the corresponding covariance matrix Cov(Z, β*) of the model, as in Eq. 14.4:

(14.4)

where the diagonal of the covariance matrix represents the individual parameter variances [86]. Monte Carlo sampling can be used to generate parameter confidence intervals (in this chapter, we recommend the use of 95% confidence intervals, which corresponds to two standard deviations from the mean) and subsequently model trajectory confidence intervals. Confidence intervals are important for gauging the predictive capabilities of the model; a model may appear to capture data well using the nominal parameter values, but if confidence intervals are large, it will be less likely to make predictions with high precision. It should be noted that, at this point, if the mechanistic model predicts well within the desired operating range with adequately sized confidence intervals, the model is unlikely to require the further addition of a machine learning component. However, if predictive capabilities are poor and/or confidence intervals are inappropriately large, introducing a machine learning component could be greatly beneficial, the first step of which is described in Section 14.2.2.

14.2.2 Time-Varying Parameter Estimation

A mechanistic modeling does not always yield the predetermined desired predictive capabilities with sufficiently low uncertainty, making them inadequate for their applications. Under the assumption that further alterations to the mechanistic model cannot confidently be made, the introduction of a machine learning component could be advantageous as it can increase model accuracy while maintaining good generalizability.

Since we have a mechanistic backbone, it can be assumed that poor model performance is due to missing information from the model structure, meaning some of the constant parameters within the model are not constant parameters but time-varying functions of state variables and operating conditions. Henceforth, we will refer to such hidden functions embedded within parameters as time-varying parameters. The most appropriate parameters to dedicate to be time-varying are parameters that have the highest uncertainty, which are identified using the covariance matrix calculated in Eq. 14.4; parameters with the highest standard deviation to nominal value ratio are deemed “most uncertain.” Normalizing standard deviation with respect to the parameter nominal value avoids potential bias introduced from the units chosen to describe the parameter. Sensitivity analysis must subsequently be conducted to ensure the chosen parameter has an appropriate effect on the mechanistic model trajectories; if not, the parameter should be removed altogether as it has a negligible impact on the model's accuracy.

Once the time-varying parameters have been identified, the end goal is to simulate them as a function of state variables and operating conditions using a machine learning model. Training the machine learning model is conducted in two stages: (1) identifying appropriate time-varying parameter profiles over the entire time course, and (2) training a machine learning model to estimate time-varying parameter profiles using corresponding state variable profiles and process conditions. Assuming that the most uncertain parameters in Eqs. 14.2a–14.2c are found to be μd, KS, and qP, identifying their respective time-varying profiles is achieved with a simple adjustment to Eqs. 14.2a–14.2c and parameter estimation Framework 14.3. The resulting parameter estimation framework is presented in Framework 14.5:

where is a weight for the regularization term that penalizes dramatic deviations time-varying parameter k, and θk(tθ) is the time-varying parameter of the nominal parameter k from time tθ to time tθ + Δtθ. We recommend that each time-varying parameter discretization step Δtθ to be no less than the time difference between consecutive measurements in order to minimize overfitting. Increasing the value of results in stronger penalization of time-varying parameter deviations, thus reducing the overfitting of noisy data. However, this will also reduce the fitting accuracy as the data-fitting term in Eq. 14.5a is prioritized less.

Once time-varying parameter profiles have been identified, the simulation of state variables should have increased in accuracy. Therefore, the time-varying parameter profiles can be assigned to corresponding state variables and necessary operating conditions for training of the machine learning component, which is discussed in Section 14.2.3.

14.2.3 Machine Learning Model Construction

Regardless of the machine learning component chosen, the overall training aim is the same: generate a data-driven model that takes state variables and key process operating conditions as inputs to predict corresponding time-varying parameter values as outputs. For the simple batch example, we have multiple inputs, CX(t), CS(t), and CP (t), and multiple outputs θμd(t), , and θqP(t), at each time-point t from solving Framework 5. The inputs and outputs can then be related in the form of an MIMO machine learning model that is not directly dependent on time. In order to train the machine learning component, a loss function that minimizes the difference between the data-driven models predicted time-varying parameters and Section 14.2.2 estimated time-varying parameters is required. A general form of the loss function is shown in Eq. 14.6:

(14.6)

which represents a Mean Absolute Error (MAE) loss function (often referred to as L1 Loss) [87, 88] where u(tθ) represents the control action at time tθ (for example, an adjustment of flowrate), w and b are the weights and biases of the machine learning component, C is the vector of state variables [CX, CS.CP], and n is the number of datapoints used in training. A similar framework uses the Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss function (often referred to as L2 loss) [88], as shown in Eq. 14.71:

(14.7)

Once training of the machine learning component is complete, the final hybrid model, with fixed weights w and biases b, takes the form shown in Eqs. 14.8a–14.8c:

(14.8a)
(14.8b)
(14.8c)

Section 14.2.3 will consistently refer to the machine learning model as a single MIMO model. However, it should be noted that using several MISO models (one for each time-varying parameter) is theoretically sound, but it may require a larger number of parameters. In this section, we will use an ANN as the machine learning model as an example. As highlighted in Section 14.1.3, ANNs are commonly implemented within hybrid models as the machine learning component due to their ability to capture highly nonlinear relationships. Smaller networks (networks with fewer hidden layers and fewer nodes within each layer) are preferred where possible, as they contain fewer weights and biases, thus reducing overfitting of the training data. However, the size of the network will vary case-by-case and a variety of different architectures should be trialed to gauge the best performance on both training and validation.

In order to mitigate overfitting, the dataset should be split into three independent datasets; a training dataset that is used to train the ANN; a separate dataset for validation of the ANN that is not used during training, where hyperparameter retuning can take place, and a third dataset for testing the final model [89, 90]. The partitioning of a dataset into training, validation, and testing subsets depends on the quantity and diversity of data available; however, multiple permutations of data partitioning should be tested in order to assess the sensitivity of training to the data partitioning. Once the dataset has been partitioned, each variable should be individually standardized or normalized. In this chapter, we follow the commonly used standardization approach where each variable is linearly transformed to have a mean of zero and a standard deviation of unity [91], which has been known to improve the training speed and accuracy of neural networks [92, 93].

Once the ANNs of varying structures are set up and the data has been appropriately partitioned, training can commence. There are several choices to be made when training an ANN that change case-by-case, examples of which include incorporating regularization terms, the number of epochs, batch size, and finally, the optimization algorithm used to train the ANN.

Regularization terms can be added to the training objective function to reduce or remove unnecessary parameters and avoid overfitting [94]. Several variations of regularization terms exist, including L1 and L2 regularization that penalize the absolute ANN parameter values and squared ANN parameter values, respectively [95]. For example, introducing the L1 regularization term to the MAE loss function results in the objective function illustrated in Eq. 14.9:

(14.9)

where λL1 is the penalty weight that can be increased to penalize weight magnitude more at the cost of ANN fitting. Similarly, adding an L2 regularization term to the MAE loss function yields the objective function shown in Eq. 14.10:

(14.10)

Epoch number and batch size refer to the way in which data is fed to the training algorithm. Batch size dictates how many datapoints per batch to process before updating the ANN parameters [96]. Batch size can be reduced from the size of the full training dataset in cases where the training dataset is too large to process in a single iteration [97]. Epochs are simply how many times the entire dataset is seen by the optimization algorithm [96]. So, increasing the number of epochs can improve the fitting of the ANN to the training data at the cost of longer computation time and an increased risk of overfitting. Early stopping is a form of regularization that assesses the trained ANN performance on validation data and terminates training if a stopping criterion is met [98], thus avoiding overfitting from using an excessive number of epochs.

Training an ANN generally involves back-propagation [99], which uses the chain rule to calculate the gradient of the loss function with respect to the ANN weights and biases. Several tools exist for ANN training, one of which is the Python package PyTorch [100], in which different loss functions, regularization terms (and weights), batch sizes, and epochs can be chosen.

14.2.4 Hybrid Model Uncertainty Estimation

Quantifying uncertainty is an important step in process model development, offering valuable insight into prediction confidence by assessing its expected precision. This effectively means that uncertainty analysis can be viewed as a form of model validation [101], despite often being overlooked as such, as excessive model uncertainty on a validation dataset can be a sign of overfitting of the training dataset [102]. Although some level of uncertainty is inevitable, especially in biosystems, minimizing model uncertainty supports the development of optimal control strategies, such as strategies used in QbD methodologies.

In the context of hybrid modeling where the most uncertain and influential parameters have been regressed by the machine learning model, it can subsequently be assumed that hybrid model uncertainty will mostly stem from the data-driven model. One such methodology for uncertainty estimation is bootstrapping, a method widely applied in machine learning for quantifying uncertainty and improvising model stability and robustness [103, 104]. Bootstrapping involves using different random samples of the training dataset to train multiple independent machine learning models. Each model is then combined with the mechanistic component to make its own hybrid model. Having several hybrid models instead of one means multiple state variable trajectories are generated; sampling the different trajectories facilitates the calculation of confidence intervals that quantify the model uncertainty.

Data sampling for bootstrapping can be completely random, or they can follow a strategy; a previous study conducted bootstrapping such that all data over predetermined periods of time within the experimental time horizon were eliminated for the training of each model [105]. Simulating scenarios where the system experiences missing information over a given duration helps assess how well a model generalizes to periods of incomplete data, an example of which is when sensors in an industrial bioprocess fail and require a fixed time horizon to be repaired. It should be noted that using GPs to simulate the machine learning component, instead of an ANN, can be beneficial for uncertainty analysis as they automatically generate the confidence interval of time-varying parameters and, therefore, the overall hybrid model. However, GPs are not always simple to implement due to their lack of an explicit model structure and are not suitable for systems with high-dimensional inputs, as discussed in Section 14.1.2.3.

14.2.5 Considerations for Hybrid Model Construction

There are multiple options when constructing a hybrid model. This section provides a brief overview of some key considerations that can be made during the construction of a hybrid model, particularly when using an ANN as the machine learning component.

14.2.5.1 Hybrid Model Greyness

Hybrid model “greyness” refers to the ratio of white box to black box modeling within the hybrid model. No metric exists for the quantification of “greyness;” however, we know when “greyness” is being increased or decreased relative to an initial model design. For example, implementing more mechanistic knowledge would be moving toward the “white” end of the “greyness” scale. Although the hybrid model “greyness” will vary case-by-case, a study investigating the effects of differing hybrid model “greyness” found that incorporating more specific mechanistic knowledge can increase the risk of incorporating incorrect inductive bias into the model [69], meaning mechanistic knowledge should only be incorporated in high confidence.

14.2.5.2 Discrepancy Hybrid Modeling

Hybrid modeling does not always require a machine learning model for the simulation of time-varying parameters; discrepancy hybrid models take the output of the mechanistic component and correct it with a data-driven component, similar to GB EL. For instance, when applied to the mechanistic model described in Eqs. 14.2a–14.2c, a discrepancy hybrid model would take the form shown in Eqs. 14.11a–14.11c:

(14.11a)
(14.11b)
(14.11c)

where ɛi(C(t), u(t), w, b) is the discrepancy term for state i that is itself a function of state variables and operating conditions in the form of a machine learning model with weights w and biases b. Comparing discrepancy hybrid models to hybrid models with time-varying parameters was investigated in a previous study for a chemical system, which found the discrepancy model to perform worse than other hybrid model structures for a dynamic system [106, 107].

14.2.5.3 Machine Learning Component

As discussed in Section 14.1.2, a multitude of machine learning approaches have been applied to bioprocesses, all of which are potentially applicable to hybrid modeling provided the limitations of the machine learning component are not exceeded by the problem at hand. For instance, when dealing with systems with high-dimensional inputs, incorporating a dimensionality reduction-based ML model, such as PCA, could be greatly beneficial. On the other hand, if quantified model uncertainty is a critical requirement for later use, then using GP could be the preferred option due to its direct computation of output mean and variance. However, if the process is known to have time-dependent or sequential mechanisms, such as the changing composition of CHO cells [108], then using an RNN would be a better option, as the hidden state is able to simulate internal memory. As such, when deciding the ML component to be used, one needs to first consider not only the amount of the data available but also the ultimate goal of the hybrid model construction.

14.2.6 Dynamic Optimization Using Hybrid Modeling

As previously highlighted in Table 14.2, bioprocess models are frequently implemented for optimization purposes. Dynamic optimization in the context of bioprocesses refers to the identification of optimal operating conditions for a process over time, such as batch, fed-batch, and continuous systems. Since a number of bioprocess models incorporate Ordinary Differential Equations (ODEs), the dynamic optimization of bioprocess must incorporate a form of numerical integration within the optimization algorithm, resulting in non-convex optimization problems that are not trivial to solve. Some optimization problems also deal with a process model with high stiffness, in which case, causing numerical issues with model discretization and resorting to gradient-free optimization algorithms, such as PSO and evolutionary algorithms, despite no guarantee of convergence to even a local optimum. Generally, it is recommended to either conduct gradient-based optimization from multiple initial points or utilize gradient-free optimization to identify a good initial guess from which gradient-based optimization can be employed, thus ensuring sufficient exploration of the solution space.

14.2.6.1 Optimal Feeding in Fed-Batch Bioprocesses

In this section, we outline an optimization framework for a fed-batch bioprocess as an example. When optimizing a fed-batch process, we can consider the degrees of freedom to be the dynamic substrate feeding rate. In this example, we propose maximizing final biomass cell density, for which the optimization problem, incorporating the hybrid model described in Eqs. 14.8a–14.8c, takes the form given in Framework 14.12:

(14.12a)
(14.12b)
(14.12c)
(14.12d)
(14.12e)
(14.12f)
(14.12g)

where C is the vector of state variables [CX, CS, CP], V is the volume of fluid in the reactor, F(t) is the volumetric feeding rate at time t, is the concentration of substrate in the feed, and F is the vector of discretized time-varying feeding rate. It should also be noted that optimization packages are often minimization-oriented, and minimizing the negative of a function is equivalent to finding its maximum. Eqs. 14.8a–14.8c have been modified to take the forms shown in Eqs. 14.12c14.12c–14.12 g to incorporate the mass balance of fed-batch operation. It should also be noted that introducing feeding can incur stiffness in the optimization framework, particularly with pulse feeding, which can pose challenges for gradient-descent optimization algorithms in some cases.

14.2.6.2 Dynamic Optimization Under Uncertainty

Uncertainty can be incorporated within a dynamic optimization framework through the objective function or constraints, depending on the application. For example, robust optimization requires an optimal solution to meet inequality constraints subject to all possible combinations of uncertain parameters within their uncertainty bounds, providing applicability to biosystems where product quality needs to be guaranteed or where certain conditions endanger cultured organisms. Therefore, robust optimization algorithms tend to identify a set of “worst-case” parameters (parameters most likely to violate constraints); the optimum is decided using the “worst-case” parameters for constraints, instead of their nominal values [109]. A study looking at robust optimization algorithms for a penicillin production case study, where cell density and substrate concentrations had maximum allowable values throughout fed-batch operation, was presented in a previous study on robust dynamic optimization [110]. Although robust optima can be found, the solutions can be overly conservative; a similar approach that overcomes this issue is chance-constrained optimization, where a predetermined proportion of solutions are allowed to violate the uncertain inequality constraints [111]. However, this does require assumptions to be made regarding the manner in which parameter uncertainties are distributed. Both robust and chance-constrained optimization methodologies are computationally expensive for dynamic systems, and there is no guarantee of finding a global optimum in most cases [112, 110].

A less computationally expensive approach involves sampling parameters to generate several parallel models; optimization of the nominal objective function is then subject to the constraints for all parallel models, thus approximating robustness or the meeting of chance constraints. This multi-modal approach (i.e. scenario tree-based approach) was proven to violate constraints in fewer instances than solely using the nominal parameters in a previous study [113]; however, it did not achieve total robustness, unlike some more computationally expensive approaches that aim to solve a bilevel optimization problem to identify the “worst-case” parameters, as demonstrated in a subsequent study [110].

When considering the uncertainty arising from the objective function instead of constraints, uncertainty can be accounted for by introducing a penalty term that penalizes the variance of the objective function [114]. Decreasing the penalization of variance allows the user to explore a region lacking in knowledge to possibly design new experiments, while increasing this penalty targets an optimum that is less likely to vary from model predictions. Again, generating a distribution of objective function values can be achieved by generating several models in parallel using different parameter samples, from which a mean and variance of the objective function can be calculated. Finally, given the complexity of dynamic optimization under uncertainty, this is not included in the current book chapter (neither is a detailed uncertainty analysis of hybrid model construction). However, interested readers can refer to [110] for a study on robust optimization of penicillin production, [115] for chance-constrained RL for batch process control, and [116] for optimization under uncertainty for beer fermentation.

14.3 Hybrid Modeling of Microalgal Lutein Production

14.3.1 Introduction to Microalgal Lutein Production

Now, in order to illustrate the potential of hybrid modeling, we will use microalgal lutein production as a case study to apply the hybrid modeling methodology explained in Section 14.2. Lutein is a carotenoid that has several health benefits for humans, including anticancer effects and prevention of cataracts [117–119]. However, humans do not synthesize lutein internally and instead rely on the ingestion of lutein from food and supplements. Although some foods naturally contain lutein, particularly fruit and vegetables [120], consuming lutein supplements can be more convenient and effective. The consumption of lutein supplements has helped drive the global lutein market to an estimated $369 million in 2024, with an expectation to grow to $461 million by 2029 with a Compound Annual Growth Rate (CAGR) of 6.1% [121]. Currently, commercial lutein production is entirely sourced from marigold flower petals [122]. However, microalgae, microscopic photosynthetic organisms that produce lutein for light harvesting [123], have the potential to become a commercially viable option for lutein production due to less labor-intensive harvesting, higher growth rate, and capacity for all-year harvesting (rather than seasonal) compared to marigold flowers [117]. Despite the potential commercial viability, several limitations exist within the microalgal lutein production process, namely the low lutein content within microalgal cells, resulting in low process yields, and high costs of microalgal biomass production compared to the marigold flower, which does not require as much energy or nutrient feeding to grow [117].

Various options are being explored to drive microalgal lutein production toward commercial viability, one of which is heterotrophic growth (the focus of this case study), where the lutein-producing microalgae grow in the absence of light, allowing ultra-high cell densities to be achieved, thus improving the potential yield and production rate of lutein [124]. In order to further optimize the production of lutein under heterotrophic growth conditions, experiments can be conducted to identify some optimal operating conditions, such as temperature and choice of substrate, as demonstrated in a previous study [124]. Additionally, another consideration is to carry out a fed-batch operation and optimize the feeding strategy, which can utilize different flow rates and feed compositions. However, the potential combinations of feed rates and compositions are numerous, making the optimal feeding strategy challenging to identify experimentally due to the multitude of degrees of freedom. Model-based optimization addresses the complex nature of optimizing a fed-batch process by efficiently exploring a wide range of potential feeding conditions, therefore reducing the need for experimental trials. In this section, we demonstrate the application of hybrid modeling to an HCD culture of lutein-producing microalgae for fed-batch optimization.

14.3.2 Experimental Setup and Data Availability

The case study in this section focuses on the growth of Chlorella sorokiniana under fed-batch conditions utilizing glucose and urea as substrates. Urea was favored over sodium nitrate as a nitrogen source for achieving higher biomass productivity in a previous study [124]. Glucose and urea are fed in a single combined feed continuously throughout the fed-batch process. The fed-batch reactor has an initial working volume of 2.5 L with a single feed rate capable of reaching up to 0.05 L/h. The feed was designed to permit feed concentrations of glucose and urea as high as 750 g/L and 60 g/L, respectively.

Measurements of cell density were collected every 12 hours, with measurements of glucose and urea concentrations taken every 12 hours for the first 24 hours, followed by more frequent sampling of 3–4 times per subsequent 12-hour interval, and lutein content was measured at 24-hour intervals. Two initial fed-batch experiments were conducted, both starting with the same initial cell density, glucose concentration, and urea concentration. The first experiment commenced with an initial 24-hour batch phase, followed by the maintenance of glucose concentration between 4 g/L and 8 g/L through frequent manual adjustment of feed flow rate until the 168-hour mark passed, when the experiment was terminated. Glucose and urea feed concentrations were fixed at 750 g/L and 46.5 g/L, respectively, throughout the experiment. For the second experiment, which also started with a 24-hour batch phase, the feed rate was only changed every 12 hours, with urea feed concentration being adjusted to a value between 0 g/L and 60 g/L every 12 hours until the experiment was terminated after 144 hours. The experimental data can be seen in Figure 14.4, where lutein content has been multiplied by the cell density to show the overall change in concentration within the reactor.

14.3.3 Constructing a Hybrid Model for Microalgal Lutein Production

Ultimately, the case study aims to identify an optimal fed-batch feeding strategy that maximizes the lutein produced by the end of the process. In order to facilitate fed-batch feed optimization, a model of the fed-batch process will be constructed and subsequently integrated within an optimization framework. The model should be capable of generating accurate predictions despite limited experimental data, enabling an efficient optimization of the fed-batch process. The hybrid model built for this specific case study is constructed in accordance with the methodology discussed throughout Section 14.2. Primarily, kinetic modeling is conducted, which is additionally used as a benchmark for the hybrid model, before introducing an ANN to enhance the model accuracy.

14.3.3.1 Preliminary Kinetic Modeling of Microalgal Lutein Production

A fundamental kinetic model of the case study system takes the form shown in Eqs. 14.13a–14.13f:

(14.13a)
(14.13b)
(14.13c)
(14.13d)
(14.13e)
(14.13f)

where CX represents cell density in g/L, CG represents glucose concentration in g/L, CN represents urea concentration in g/L, LC represents lutein content in mg/(g biomass), and CL represents the overall lutein concentration within the reactor. The mechanistic model relies on the assumption of Monod kinetics for substrate uptake and growth, as well as first-order cell death. The use of Monod kinetics for the backbone of the model is justified by its successful incorporation within several models of lutein-producing microalgal systems seen in literature [125–127]. Urea was decoupled from cell growth in Eq. 14.13c because the experimental data in Figure 14.4 illustrates the ability of cells to continue growing in the presence of little to no urea; the undisclosed relationship between urea and biomass growth rate will be quantified by the machine learning component when constructing the hybrid model. It should be noted that lutein content is an intracellular concentration. Hence, dilution is accounted for in Eq. 14.13d. The parameters in Eqs. 14.13a–14.13f are estimated using the parameter estimation framework described in Framework 14.3, subject to Eqs. 14.13a–14.13f instead of Eqs. 14.5b–14.5d.

The kinetic model fitting can be seen in Figure 14.4 with the parameter values provided in column two of Table 14.3. Despite fitting cell density well, with an R2 value of 0.932 across the two fed-batch experiments, the kinetic model particularly struggled to capture the substrate concentration profiles, which is evidenced in the R2 values of −1.073 and 0.123 for glucose and urea, respectively, across the two fed-batch experiments. The kinetic model fitting of both fed-batch experiments 1 and 2, shown in Figure 14.4, generally shows the kinetic model is underpredicting the substrate concentrations, particularly beyond the first 24 hours, which means that the kinetic model is overpredicting their respective consumption rates. By the 24-hour mark, the cell density has already increased by over 600%, meaning the overprediction of consumption rates could be due to mass transfer limitations or intracellular competition as a result of increased cell density, which the mechanistic model does not explain. Since the mechanistic understanding of the process is evidently incomplete, a data-driven component can be introduced to capture the remaining relationships within the system while not requiring the additional assumptions of a more intricate kinetic model, therefore avoiding the introduction of further inductive bias. The kinetic model constructed in this section provides a foundation for the hybrid model and will henceforth be used as a benchmark for further comparison.

14.3.3.2 Artificial Neural Network Implementation for Time-Varying Parameters

Due to the inadequate fitting of the kinetic model, as discussed in the previous section, a data-driven component is introduced to improve the model accuracy. For this case study, a Feed Forward Neural Network (FFNN) is chosen as the data-driven model due to its ability to capture any nonlinear relationships that we may find in the fed-batch fermentation process. The first step is to identify the time-varying parameters, which in this case were found to be μmax, , and (whose time-varying parameters are and respectively) as these parameters presented the highest uncertainties to which the fit of the model also demonstrated sufficient sensitivity to their values. The parameter estimation framework in Framework 14.5, subject to Eqs. 14.13a–14.13f, is then used to identify time-varying parameter profiles.

Following the identifications of time-varying parameter profiles, whose mean (μ) and standard deviation (σ) are shown in Table 14.3, the FFNN is trained to model the relationship between the time-varying parameters as outputs and the state variables and control actions as inputs. In this case, the state variables and control actions used as inputs to the FFNN are CX, CG, CN, FG (the feed rate of glucose in g/h) and FN(the feed rate of urea in g/h). Control actions are included in the FFNN input because the state variable values alone (at the time the parameters are updated) do not provide the full information of the system before the next parameter update occurs. The FFNN is trained using the L1 Loss function (Mean Average Error, or MAE), shown in Eq. 14.6, with L1 regularization penalizing the absolute values of the ANN weights and biases, as illustrated in Eq. 14.9. The L1 regularization term converges redundant parameters to a value of zero to reduce overparameterization and overfitting of the FFNN by encouraging the training to focus only on the most influential weights and biases.

The FFNN, consisting of 2 hidden layers with 8 nodes in each layer, was trained using augmented data; each augmented dataset is a copy of the training dataset with the inputs being subject to Gaussian noise. Augmenting data improves the performance of neural networks by expanding the training dataset and making the model more robust to noise, thus reducing overfitting [128, 129]. In this study, 100 augmented datasets were generated using a Gaussian noise distribution and a standard deviation of 0.01 (1% of the standard deviation of the standardized data). It is important to include enough noise to improve the FFNN robustness, while not introducing so much that it inhibits the FFNN fitting capabilities. The combination of parameter regularization and data augmentation helps combat potential overfitting using the very limited dataset of just two fed-batch experiments. Training was conducted over 40,000 epochs, as in a previous hybrid modeling study [130], to ensure convergence over the large augmented dataset. The precision plots for the augmented dataset training are shown in Figure 14.3, which illustrates the strong fitting capabilities of the FFNN, which converged to an MAE (or L1 loss) of 0.014 and R2 values of 0.999, 0.998, and 0.999 for the standardized time-varying parameters , , and , respectively.

To illustrate the improvement made by introducing a data-driven component, we must compare the fitting of the benchmark kinetic model to the hybrid model. Figure 14.4 shows the fitting of both the initial kinetic model and the overall hybrid model, which improved the mean R2 value from 0.219 to 0.974 across the two fed-batch experiments. The first fed-batch experiment (shown in Figure 14.4a) saw a large improvement in the mean R2 value, going from 0.263 to 0.962. The second fed-batch experiment (shown in Figure 14.4b) saw a slightly larger improvement in the mean R2 value, going from 0.174 to 0.986. In terms of the simulated state variables, the smallest improvement in R2 value was from 0.932 to 0.996 for cell density, meaning the original kinetic model provided a good estimation of the yield of cells from the glucose fed to the reactor. Since the overall lutein concentration is found to be strongly linked to cell density, this saw a similar change in R2 value from 0.892 to 0.965, which further supports the decision to not implement a time-varying parameter for lutein content in Eq. 14.13d. However, urea and glucose saw much larger improvements in fitting with their R2 values increasing from 0.123 to 0.972 and −1.073 to 0.963, respectively, which accounts for the vast majority of the overall fitting improvement. The hybrid model is able to improve the fitting of the substrate concentration profiles because the FFNN can account for changes in parameter values that may be caused by various phenomena, such as metabolic activity or mass transfer limitations, without the need for a detailed physical model. On the other hand, the benchmark kinetic model is limited to the assumed structure and therefore lacks generalizability in comparison to the hybrid model.

Since the implementation of an FFNN introduces additional parameters, the corrected Akaike Information Criterion (AICc) can also be accounted for to compare models of differing sizes, as demonstrated in a previous hybrid modeling study [131]. For fed-batch experiment 1, the hybrid model improved the AICc from a value of 521.0 for the kinetic model to 419.3 for the hybrid model, with fed-batch experiment 2 seeing a similar improvement in the AICc from 460.1 to 381.3, therefore demonstrating that the introduction of an FFNN is justified and has not inappropriately increased the model complexity.

The drastic improvement in the fitting of the dynamic model highlights the potential of incorporating machine learning to capture dynamics that preliminary mechanistic modeling may overlook. Since the model is sufficiently accurate, it is ready to be integrated within an optimization framework to design experiments that maximize the production of lutein, the results of which are discussed in the next section.

14.3.4 Dynamic Optimization of Microalgal Lutein Production

The dynamic optimization framework aims to maximize the final lutein mass in the reactor at the end of the fed-batch process spanning 5 days (120 hours) with feeding updated every 12 hours to allow for automated operation. The overall optimization framework is illustrated in Framework 14.14:

where the parameters , , and in Eqs. 14.13a–14.13f are replaced by their corresponding ANN outputs, the overall lutein production mL is taken as the product of lutein concentration and working volume, as in Eq. 14.14e, and the control vector at time t is defined by u(t) = [F(t) (t), F(t) (t)].

For the purpose of this case study, a computational experiment has been conducted to examine the optimization results of the current hybrid model using a more comprehensive hybrid model validated over a wide range of operating conditions as the “ground-truth.” Figure 14.5 shows the results of optimization Framework 14.14, which predicted a final lutein production of 290.3 mg, with an actual final concentration of 366.0 mg. For comparison, the second fed-batch experiment used for hybrid model construction was also designed with 12-hour feeding stages and achieved a total lutein production of 466.8 mg. Although this is a reduction in overall lutein production due to the shorter batch time, the optimized experiment takes place over a shorter time horizon (120 hours instead of 144 hours) and achieved the highest lutein yield of 0.702 mg/(g glucose) in comparison to the yields of 0.611 mg/(g glucose)− and 0.675 mg/(g glucose) achieved in fed-batch experiments 1 and 2, respectively. In terms of the predicted feed rate, the steadily increasing feed rate shown in Figure 14.5 does make sense from a physical point of view because the increase in cell density will have a higher demand for substrate to maintain the larger cell density. Both glucose and urea feed concentrations maintained their maximum permitted values of 750 g/L and 60 g/L, respectively, thus ensuring sufficient substrates are provided for growth.

The model prediction mismatch in the latter stages of the simulation in Figure 14.5 highlights where further information is required to better train the model. Dynamic models can be particularly susceptible to error propagation (small errors early in the simulation that snowball into a larger offset further along the simulated time horizon). For example, the largest errors in the glucose and urea concentration profiles shown in Figure 14.5 exist beyond a time of 100 hours, emphasizing the need for improved training in the latter stages of the process. One cause of this mismatch could be the prediction of cell density, the fit of which has an R2 value of 0.799, where the hybrid model initially over-predicts cell growth, leading to the over-predictions of substrate consumption rates. Subsequently, the over-prediction of substrate consumption rates means that the substrate concentrations are generally under-predicted from a time of 25–30 hours onward, resulting in an underprediction of cell growth. The suboptimal prediction of cell density is likely to be due to the training dataset; despite augmenting the data with 100 new datasets, Figure 14.3 shows that the time-varying parameter has a noticeable gap in the augmented training dataset where no training data exists for time-varying parameters between standardized values of 0.5 and 1.5, despite the use of a penalty term that penalizes the deviation of time-varying parameters in the objective function shown in Eq. 14.5a. Moreover, the increasing cell density throughout the process increases the sensitivity of the system to propagated errors, for example the glucose consumption rate in fed-batch experiment 1 increased from 1.91 g/L/h to 6.97 g/L/h from when the feeding commenced at the 24-hour mark to the final time of 168 hours, meaning simulation errors have a larger effect on simulated trajectories later on in the time horizon. A similar trend is shown in the feeding profile in Figure 14.5, which reflects the increased glucose consumption rates in the optimization result over time, thus increasing the sensitivity of the model to errors in the prediction of substrate uptake. The worst performing component for prediction was urea, with an R2 value of −0.115. However, this is due to two main limitations of the dataset; (1) there exist gaps in the training for as aforementioned, which directly affects urea (as the consumption rate is shown to be directly proportional to cell density in Eq. 14.13c), and (2) both fed-batch experiments used for training saw the urea sit at low concentrations for prolonged periods, meaning the FFNN anticipates a high consumption rate of urea (and therefore ) regardless of the FFNN inputs, which will not always hold true. The low urea concentrations in the training dataset will also inhibit the ability of the FFNN to recognize the effects of urea on growth – the only information the data provides is that growth can still occur when subject to low urea concentrations. Similarly, the glucose concentration in fed-batch experiment 1 remained in a narrow region between 4 and 8 g/L beyond a time of 36 hours, which again limits the ability of the FFNN to adequately capture the effects that glucose has on the time-varying parameters. The poor predictive capabilities for urea and glucose emphasizes the need for data covering a broad range of operating conditions.

Although the predictive performance may seem suboptimal during certain short phases of the process, it must be emphasized that only two fed-batch experiments were available for training, making the construction of a high-fidelity model extremely challenging. So, in this context, the hybrid model predictions are satisfactory. In cases where a limited number of experiments can be designed, careful DoEs should be conducted to maximize the information obtained from each experiment. In order to improve the hybrid model predictions in the future, constraints could be added to reduce the excess remaining substrates at the end of the experiment to improve the process yield. In addition, feed strategies that differ more from existing experiments could be tried, through the use of a penalty function in the optimization framework objective that encourages the exploration of a wider range of operating conditions for when the model is updated, thus highlighting the importance of Model Based DoEs (MBDoE) in model training and the subsequent process optimization. In its current state, the most effective way to utilize this hybrid model would be with online updating of the data-driven component from real-time data, as retraining the FFNN can be done quickly and accurately.

14.4 Summary

The chapter began by highlighting some key literature that illustrates a variety of ML applications to bioprocess development and optimization. An observation was made that existing models generally fall within the spectrum between mechanistic (“white box”) and purely data-driven (“black box”) modeling, with their respective strengths and weaknesses explained in depth. In order to simultaneously address the limitations of both mechanistic and data-driven modeling and utilize their respective strengths, the authors present the concept of hybrid modeling (or “grey box”) for the integration of ML within a mechanistic model. Several applications of hybrid models in bioprocessing from literature are explored, demonstrating extensive capabilities for the enhancement of bioprocesses.

The chapter then outlines a comprehensive methodology for constructing hybrid models, commencing with a mechanistic model based on mass balances and simple kinetic laws. For the cases where a mechanistic model performs in a dissatisfactory manner, sensitivity and uncertainty analysis are used to identify the most uncertain parameters, which are then reformulated as time-varying functions. Machine learning models can then be trained to estimate the time-varying parameters using experimental state variables and control actions as inputs. Detailed procedures are provided for training ANNs, including regularization, data augmentation, and partitioning into training, validation, and test sets. Bootstrapping is also introduced as a strategy for quantifying uncertainty in hybrid model predictions and improving hybrid model robustness.

The methodology described in this chapter is then applied to a detailed case study on lutein production by Chlorella. sorokiniana microalgae under heterotrophic fed-batch conditions. Initial mechanistic modeling based on Monod kinetics could not accurately predict glucose and urea concentrations, despite performing well for cell density, and so an FFNN was introduced to model three key time-varying parameters: maximum specific growth rate, maximum specific glucose uptake rate, and maximum specific urea uptake rate. The hybrid model significantly outperformed the purely mechanistic model, improving mean R2 values across key state variables from 0.219 to 0.974.

Finally, the hybrid model was incorporated within a dynamic optimization framework to maximize lutein production over a 120-hour fed-batch operation. The optimization degrees of freedom were provided as the dynamic feed flow rate and substrate feed concentrations, demonstrating how model-based optimization can assist in efficiently identifying optimal operating conditions. Overall, the modeling and optimization of the lutein-producing microalgal fed-batch process demonstrate the potential of hybrid modeling for dynamic bioprocesses, particularly under conditions of limited data availability. Although not explicitly explored in this chapter, it is important to note that online model updating can be employed to incorporate new data and enhance predictive accuracy. Equally critical is the availability of informative and diverse datasets to ensure robust hybrid model training.
